title: Amid zoning changes, long-term residents plan their exit from Camberwell
content: Just before new residential zoning rules came into force, a real estate pamphlet arrived in Richard Arbon's letterbox. "It talked about the activity centres and was encouraging us to talk to them if we wanted to sell our property," he said. Mr Arbon lives in the leafy and historic suburb of Camberwell in Melbourne's inner east, where huge zoning changes designed to create more housing near established infrastructure are expected to significantly change his neighbourhood. Across Melbourne, the Victorian government has announced it will create 60 of these "activity centres" — where it hopes much greater density, higher building limits and faster approval processes will speed up development and significantly increase housing supply. Camberwell is one of 10 pilot centres where the zoning changes have just been gazetted and where residents will first see change. Developments between six and 12-storeys are now possible around the railway station and shopping precinct under the new zoning, which is largely consistent with development that was already occurring. But it is in the surrounding "walkable catchment" that the biggest changes are likely. Streets within about a 10-minute walk of Camberwell's centre — which currently feature freestanding homes and some double storey apartment blocks — will now see developments of up to six storeys allowed. Areas where multi-storey housing will be allowed in Camberwell under the state government's activity centres policy. (Supplied) While the new zoning is just three weeks old, the property market is already responding. For Mr Arbon, the pamphlet in his letterbox was "the first foray we've seen from a real estate agent jumping onto the proposed, and now actual, changes," he explained. He suspected the new zoning rules could further drive up property prices as developers compete for land on which to build apartment blocks. "You might see groups of neighbours amalgamating to put blocks together to maximise their return," he predicted. Four neighbouring properties have been listed for sale and development in Glen Iris. (ABC News: Rudy De Santis) Indeed, the ABC saw a property sale sign in nearby Glen Iris where four houses were being sold on a single lot — the sign alerting potential buyers to its changed zoning status as part of an activity centre. Real estate agents and buyers' advocates told the ABC they had also noticed the zoning changes having an early impact on the property market. Jeff Anderson has been a real estate agent for 40 years. He has run over 4,000 auctions and now has his own business helping people buy homes and advising large businesses on Melbourne's property market. He said there was a range of ways the zoning changes could impact on the price of a property. "If you're getting a six-, eight-storey block built next to you, and you are going to have your view completely lost, you are just going to look at a brick wall … then that is going to devalue the property of the existing owner," he said. But for freestanding houses which do not end up with a larger development near them, Mr Anderson said, their value will only continue to increase over time. "The scarcer land gets, the more that appreciates because people are always going to want a backyard and somewhere for the children to play with security and privacy, so those properties I see as continuing to outpace the market generally, but any other property without land is going to be under pressure," he said. Residents worry about large apartment buildings overlooking single storey homes. (ABC News: Rudy De Santis) The real estate agent said the area could see much flatter prices for apartments if the supply significantly increased — which he said was already worrying existing apartment owners. "People with existing quality apartments are selling pretty consistently due to the uncertainty," he noted. He said he was already seeing some long-term Camberwell residents selling, or planning to sell, because of the zoning changes. "There's a lot of talk, a lot of people moving bayside to the Peninsula, both sides, and people are wanting a sea or a tree-change," he said. "They want to get out of the congestion of what is to be in a few years." Many homes in Camberwell have been subject to heritage protections. (ABC News: Rudy De Santis) Buyers advocate Cate Bakos agreed new zoning rules in Camberwell were being seen as a money-making opportunity by some, and a reason not to purchase by others. She warned potential buyers needed to understand "exactly where the areas poised for change are and knowing exactly what your amenity is and what your neighbouring changes will be," she said. Cate Bakos says the market was showing a mixed reaction to the Victorian government's activity centres. (Supplied: Cate Bakos) But, while some might be keen to cash in, Linda Allison, the Victorian chief executive of the Urban Development Institute of Australia, warned change was likely to be slow, even with the new zoning rules. "The planning process to go from a concept to actually coming out of the ground is a very lengthy process — it can take five to seven years," she explained. While Ms Allison said the new higher density limits in the activity centres could help stack up the financial viability of projects, she listed high interest rates, construction costs, and Victoria's property taxes as still holding back apartment builds. The Urban Development Institute said construction of new homes would still take time, despite with the new zoning rules. (ABC News: Rudy De Santis) The development boss acknowledged that the changes were still unpopular with some residents but said the need for more housing was very real. "The bigger picture here is making sure future generations have access to a home of their choosing in the area they want to live in, and we know we have strong population growth, and we know we have record lows in rental availabilities," she said. "So, if we want our kids and grandkids to be able to enjoy the same kind of benefits that we as Melburnians have had for generations, then we need to be more open to all different types of housing." That sentiment was shared by Premier Jacinta Allan when she announced the new height limits for activity centres in February, saying the state needed to build its way out of its housing crisis. "We want more homes for young people and workers close to jobs, transport and services," she said. How Melbourne and its inner east creates more housing and what that means for existing residents are still deeply divisive issues. In the 10 pilot activity centres, the Victorian government said it hoped to add 60,000 new homes. It pointed out that there had been low housing growth rates in many of these established centres in Melbourne's east compared with the housing and population growth seen in many of the city's outer suburbs. But the scale of that intended change has shocked and angered many residents in these neighbourhoods. Mr Arbon was so angry at the real estate agent's brochure in his letterbox that he ripped it up. What upset him about the planning changes was the size of developments now allowed in residential streets away from the shopping precinct and the possible degradation of the suburb's heritage values. "While people understand the need for some more housing densification and affordable housing, they are horrified, they feel powerless," he said of the atmosphere in his community. Christina Branagan doesn't believe the government's plan to create affordable housing will work in Camberwell. (ABC News: Rudy De Santis) Christina Branagan has lived in Camberwell for more than 20 years and has been so deeply concerned by the zoning changes, she's been out speaking to her neighbours about it. "One of the things I really love about living here is that we are looking after heritage places for the future that, I truly think, are world class heritage suburbs," she explained. And while she said she wanted to see more affordable housing so her children's generation can buy their own homes, she was sceptical that these changes would create affordable housing in Camberwell where land prices were very high. "What I am actually seeing around my area is a lot of more affordable places like 1930s houses and art deco flats and 1950s units with shared gardens they are actually being demolished … and everything that goes up is luxury apartments, luxury townhouses," she said. The residents have the support of the City of Boroondara, which has also shared its concerns about heritage protections and the scale of change planned for the "walkable catchment zones". The Deputy Mayor Victor Franco has described the state government's suburban rezoning as the most significant changes to Victoria's planning system in 30 years. Christina Branagan fears affordable apartments will be demolished. (ABC News: Rudy De Santis) Cr Franco said while heritage overlays remained intact, how much weight these overlays were to be given under the new zoning was not clear. He said that was because the previous residential zoning scheme told councils they needed to respect the character and heritage values of an area while the new zoning's purpose was to encourage more development. "Ultimately it will end up being decided by VCAT (the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal) and the Supreme Court," he predicted. But until a test case ends up in the courts, he said, there was a lack of clarity for residents and developers. "I don't think these changes will lead to the widespread demolition of significant heritage-listed homes, but rather over time new and inappropriate developments will degrade the look and feel of areas currently covered by heritage overlay protections." He's not the only planner with concerns. The Victorian government appointed a standing advisory committee made up of planning experts who were asked by the Victorian planning minister to investigate several issues around the new activity centres. The panel was appointed on August 22 last year and delivered its report in November, but its was only released to the public on April 14, just after the zoning changes had been made in the pilot activity centres. One of the report's recommendations was that walkable catchment zoning should not be applied to areas that have a heritage overlay or a neighbourhood character overlay. But the Victorian government insisted the new activity centres would not change heritage overlays or policies, with a spokesperson saying "we want more homes for young people and workers close to jobs, transport, and services — so they can live where they want, near the things they need and the people they love". A parliamentary inquiry into the zoning changes has been holding hearings in April, with a report due later this month.

title: Property prices lift and growth in house values continues to outpace units
content: House prices are on track to continue rising across the country as interest rates fall and supply continues to remain tight. As voters head to the ballot box prepared to cast votes on the issue of housing affordability, data from Cotality (formerly CoreLogic) shows that house prices trended higher in April. Its national Home Value Index recorded a third straight month of growth in April, with dwelling values up 0.3 per cent to reach a new record high. This rise in values added about $2,720 to the median value of an Australian dwelling over the month. Nationally, the median value is now standing at $825,349, according to Cotality. Sydney maintains the highest median value at $1,194,709, while Darwin has the lowest at $526,410. The monthly lift in home values was recorded across every capital city, with gains highest in Darwin (up 1.1 per cent in the month of April). However, the annual pace of gains slowed to 3.2 per cent nationally in April, the slowest annual rise since the 12 months ending August 2023. Over the year, all states except Melbourne and Canberra recorded gains. Melbourne's values fell 2.2 per cent over the year, while Canberra saw a slight 0.6 per cent drop. Conversely, Perth saw the highest annual gain, lifting 10 per cent. Cotality's head of research, Eliza Owen, says house prices have stayed strong are expected to trend higher in the coming months. "However, it's going to be hampered by economic uncertainty and what that could do to the labour market. It's an evolving picture, but ultimately, I think we're looking at a more modest growth rate for 2025." Eliza Owen expects house prices will keep rising but possibly at a slower pace. (ABC News: John Gunn) Cotality's data was in line with the PropTrack Home Price Index, which found national home prices hit a new peak in April, but growth has slowed compared to the start of 2025. The report found that national home prices lifted 0.2 per cent over the month, and 3.7 per cent year-on-year in April 2025. A slight slowdown in buying and selling over the Easter break was evident in weekly auction numbers, which dropped to 644 auctions scheduled for the week of April 20 across the combined capitals. Builders take out insurance designed to cover clients' costs in the event they go bust. But some people are waiting for years for a payout and facing potential bankruptcy. Cotality says outside of the initial COVID impact in 2020, this is the lowest Easter auction week since 2019, when the housing market was nearing a cyclical trough, and a federal election was dominated by conversations of housing policy reform. It found the flow of new listings also dropped off substantially, with new listings for sale across the combined capitals falling to 19,650 in the four weeks to April 27. Much like with the auction numbers, this is the lowest number of new listings for this time of year since 2019 (outside of COVID impacts in 2020). Ms Owen said during the period measured "there was so much going on between tariff announcements, the federal election, the extended public holiday period". There was a slight slowdown in buying and selling over the Easter break. (ABC News: Nassim Khadem) Growth in house values is continuing to outpace the unit sector. A moderate fall in home values may be just what Australia's economy needs in the long-term. Cotality noted the past three months have seen the value of houses rise by 1.1 per cent across the combined capitals, more than double the 0.5 per cent rise recorded across the unit sector. It found this trend was mostly being driven by Sydney, where house values were up 1.4 per cent over the rolling quarter compared with a 0.3 per cent fall in unit values over the same period. Hobart had the largest disparity between house and unit growth in the period, with houses rising 1.4 per cent against a 1.1 per cent fall in units. Regional housing values have continued to outpace the capitals, with values up 0.6 per cent and 0.2 per cent respectively over the month of April. Rental growth also firmed, with the national rental index rising by 0.6 per cent over the quarter. But Cotality said that adjusting for seasonality, the pace of growth is milder, with rents rising 0.4 per cent nationally in April. Over the year, the pace of rental growth has more than halved, from 8.3 per cent over the 12 months to April 2024, to 3.6 per cent over the most recent 12-month period. Eliza Owen says the slowdown in rents is "a good sign for renters, and it's well down from the eight to 10 per cent increases we'd seen in 202, 2022 and 2023".

title: Coalition to release 'materially better, in double digits' budget costings
content: The Coalition is making a last-minute claim for the mantle of superior economic management with a promise its deficits would be at least $10 billion smaller than under Labor over the next four years. Despite an election campaign in which both sides have downplayed or left silent questions over how they would address longer-term budget repair, the Coalition will claim its plan would trim $40 billion of gross debt in 2028/29 from the government's $1.22 trillion prediction. It's understood the budget bottom line will be "materially better", according to a Coalition source, boosted by a narrowing of deficits over the forwards in the "low double digits". Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues That headline promise compares to Labor's forecast deficits over four years of about $150 billion. Shadow Treasurer Angus Taylor will release details of the costings on Thursday. "Labor has delivered the longest per-capita recession on record and the biggest collapse in living standards in the developed world," he will say. "That's not bad luck, that's bad management. "After raking in almost $400 billion in extra revenue, Labor chose to splurge instead of save, leaving Australians more exposed to the next economic shock. "We will rebuild the nation's fiscal buffers, reduce debt, and begin budget repair because that's what economic responsibility looks like." Angus Taylor says Coalition will release costings in the 'next day or so'. (ABC News Breakfast) In the lead-up to and during the campaign, Mr Dutton promised at least $48 billion in extra spending for defence, fuel excise relief, a temporary low and middle income tax offset, and Medicare bulk billing. This election season politicians have tried to sell you the world. The team at Gruen isn't about to buy it. They've taken a big swing at the election, showing you how the democracy sausage is made, all the sizzle and none of the meat. Offsetting those promised costs, the Coalition has said it would target more than $100 billion in Labor spending and so-called "off-budget" debt-funded investments for electricity transmission and housing, in addition to public service cuts and dumping Labor's student debt relief plans. The opposition's full costings will come just days after one of the world's top ratings agencies warned both sides of politics that without changes to spending or tax plans, Australia's coveted AAA credit rating could be threatened by a sudden collapse in commodity prices or other setbacks. Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the federal budget will be about $1 billion better off over four years compared to the March budget. Mr Taylor said on Wednesday that he is "solving for two budgets". One is for households, he said, and their need for support after being "absolutely wrecked" by Treasurer Jim Chalmers. The second is the government budget, which he said "has been wrecked again by a treasurer who doesn't understand the basics of how an economy works and how to manage a government budget". Labor — which released its costings in the 2022 election on the Thursday before election day — has been challenging the Coalition this week to "come clean" over how it plans to fund Mr Dutton's signature nuclear power plan and where it will find the savings. The Coalition's most expensive commitments include a $21 billion boost to military spending over the next four years, a $1,200 tax offset at a cost of $10 billion, and a 25-cent-a-litre fuel excise cut wiping $6 billion from the budget. The Coalition is also expected to claim that the budget will be in better shape under its watch because productivity growth will improve. Labor on Monday announced costings showing it had found more than $6 billion in savings via reduced reliance on consulting firms, helping offset around $10 billion in election campaign announcements. The $4 billion difference was already accounted for in the budget. Jim Chalmers warned of "dodgy assumptions" in the Coalition's costings. (ABC News: Matt Roberts) "When the Coalition finally gets around to releasing its costings, keep an eye out for some dodgy assumptions around productivity, pumping up their numbers," Mr Chalmers said on Wednesday. "Keep an eye out remembering that David Littleproud said they'll start building nuclear reactors the day after they are elected. "The reason they haven't released their costings yet is because they don't want to come clean on the savage cuts that they will need to make to pay for their nuclear reactors." title: Election could change the future of Australia's hydrogen capital
content: With a view across the southern Great Barrier Reef and shrouded by state forests, it is easy to forget Gladstone is one of the most emissions-intensive places in Australia. But the city is a major Australian producer of cement, alumina, aluminium, and ammonia, while the Gladstone Port — one of the biggest bulk commodity ports in the world — facilitates tens of billions of dollars' worth of trade annually through its exports of products like coal and gas. State and federal governments have earmarked the city's future as a possible green hydrogen powerhouse. Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues This is something some experts and residents believe would shore up its future if a government could pull it off. Last year Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced temporary tax credits that would see producers of green hydrogen receive $2 per kilogram of renewable hydrogen produced for a period of up to 10 years. The Gladstone port is a major exporter of coal. (ABC News: Scout Wallen) The initiative would cost the government an estimated $8 billion across 10 years initially, and then an average of $1.2 billion per year from 2034-35 and 2040-41. The LNP has vowed to scrap the policy if it is elected. Green hydrogen — what is it? Green hydrogen can be produced when it is extracted from water through electrolysis, which is powered by a renewable energy source. Gladstone resident Jade Wright is a student nurse who worked as a deckhand on boats and has done maintenance work at industrial facilities. Gladstone local Jade Wright would like to see the hydrogen industry flourish in the city. (ABC News: Jasmine Hines) Having been a teenager during Gladstone's last boom and bust cycle from LNG in the 2010s, she is worried about the city decarbonising and what it could look like. Ms Wright said government investment should be made to kickstart the green hydrogen industry. "If hydrogen can't get off the ground, the whole of Gladstone continues to struggle," she said. Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen But on the other side of politics, the LNP takes a different view. Its flagship election energy policy is to build small nuclear power plants around Australia. One of these would be just over 100 kilometres to the west of Gladstone, near Biloela. Local scaffolding business owner David Nunn co-founded the CQ Nuclear Alliance three years ago and believes it is the way forward. Gladstone businessman David Nunn co-founded the CQ Nuclear Alliance. (ABC News: Jasmine Hines) He is wary of the government support provided to the private sector for renewable projects, including for green hydrogen. "I support any industry that stacks up financially." Mr Nunn said the nuclear industry had been proven overseas, while he believed green hydrogen was still in an experimental stage. But if Gladstone's green hydrogen dream crumbled, and emissions-intensive industries were wound back, Ms Wright believed Gladstone would suffer. "Without the jobs, without the heavy industry, as a town, we're kind of flailing," she said. Fortescue has the largest hydrogen electrolyser manufacturing plant in the country in Gladstone. (Supplied: Queensland government) CQUniversity Professor Jonathan Love said the developing industry would need incentives to become competitive and give investors confidence. Professor Love said Gladstone had the potential to be a major exporter of hydrogen, but only if the industry was incentivised by the government. "If Australia is too late getting there then there'll already be a market that the likes of Japan and South Korea will be tapping into." A hydrogen electrolyser. (ABC Illawarra: Tim Fernandez) A paper published by the Nature Energy journal earlier this year tracked 190 green hydrogen projects globally, finding only seven per cent were completed on time. It found to keep global warming at 1.5 degrees above pre-industrial levels, production needed to grow 380-fold and double each year. He said current production methods using natural gas and coal were carbon-intensive, and green hydrogen was essential to meeting net zero emissions by 2050. Renewable hydrogen is already being used in the city's gas network, while billionaire Andrew Forrest's company Fortescue is manufacturing hydrogen electrolysers in Gladstone. The next stage of the company's project will see the electrolysers produce green hydrogen. An electrolyser built by Fortescue. (Facebook: Glenn Butcher MP) A Fortescue spokesperson said incentives were critical to developing a green iron industry, which required large amounts of green hydrogen as a fuel source. "This kind of government support will help attract large-scale investment, foster innovation, and secure thousands of new jobs in advanced manufacturing," it said. 1 / of 11 All fields are required unless marked optional. title: Anger over highway 'patch jobs' amid less federal cash for SA roads
content: Many drivers in regional South Australia have voiced frustration with the condition of the state's roads, telling the ABC they are worried about safety. In November 2023, the federal government announced it would be switching to a 50:50 deal when it came to funding certain national infrastructure upgrades, which included national highways, when it used to be 80:20. While January's announcement of a $9 billion revamp to Queensland's Bruce Highway reverted back to the 80:20 model, it looks likely SA will fall under the 50:50 model. Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues SA Minister for Infrastructure and Transport Tom Koutsantonis said the state continued to work with the federal government to deliver critical safety improvements at high-risk locations. "Discussions with the Commonwealth on cost-sharing arrangements, particularly for regional roads, are ongoing, and we recognise the significant contributions made towards major projects on a 50:50 funding split." Tom Koutsantonis says funding-split discussions are ongoing. (ABC News: Che Chorley) One consequence of the extra weight the SA government might be expected to carry in funding national highways could be less funding available for state and local road networks. Shadow Minister for Transport Ben Hood said a 50:50 funding model would hold SA back. "The premiers of Tasmania and NSW pushed back against the government on changing the split, but we heard nothing from the SA premier or Minister Koutsantonis." Ben Hood says the 50:50 funding split will jeopardise road projects. (ABC South East SA: Todd Lewis) The model also has local councils concerned. "South Australia receives the lowest amount of federal road funding of any state, both on a per capita basis and per kilometre of road," a spokesperson for Local Government Association SA said. The federal government made the change after a review of government spending. A spokesperson for federal Transport Minister Catherine King said the Commonwealth's approach to infrastructure funding was recommended by an independent review. "It means states need to undertake proper planning on projects, minimise cost blowouts, and it means we can invest in more projects in South Australia while maintaining the same amount of funding overall," they said. The Coalition said it was committed to the 80:20 model used previously if successful in the upcoming federal election. In South Australia's South East, the Southern Ports Highway runs along the coast and connects busy beach towns like Robe, Beachport, and Southend. The road is derided by locals as narrow, undulating, and rapidly deteriorating, and was named number six on the RAA's recent Risky Roads list for South Australia. Margie Bowman knows the highway as well as anyone, having recently retired from driving Beachport's school bus along the road to the nearby Kangaroo Inn Area School. Margie Bowman recently retired from driving a school bus along the Southern Ports Highway. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook) "It's my worst nightmare — I don't have to worry about it anymore, but I worry about anyone else having to drive the bus," she said. Plans are in place to completely rebuild the highway between Beachport and Southend, but Ms Bowman said recent roadworks had done little to ease locals' concerns. Sections of the Southern Ports Highway are slated for a $168 million upgrade. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook) "Patch jobs aren't even compacted down anymore … so when we get rain, it just washes away again," she said. "It's uneven and until you've got a decent base, it's never going to change." Shoulder sealing is part of the work designated for the Southern Ports Highway. (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook) Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen It's a similar story in the Riverland. The ongoing $87.5 million Sturt Highway Corridor Upgrade has included works along approximately 210km of the highway. Jodie Harriss lives in Waikerie and drives along the Sturt Highway daily to work in Berri, approximately 60km away. "There are several points along that road where there's been repairs, but … it's just a bandaid fix," she said. "Before you know it, you've got that hole and that ditch again. The Sturt Highway is a critical transport link between Sydney and Adelaide. (ABC Riverland: Elyse Armanini) "For a major highway connecting interstate, it's not up to scratch at all. "You get what you pay for, and the government says it will pump all this money into our roads — well, I don't see it on the highway … it's lethal." The Sturt Highway received funding under the 80:20 model. (ABC Riverland: Will Hunter) The Flinders Highway connects the SA towns of Ceduna and Port Lincoln, past 396km of sand dunes, arid landscapes, and countless dusty offshoots leading to deserted beaches and iconic surf beaches. In recent years, caravans and trucks have become more common. Grain trains ceased operating in the region in May 2019, when Viterra moved its business from the rail to the road, meaning a huge increase in the number of trucks in the area, especially during harvest months. Streaky Bay and Districts Road Safety Committee president Mischa Karp said tourism had increased in the area, and transport authorities needed to take a look at the width of the road. Hear the latest election news as it happens on the Election Central Playlist. Only on the ABC listen app. "The roads are incredibly narrow with very small or no shoulders, and you're often competing with high numbers of cars, caravans, and grain trucks, and a number of undulating surfaces." ABC measured the road at several sections of the Flinders Highway. The 8.85-metre width of the road on the Western Approach Road at Duck Ponds near Port Lincoln, including bike lanes, leaves plenty of room for everyone. Twenty-five lives were lost on the Flinders Highway from 2019 to 2023. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Tim McGlone) But it is a different story near Talia, between Port Kenny and Elliston, where the road measures just 6.04m — from each edge of the bitumen — and near the Cummins Monument Lookout north of Mount Drummond, where it is 6.09m wide. In Australia, caravans have a maximum legal width of 2.5 metres. It means the common occurrence of two caravans passing each other on the Flinders Highway leaves only around a metre of wriggle room. 1 / of 11 All fields are required unless marked optional. title: Record dry hurting small businesses in country SA
content: Small businesses in South Australia say they are struggling after some of the driest years on record in many regions. Most years, the average annual rainfall in the lush wine region of Clare, around 145 kilometres north of Adelaide, is 527 millimetres. But according to the Bureau of Meteorology, in 2024 the Clare Valley recorded just 287mm – 53 per cent of its average. Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues Lowest annual average rainfalls were also recorded for Snowtown, almost the entire Yorke Peninsula and several Eyre Peninsula towns including Cummins and Ceduna, and on Kangaroo Island at Cape Willoughby. Clare hair salon owner Erin Pearse said locals' spending had been "slowing", as clients — many of whom worked in agriculture — stretched out their regular appointments and opted for cheaper services. Erin Pearse says spending around Clare has been "slowing down" in recent months. (ABC North and West SA: Viki Ntafillis) "Instead of going for their six weekly appointments, they're sort of stretching out to eight to 10 weeks," she said. Ms Pearse said she took on more cost-effective products to combat spending cuts and stay affordable, and recycled most of the rubbish from her business locally. Clare retailer Buff Byrne said March was "probably the worst month we've had in years" for her retail and embroidery business. Clare small business owner Buff Byrne says many locals are "treading carefully" with money. (ABC North and West SA: Viki Ntafillis) "It was 50 per cent down," she said. "Everyone's just treading carefully with how much they're spending. "I've definitely had primary producers in talking about [the dry conditions] and it's not only them — it's everyone." Ricardo Rivas said he normally saw an influx of up to 40 new clients at his Clare gym during harvest, but there had only been about 12 this year. "There hasn't been that much to harvest … so that tends to affect that cash flow and that trickles down to the locals," he said. Ricardo Rivas says new gym memberships are low for this time of year. (ABC North and West SA: Viki Ntafillis) "The first thing to go is the gym. They need to eat." In early 2024, Mr Rivas began helping out the rural health initiative Fat Farmers by hosting weekly workouts. "Mainly it's a physical activity, but … the extra 40 minutes of catch-up between all of them that they have afterwards, that keeps them coming all the time," he said. Clare was one of several regions in SA that recorded its lowest rainfall on record in 2024. (Supplied: Bureau of Meteorology) "It just feels good to be around more people that are doing the same and they're all struggling, and at least they help each other. Over on the Eyre Peninsula, Michelle Rayner in Kimba said her cafe's sales hit an unprecedented low over summer. Michelle Rayner says sales at her cafe in Kimba have been down 60 per cent. (ABC North and West SA: Viki Ntafillis) "I had to cut down the staff and I reduced my menu as well," she said. "We were down over 60 per cent. "We're into our 10th year this year and we've never seen anything like that." Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen With a federal election around the corner, Ms Rayner said she wanted politicians to offer solutions that "would actually help farmers get through the drought". "They''ll quite often offer up all these feel-good things, all this counselling … but it's not actually going to help," she said. Water carter Grant Fidge said he had been "pretty busy" trying to keep up with demand, as many locals from Clare and its surrounds relied on tank water rather than mains water. "On an average year, I sort of just work 8am-5pm and have a bit of a lunch break and keep up fairly easily," he said. "This year I'm … more 7:30am-6:30pm … and I can come do the odd Saturday just to keep up." Water carter Grant Fidge says most locals relying on tank water are running low this year. (ABC North and West SA: Viki Ntafillis) Mr Fidge said he was receiving calls from people in the Mid North who he had never delivered to before. "Everyone's hanging out for the rain but usually it doesn't start until around June here, it seems, the last few years." Rural Business Support (RBS) chief executive Brett Smith said the organisation was currently assisting 540 agricultural businesses across regional South Australia, and around 15-20 small businesses not directly tied to agriculture. "We only have half a [full-time equivalent employee] servicing the entirety of SA [for regional small businesses] and that … is at capacity," he said. Mr Smith said with new funding from the recently announced drought relief package, RBS hoped to take on more small business clients soon, as the situation was "quite serious". Rural Business Support CEO Brett Smith says the situation is "quite serious" for many small operations. (ABC Adelaide: Luke Pike) "It's an ecosystem, everyone relies on each other," he said. "Once you lose a family … if they leave town, there's less people at the school, less people at sport, and there are less people doing the volunteer things, which really make our small towns flourish." In a joint statement, Liberal MP for Barker Tony Pasin and candidate for Grey Tom Venning said a Coalition government would commit $1.8 million over six months to extend the Rural Financial Counselling Service for eligible farmers, fishers, foresters and small related businesses "experiencing, or at risk of, financial hardship". Hear the latest election news as it happens on the Election Central Playlist. Only on the ABC listen app. South Australian senator Karen Grogan said Labor had "backed in" regional resilience through the $519 million Future Drought Fund. "We are also providing help for struggling farmers, including through concessional loans, Farm Household Allowance, and access to the Rural Financial Counselling Service," she said in a statement. "Labor's National Drought Agreement with states and territories ensures a coordinated, long-term approach to resilience." 1 / of 11 All fields are required unless marked optional. title: PM shrugs off Trump's 'throwaway comment' on Australia's efforts to call
content: US President Donald Trump has acknowledged Australia's efforts to talk to him about trade and indicated he intended to speak to the Australian prime minister about the issue. As he prepared to board a flight in Washington, Mr Trump was asked: "The Australian prime minister is having an election this weekend. Will you speak to him about trade?" Mr Trump replied: "They are calling and I will be talking to him, yes." Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues Anthony Albanese later called it a "lighthearted throwaway comment from the president". "I assure you, I'm not staying up at night trying to ring anyone at the moment. I'm in an election campaign," he told ABC Radio Melbourne. "I'm sure, if we are successful, we'll have a discussion after Saturday." Donald Trump's first 100 days back in the White House have been extraordinarily eventful. Here's some of what you might have missed. The Australian government has been attempting to negotiate with the Trump administration over its controversial tariffs regime, which includes a minimum 10 per cent tariff on almost all imports, and 25 per cent tariffs on specific products including aluminium and steel. Australia's failure to secure an exemption from any of the tariffs, despite running a consistent trade deficit with the US and putting a significant diplomatic effort into negotiations, has been a dominant issue in the election campaign. Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen Mr Trump had told Prime Minister Anthony Albanese he would consider exempting Australia from the metal tariffs in February. But in March, White House spokeswoman Karoline Leavitt told the ABC: "He considered it, and considered against it. There will be no exemptions." Mr Albanese later called the decision "entirely unjustified" and "against the spirit of our two nations' enduring friendship". The next federal government faces a world with drastic US policy changes, trade disputes, and ongoing wars in Europe and the Middle East. The opposition has frequently criticised the prime minister for not making more effort to speak directly to Mr Trump about the tariffs. Many of America's trading partners have been targeted with much higher tariffs, but their implementation is on hold to allow for negotiations towards new trade deals. Earlier on Tuesday, local time, US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick told business network CNBC a deal had been struck with one trading partner, but he would not say which one. "I have a deal done," Mr Lutnick said. "But I need to wait for their prime minister and their parliament to give its approval, which I expect shortly." Meanwhile, the White House criticised online retailer Amazon over reports it was considering displaying the effects of tariffs on prices listed on its website. Ms Leavitt described the reported move as "a hostile and political act by Amazon". Amazon later ruled out the idea, prompting Mr Trump to praise its high-profile executive chairman, Jeff Bezos. "He solved the problem very quickly," Mr Trump said. "He did the right thing. Good guy." 1 / of 11 All fields are required unless marked optional. title: Despite new laws, salmon farming assessment still 'active' for Macquarie Harbour
content: The future of salmon farming in Tasmania's Macquarie Harbour remains under "active" assessment by the federal government, despite the passing of legislation designed to nullify the issue. Tasmania's salmon industry was relieved, and environmental groups were outraged, when parliament approved contentious amendments to national environmental laws late last month. The changes were primarily intended to end Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek's assessment of salmon farming's impact on an endangered species in the harbour. Had Ms Plibersek chosen to conduct a broad review, it could have led to the shutdown of the local industry — a politically precarious prospect for the government ahead of the election. But documents seen by the ABC show the deliberation process is ongoing, with the minister's consideration yet to be formally concluded. Tasmanian voters divided over salmon farming industry (Selina Bryan) Opponents of salmon farming addressed a packed Hobart Parliament House lawn to rally against the state's salmon industry, following a mass mortality event over summer. The details emerged in correspondence sent by the federal environment department to former senator Rex Patrick on April 16 — almost three weeks after the amendments became law. Mr Patrick, a South Australian transparency advocate and current Senate candidate for the Jacqui Lambie Network, had submitted a Freedom of Information (FOI) request for departmental advice and a briefing given to the minister in January and February this year. But his application was rejected, partly on the grounds the documents included deliberative information, advice and recommendations, which the department said were exempt. "The documents contain the weighing up of options by the minister to assist with the decision-making process, which is still current and subject to ongoing deliberative processes," its decision letter states. "The documents also include content and recommendations which remain under assessment and consideration by the Minister and are subject to further development and change." Anti-salmon farming groups held a rally in Hobart on Sunday. (ABC News: Jake Grant) The ABC approached the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) for further clarity. It confirmed the matter "remains subject to deliberative processes". The department's online portal also confirms the assessment of marine farming in Macquarie Harbour is still "active". Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen A map showing the location of salmon farm licences in Macquarie Harbour, on Tasmania's west coast. (ABC News: Magie Khameneh) Federal Labor pushes through legislation that could derail a legal battle over salmon farming's impact on an endangered ray and safeguard the industry's future in Tasmania. The government rushed through the amendments with the support of the opposition on March 26 during the final sitting week before the election was called. "We won't stand by and let workers in Strahan lose their livelihoods because of a broken law," a government spokesperson said at the time. "Under existing law, an industry could be shut down overnight when an environmental assessment commences. Anthony Albanese speaks to Tassal employees at a fish farm enclosure during visit to Tasmania in December 2024. (Tassal) But Rex Patrick told the ABC the FOI process had confirmed the matter was not yet over. "The FOI has revealed an inconsistency between the public's perception and the department's treatment of the matter," he said. The opposition's environment spokesperson, Senator Jonno Duniam, said the revelations were "an outrage". "The fact is, these documents reveal that the minister still can make a decision to shut down salmon farming in Macquarie Harbour, contrary to the promise she made to us, the opposition, to the parliament and to the people [in the electorate] of Braddon." A government spokesperson told the ABC the "government, as always, will follow the law". Federal Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek. (ABC News: Maren Preuss) Ms Plibersek's assessment was sparked in November 2023, when three environmental groups asked the minister to reconsider prior approvals given to the industry in 2012. Foreign companies now own Tasmania's big three salmon farming operations. Here's a look at how industrial fish farms are run overseas — and the problems operators have encountered when there's opposition to their practices. The groups argued salmon farming was putting the endangered Maugean skate, a ray-like fish species only found in Macquarie Harbour, at risk of extinction. The left-leaning think tank Australia Institute was one of the groups that requested the review. Its Tasmanian director, Eloise Carr, said the FOI documents showed the department was following due process and listening to the science. "Fish farming in Macquarie Harbour should be called in for a comprehensive assessment under national nature laws," she said. The recent amendments would not achieve the government's aim, she added. The Bob Brown Foundation, one of the other groups that requested a ministerial review, has launched a legal challenge against the new laws. The matter is expected to be heard in the federal court next month. Salmon Tasmania did not respond to a request for comment. Eloise Carr says the Australia Institute considers the law to be "so poorly drafted" it does not apply to "Macquarie Harbour fish farming". title: Australia faces 'lonelier' world with rules-based order crumbling
content: The global rules-based order is shifting in a way not seen for decades, with some experts saying the next government inherits a "world in disarray". There are concerns Australia has wasted time prepping its defence capabilities at a time when China seeks to become a dominant force in the Indo-Pacific. Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues The next federal government faces a world with drastic US policy changes, trade disputes, and ongoing wars in Europe and the Middle East. Security alliances are being challenged, and economic security is volatile, prompting voters to question what this means for Australia's place in the world. The ABC asked a group of former industry players, analysts, economists, and defence experts for their advice on what the next Australian prime minister needs to address first to ensure the country is stable, safe and successful. Peter Jennings is the director of Strategic Analysis Australia and former deputy secretary for strategy in the Defence Department. He said Australia was in "a very difficult situation". Peter Jennings, director of Strategic Analysis Australia, said the Australian Defence Force was losing capabilities very quickly. (AAP: Mick Tsikas) China was seeking to up-end the global order and make itself the dominant strategic player in the Indo-Pacific, while global "bad actors" such as Russia, North Korea and Iran were "out to create mayhem in their immediate regions", he said. Mr Jennings said the next government needed to stop wasting time. The next three years would be crucial for building stronger defence capabilities and alliances to help deter China in particular, he said. But right now, the defence force was "losing capabilities very quickly". Experts agree that Australia needs to boost its military capabilities. (Department of Defence: Lance Corporal Riley Blennerhassett) He singled out AUKUS as being "a real crisis" for the next government, warning it was in danger "of slowly sinking into the quicksand". Australia needed to focus on short-term solutions and local production that was driven by the private sector. Mr Jennings said Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's strategy to deal with the Trump administration had worked quite well so far. That was to "remain at arms-length … But we can't ignore it any longer". There are concerns about Donald Trump's self interests and whether the US would remain a reliable ally. (AP: Evan Vucci) The US is Australia's most vital strategic ally and represents one of its most important economic relationships. But there were dramatic changes occurring under the Trump administration, leading to uncertainty about the reliability of the US as a reliable military ally. Sean Turnell is an honorary professor of economics at Macquarie University and a non-resident fellow in the South-East Asia program at the Lowy Institute. Professor Turnell was held hostage for 650 days in Myanmar after being accused of espionage during his time working as an economic adviser to the now-deposed leader Aung San Suu Kyi. "The biggest thing we face is a highly volatile international economy," he said. Sean Turnell has been a senior analyst at the Reserve Bank of Australia, and said he was concerned with the lack of drive to grow the economy. ( ABC News: Keana Naughton ) The extent to which arbitrary policymaking spills over international financial markets could have "have huge implications on the Australian economy", Professor Turnell said. He wants the next prime minister to get serious about future-proofing the budget and growing the economy. Right now, the economy was doing well, but neither party was addressing what may lie ahead, Professor Turnell said. "It worries me. It's not time to sort of slacken off," he said. The International Monetary Fund says the US will be hardest hit by its own increased tariffs, which the organisation says is the biggest upheaval to global trade in 80 years. "Australia is entering into a new era. The old things that we were dependent on for decades and really took for granted are now in doubt." He said the next government needed to create a "fortress balance sheet" and get the budget in a place where it could withstand the volatile global environment. "Neither party seems to be directly addressing this issue," he said. Opposition Leader Peter Dutton announced an increase in defence spending but details have been thin. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore) Economic and national security are closely entwined. If the budget was in the right place, it would make space for increased defence spending, Professor Turnell said. Labor has not announced any election commitments specific to defence. The Coalition said it would spend an extra $21 billion between now and 2030 to reach its goal of lifting overall military spending. "The other thing I worry about is that there doesn't seem to be much focus on how to drive economic growth," Professor Turnell said. "It seems to be more about how to divide up the pie rather than increase the size." The first international visit taken by a prime minister often says a lot about the country's most important relationships. Most experts and analysts who spoke to the ABC said the first visit of a newly-elected prime minister should be in the Indo-Pacific. The first phone call should be to US President Donald Trump, they said. Since Paul Keating in 1992, almost every newly-elected prime minister has made Indonesia their first official international visit. Julia Gillard bucked the trend by heading to Afghanistan as her first port of call. Then, Anthony Albanese headed to Japan for the Quad meeting, which had already been scheduled, days after he was sworn in as prime minister. Jennifer Parker is a former naval officer and maritime security expert at the ANU National Security College and has more than 20 years' experience at the Australian Department of Defence. She said the choice of where the next prime minister visits after May 3 will be decisive. "I think also a visit or some sort of direct call quickly with the president of the United States is important." Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen Ms Parker believes both sides of the political divide need to better address the significance of the global shifts. Jennifer Parker from the Australian National University's National Security College said both major parties have failed to explain the need to boost defence spending to the public. (Supplied) Ms Parker said the key role of the next government would be to have a whole-of-nation view on defence. Australia needed to highlight its achievements as a reliable middle power in the region, Ms Parker said. While 70 per cent of Australians surveyed hold a "very unfavourable" view of Russia, that's only the case for 6 per cent of Indonesians. "That requires investment in both our diplomatic architecture, which includes our aid investment, but also our defence architecture," she said. She singled out Indonesia, saying strengthening the relationship with our close neighbour was paramount — both due to geography, and because two-thirds of Australia's maritime trade goes through the Indonesian archipelago, including most of our fuel. Ms Parker said the next government would need to bolster defence spending, to plug significant gaps in Australia's capabilities. She blamed both sides of politics for failing to explain the need for increased spending to the Australian public. Hear the latest election news as it happens on the Election Central Playlist. Only on the ABC listen app. There was often the idea that Australia was too isolated from the world to be attacked, but distance could also be a weakness, she said. It meant that supply lines, such as ammunition and maritime access, could be quickly cut off. She added that moving away from the US relationship was not the way to go — America remained a reliable partner. "The messaging that we're seeing from the current Trump administration is that the Indo-Pacific matters to the US," she said. Richard Maude is a distinguished policy fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute and a former deputy secretary in the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. "The next Australian government inherits a world in disarray," Mr Maude said. Richard Maude is a former deputy secretary in the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade. He believes Australia must prioritise relationships in the Indo-Pacific. (Supplied) Mr Maude said the major parties were lacking any compelling vision of how Australia could successfully navigate "a lonelier and more dangerous world". With no comprehensive plan, it seemed Australia was hoping to "ride its luck". The to-do list for the next prime minister was long, but he narrowed it down to a few key points. Fixing the nation's finances and making space in the budget to increase defence spending was a key priority, Mr Maude said. But Australia also needed to hedge against a "disruptive and narrowly self-interested" United States by investing more in a diverse set of regional and global partnerships. "If you strip out the politics, both major parties have actually invested pretty heavily in core relationships within our own region, and we really need to keep doing that," Mr Maude said. He said key relationships with Japan, Korea, India and Indonesia would need to keep being prioritised. The Albanese government has put in a significant effort with Pacific nations since taking office in 2022. (Supplied) He also highlighted the Pacific, saying that we had tried to "lift our game" in the region through successive Australian governments. European relationships were also becoming more important, especially the "core group" of France, Germany, the United Kingdom and Poland. "Those countries, in many ways, now share a much closer alignment of interest and values than we do with our alliance partner, America, at least under President Donald Trump," he said. 1 / of 7 Gorana Grgić, from the University of Sydney, specialising in US politics and foreign policy, said the next Australian government needed to continue to deepen and expand partnerships with other countries. "The next Australian prime minister must prioritise making Australia more resilient in an era of profound global uncertainty and the fracturing of the rules-based international order," she said. Gorana Grgić from the University of Sydney said Australia needed to be ready to adapt and be flexible with its foreign policy in a changing world. (Supplied: University of Sydney) Dr Grgić believes whoever leads the country after the election on May 3 will need to navigate a very different international landscape to previous modern Australian prime ministers. The current global landscape is marked by intense strategic competition, increasing fragmentation, and the contesting of established rules and norms. "Australia's diplomacy must be anchored in a clear articulation of its interests as a liberal democracy and a firm commitment to standing up for its values," she said. Lydia Khalil is the program director of the Transnational Challenges Program at the Lowy Institute and specialises in international relations, national security and strategic intelligence analysis. She echoed the sentiment shared by other experts about the worrying trend of international rules and norms being up-ended by shifts in the United States. Lydia Khalil is the Program Director of the Transnational Challenges Program at the Lowy Institute. She said leaders needed to clarify the importance of democracy to the public. (Supplied) The next prime minister must communicate the value of Australia's democracy to the public, Ms Khalil said. She said that the world was going through a significant democratic recession and that democracies had been in decline for the past 17 years. "Despite our challenges, Australia is a rare bright spot; our democracy is worth protecting and should not be taken for granted," she said. All fields are required unless marked optional. title: Outcry as dumping of PFAS-contaminated waste gets go-head at WA tip
content: Residents of a small community in Western Australia's South West have been left outraged by a state government decision to green-light the disposal of toxic chemicals at their local rubbish tip. The Department of Water and Environmental Regulation (DWER) has approved a licence amendment for the Cleanaway-owned rubbish facility at Crooked Brook on the outskirts of Dardanup, 180 kilometres south of Perth. The change will allow for waste contaminated with PFAS, and other dangerous chemicals, to be buried at the landfill. PFAS synthetic chemicals are found in low levels across much of Australia, as they have been used for more than 50 years in common residential and industrial items. They are considered "forever" chemicals, as they are highly persistent in the environment and take a long time to break down, and some varieties are recognised internationally as being toxic to humans and wildlife. Dardanup Environmental Action Group (DEAG) spokesperson Jill Cross said she was "angry, disheartened and gutted" by the decision, after 1,700 locals signed a petition against the proposal. Dardanup woman Jill Cross says she is "gutted" over DWER's decision. (ABC South West WA / Georgia Loney ) She said residents were concerned the waste site, which was already controversial with locals, could contaminate the local water supply. "It's not just groundwater [which is a concern], but also dust from that site," Ms Cross said. "Everyone is relying on those liners to make sure the aquifer is protected … and at some stage they will fail. Dardanup Shire President Tyrrell Gardiner said the potential for contamination was also front of mind for the council. Cr Gardiner said the council had objected to the change on several grounds, including the potential for contaminated dust and the life span of the landfill's liners. "Hopefully it doesn't happen at all, but it is likely to happen in the long-term future," he said. "We've got to support our community on this one. "It's just another approval to that site, which adds to the concerns of the people who live around it." Mr Gardiner said decisions to expand operations at the site had been subject to state government discretion since its construction in the 1990s. "As a local government authority, we are absolutely hamstrung in trying to get some control," he said. A cleanaway truck driving through the Dardanup townsite. (ABC News: Kate Stephens) Environment Minister Matthew Swinbourn said DWER had undertaken a detailed risk assessment of the application and fully considered the community's concerns. "DWER has assessed that the site does not place an unacceptable risk or impact on the environment, to drinking water, or to the public," Mr Swinbourn said. The DWER approval referenced an independent investigation in 2021 that indicated the landfill was not located on a vulnerable groundwater system. The report also found containment measures were sufficient to manage the risks associated with PFAS-contaminated waste. PFAS chemicals are used in a vast number of waterproof, non-stick and stain-resistant products. But concerns about their environmental and potential health impacts have intensified in recent years. "PFAS are persistent chemicals that require careful management," the DWER spokesperson said. "Our assessment considered the construction and lining of the landfill cells, leachate controls, and long-term groundwater monitoring." As part of the decision, DWER also reviewed Cleanaway's monitoring report from last year and found that PFAS concentrations in groundwater were consistent with background levels and below guideline thresholds. The amendment is now open for a public appeal period until May 14.Minister for Water and the South West Don Punch declined to comment.

title: The cost-of-living debate this election shows how many people are being left behind
content: There's not much that unites politicians across the spectrum but over the past five weeks they've been in agreement about what the biggest issue is this election: the cost-of-living crisis. It's a phrase being thrown around like there's no tomorrow, with leaders and candidates often repeating that it doesn't have a postcode. Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues And it's true. Across the country people are struggling, but while this problem might not have a postcode it does have a bank balance. I've spent the past five weeks crisscrossing the country, following the leaders on the campaign trail as they visit electorates on tight margins where voters will have a particularly high impact on who forms government. And the more people you speak to, the more it becomes clear that there's a difference between those who are inconvenienced and those who are in crisis. The space between them isn't a gap, it's a chasm. The media circus still has a little while to run yet, but when it comes to how politicians will help those at the forefront of this crisis, it's unclear if that will take centre stage. A huge media pack follows the leaders on the campaign trail. (ABC News: Matt Roberts) Being prime minister means getting the keys to some prime real estate — living in The Lodge in Canberra or Sydney's Kirribilli House with its panoramic harbour views. "I was actually living in a tent at Musgrave Park and I'd been there for a while," Alethia, who didn't want to give her real name, says when I meet her in Brisbane. Unlike whoever wins government on May 3, she — along with thousands of people across the country — is facing the harshest side of the housing crisis currently engulfing Australia. After she fled interstate to escape domestic violence, she made it into a rental in Brisbane but was then evicted in the middle of the pandemic. "I had a massive meltdown when they said they were going to move me from there, because I was so afraid of being moved around," she says. Alethia is living in crisis accommodation in Brisbane after fleeing domestic violence. (ABC News: Liz Pickering) Now she's in crisis accommodation, assisted by housing not-for-profit Micah Projects, but it's not somewhere she can live with her sons who have been forced to move interstate. This election, housing has been one of the most talked about topics of the campaign. But can you recall homelessness being discussed beyond a passing mention? "Politicians need to really acknowledge that a lot of people that don't have housing, it's not because they don't want to have a house. It's because they can't afford it," Alethia says. "I've applied for many private rentals… it's not like I'm asking for a $900 home, I'm looking $350, $400 and that's between two people." Sauvi was planning to go on holiday in his retirement, he'll be 70 next year, but now he looks after his young granddaughter in emergency accommodation. "I just do my best, try my best to do it myself," he says. Sauvi is a renter in Brisbane struggling to make ends meet. (ABC News: Liz Pickering) She draws in a pink colouring book while we chat and, like Alethia, Sauvi wishes politicians understood how hard things are for people who aren't first homebuyers or owners. "As long as we've got the roof on top of our head, that's the main thing, not on the street." Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen In Brisbane, the median house price is $843,231, five per cent of that is $42,161.55. In contrast, the fortnightly Jobseeker rate is $781.10 if you're single and don't have a dependent: that's $18,746.40 a year. Brisbane's Micah Projects, where Karen Walsh is CEO, is just down the road from where both the prime minister and opposition leader spent their first day on the campaign trail. "I'm very frustrated, because we know the solutions, we just don't have the political will to do it," she says. Researchers say women are feeling under represented in politics and struggle to speak up about the issues that matter to them. Ms Walsh welcomes plans to build more homes but says the one size fits all approach to social housing isn't working. "We can't just keep putting very vulnerable people, people with disabilities, serious mental illness, in the mix of social housing, it doesn't work." And she's sick of the federal government palming off a number of housing issues as matters for the states and territories. "There's nothing that's just a matter for the states…the mental health system isn't working properly, child protection isn't working properly, domestic violence [system] isn't meeting the housing needs that women are presenting with, we've got to get together and really make sure we start doing this instead of just talking about it." All sides of politics acknowledge that not enough has been done to prevent Australia's housing shortage. They say you reap what you sow but looking around Micah Projects that doesn't quite ring true. Here, it's constituents like Sauvi and Alethia who reap it instead. Anthony Albanese meets voters in Brisbane during the election campaign. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson) A few days later, I'm on the campaign bus with the prime minister who's spruiking a new development in Adelaide fresh off the back of his campaign launch in Perth the day before. I put some of what Alethia told us to him — that crisis accommodation isn't working for women fleeing violent homes but who want to live with their sons or who have needs that aren't straightforward. This election season politicians have tried to sell you the world. The team at Gruen isn't about to buy it. They've taken a big swing at the election, showing you how the democracy sausage is made, all the sizzle and none of the meat. "Well," he says, "the Housing Australia Future Fund had a portion of that housing that was about emergency accommodation for women and children escaping domestic violence. "That was something pointed out when the Greens and the Liberals and the Nationals in the Senate held it up for month after month after month after month." It was a quick pivot back to one of Labor's central campaign messages, but the prime minister noted it was just one thing among the multiple measures the government had implemented for women and children in this situation. He acknowledged there was more to be done, but frontline workers have repeatedly said the government had already failed to meet even basic requests from the sector and had described some of its measures as "trickery and deception". Like homelessness, violence against women has barely been on the political agenda in the lead up to the election — despite a number of women being killed while the campaign rolled on. That is until late last week, when the Coalition matched Labor's commitments and released its new $90 million package which includes a national domestic violence register. But, once again, those on the coal face have said this was a welcome boost but still not enough. Albanese campaigns in the Hunter in early April, MP Dan Repacholi is on the far left. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore) Later in the week, I visit the electorate of Hunter via Newcastle. On the way into the city, taxi driver Yogesh says he's voting Greens because he doesn't think the major parties are doing enough to make housing affordable or deal with how expensive the supermarket is getting. "They're changing all the time, their priorities," he says of the major parties compared to the Greens leader Adam Bandt who he believes "thought about young people and how much they're spending and they're renting". Yogesh is a chef by profession but drives the taxi because he needs two jobs to pay the rent on his apartment. "Sometimes seven days a week I have to work, I woke up today at 3:30 actually." "Yesterday I worked until 10 o'clock [at the restaurant]." Around the country, people are picking up extra shifts, sometimes working dangerously long hours like Yogesh, doing everything they can to try to get by. But what happens when you can't do that? In Kurri Kurri, under the watchful eye of the giant kookaburra, grandad Graham has just met the Nationals candidate for Hunter, Sue Gilroy. He's taking his grandkids out for the day and just as they were getting in the car, saw us interviewing the candidate and wanted to chat with her. "I'm on the disabilities pension, I hurt my back out at Alcan when it was going –that's an industrial aluminium smelter," he says. In Kurri Kurri, under the watchful eye of the giant kookaburra, grandad Graham has just met the Nationals candidate for Hunter, Sue Gilroy. (Carey Harris) Kurri Kurri is at the eastern edge of Hunter in NSW coal country — a long-time Labor heartland. But that's begun to shift, with Labor's first-preference vote trending downwards since 2010, the seat is now held by Labor MP Dan Repacholi on a margin of 4.8 per cent. This election, Graham's shifting his support to the Nationals after being a lifelong Labor voter. "When I was younger, growing up and working, Labor was always for the working man," he says. "We had unions that looked after us as well, but now they've just got off track and not looking after families or the working man." It was meeting Sue that sealed the deal. "She sounds honest," he says "and she's trying to get fuel down… and doing the right thing." His view that the Nationals are best placed to help working people isn't shared by everyone in the electorate. The day before, walking down Cessnock's main street with Repacholi you couldn't get more than a few steps without someone shouting out in support, tooting their horn or wanting to have a chat. But with voters like Graham who've stood by Labor their whole lives changing their mind, those in the party are hoping that love extends beyond Cessnock. By the time I reach the seat of Bradfield on Sydney’s North Shore, polls have opened. Millions of people will vote early this election, hundreds of thousands already have, breaking pre-poll voting records set at the last one. At the Uniting Church polling place in Willoughby, there are more volunteers than voters. But a steady stream of them have been battling the wind to come in and cast their ballot. The two candidates going head-to-head for the seat are here too: Liberal Gisele Kapterian and independent Nicolette Boele. Bradfield is a microcosm of the national contest, with candidates making their case for how they can put a lid on the rising cost of everything. (ABC News: Liam Patrick) The latter came close to winning the seat in 2022 but was pipped at the post by then-cabinet minister Paul Fletcher off the back of a 12.3 per cent swing against the Liberals. You wouldn't know it at this booth though, almost everyone who comes through takes a Liberal how-to-vote card and Kapterian is in her element meeting voters on their way in. "I'm an international trade lawyer by background, so all the stories I used to tell about tariffs and trade that used to put people to sleep over the dinner table and now become very relevant when we have a US president whose favourite word is tariff," she says. It's an issue her potential constituents are raising with her along with cost of living. "Cost of living is postcode agnostic, it means different things to different people in different contexts," she says. "It means everything from I would like to choose where to buy my home or I want to choose to live closer to my parents because I want my parents to be involved in the upbringing of my children. "It's got to do with I want the choice to send my children to the right school, the school of their choosing whether it be private or public. "People who worked so hard to secure these choices for themselves but just can't seem to make ends meet, that's the problem." Liberal Gisele Kapterian is hoping to win the seat of Bradfield in Sydney. (Jack Ailwood/ABC News) Kapterian and Boele are at odds on many things, but they both agree that cost of living is one of the key issues faced by the constituents in the electorate they want to represent. "People are hurting right across the stages of life," Boele says. "Everything is more expensive and that is madness because we should be one of the countries in the world with the cheapest energy bills."' While the pair agree that it's a pressing issue for their constituents-to-be, they're not on the same page when it comes to how to tackle it. It's a microcosm of the contest that will play out around the country this week, with candidates making their case for how they can put a lid on the rising cost of everything. In 1942, Australia's 12th prime minister Robert Menzies spoke of Australia's "forgotten class" in a speech that's impact has echoed through generations of Australian politics. A speech with the promise of a home of your own as its driving force. Now, the middle class he spoke about is at the centre of our political debate, with policy pitches focused squarely on this hefty group of voters. Certainly no longer "taken for granted by each political party in turn". But while much has changed since the 40s, if the cost-of-living debate shows anything this election, it's just how many people still feel forgotten. 1 / of 11 All fields are required unless marked optional.
