title: Side hustles on the rise as Tasmanians lowest paid but working the most jobs
content: Bruno Cabral was a lawyer in Brazil before he moved to Australia in search of a fresh start. But when he arrived in Tasmania three years ago, finding a full-time job proved difficult. "It was really hard, because I arrived in here in June … and Tasmania is really seasonal, you know, and there weren't many job vacancies available," Mr Cabral said. More people than ever before are picking up multiple jobs as the high cost of living pushes Australians to take on extra work, but the tax office warns people not to get caught out and know their obligations. Faced with a tough job market in Hobart, and a desperate need to pay the bills, he turned to an online job marketplace that outsources small jobs. Mr Cabral picked up some home removalist jobs on the platform, which he said "was the easiest and the quickest way to make some money". "When I started, I just realised that it wasn't that hard to be honest, and I was good at it, so I just decided to stay doing it," he said. He has since used the experience to help him land a permanent job in the industry. But that hasn't stopped him from side hustling. "Being a removalist, we're not really sure about our schedule, so sometimes when I know that I'm gonna finish earlier, I just open [Airtasker] up and I look for something else to do," he said. Airtasker is an Australian company that allows people to outsource everyday tasks. Mr Cabral estimates that he makes about an extra $300 a week by picking up the few odd jobs. Tasmania is leading the nation when it comes to working multiple jobs. (Unsplash: Robert Anasch ) The latest statistics from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) show that Tasmania is leading the nation when it comes to working multiple jobs. In December last year, the ABS found 8 per cent of employed Tasmanians, or 1 in 12, held two or more jobs, a number that was slightly higher in its capital, Hobart, at 8.5 per cent. Meanwhile, the national average is 6.7 per cent. Dr Paul Blacklow says low wage is one of the factors driving people to work multiple jobs. (ABC News) University of Tasmania economics lecturer Paul Blacklow said two main factors drove people to hold multiple jobs: their primary job not being full-time hours or it having a low wage. This is particularly true in Tasmania, where wages are lower compared with the mainland. The most recent figures from the ABS show Tasmanians have the lowest average weekly earnings for full-time workers in the country. Source: ABS, based on mean "And so for that reason, Tasmanians may well be taking on additional jobs, more so than their counterparts in the other states," Dr Blacklow said. Data from the ABS shows the number of multiple job holders across Australia is at an all-time high. Between 1995 and 2019, the multiple job-holding rate fluctuated between 5 per cent and 6 per cent. But after the COVID pandemic restrictions began to ease, the multiple job-holding rate rose and has remained at a historical peak of between 6.5 per cent and 6.7 per cent since December 2022. Dr Blacklow said this recent increase is likely attributable to "the cost-of-living crisis, and also because nominal wages haven't been growing that much". "We've noticed throughout history that other times when Australians have increased the amount of the incidence of holding multiple jobs, it's typically been when the economy has not been too well, or that inflation is high, or the wage growth is low," he said. ABS statistics show that workers aged 20–24 years old are the most likely to be working multiple jobs. This rings true for full-time university student Aya Gibson, who also holds three jobs. The 21-year-old's packed schedule sees her work at least three nights a week as a waitress, serve customers at a market stall at least once a fortnight, and coach a soccer team for a couple hours each week. She works up to 30 hours a week on average across all three jobs, as well as studying a double degree in marine biology and Antarctic sciences, which takes up about 38 hours a week. Aya Gibson works up to 30 hours a week on average across three jobs. (Supplied: Aya Gibson) Ms Gibson lives at home, which she says makes her daily expenses "probably lower than your average uni student", but that she is conscious of the current economic climate as "things are getting increasingly more expensive". "And so who knows what it's going to look like when I'm coming around to that kind of time in my life. "I may as well work and put towards savings and that kind of thing, and some life things that are good to save for."

title: Byron Bay to trial relaxed rules to boost 'waning' nightlife
content: Businesses in one of the country's most popular tourist destinations hope an upcoming trial will reinvigorate the town's nightlife. Byron Bay will be the first town outside of Sydney to trial a special entertainment precinct (SEP) under a New South Wales government plan announced on Saturday to boost the night-time economy. The precincts, known as SEPs, enable local councils to designate areas where trading hours and sound conditions can be relaxed to help drive successful hospitality venues, live music, performance and events. Matt Williamson says the trial will enable CBD venues to build on the success of larger regional music events. (Supplied: John Graham) Wirrun 'Wizz' Sky was one of the businesses pushing for the Byron CBD precinct, which will be encompass the Bay Street beachfront, Jonson Street, the rail corridor and Middleton and Browning Streets. He said relaxing trading restrictions would help revive the town's nightlife. "Byron has become a global destination because of the vibe, energy, live music and the cultural scene, which has been waning over the last few years," Mr Sky said. "This opens the door for small businesses like mine to re-engage with the soul of Byron to bring that energy and cultural essence back to town." Byron Shire Chamber of Commerce president Matt Williamson said the precinct would open up possibilities for new events. "[Business owners] can have events in laneways and put on little festivals that they have been wanting to for ages, but haven't been able to, because of restrictions," he said. Mr Williamson said it was hoped the trial would enable more activities in the CBD off the back of major music festivals and other local events. The Byron Shire Council will receive a kickstart state government grant of $162,800 for community consultation and to develop new opening hours and sound rules during the trial. Sarah Ndiaye is pushing for the precinct to bring nightlife back into town after difficult years of COVID and floods. (Supplied: John Graham) Byron Shire Mayor Sarah Ndiaye said she wanted to work with local businesses and the community to make the most of the trial, which was expected to start at the end of the year and run for 12-18 months. "There's a possibility here to get rid of some of the red tape and making sure that we're facilitating the economy, rather than creating roadblocks," she said. State Minister for Music and the Night-time Economy, John Graham, said the Byron precinct trial aimed to make it easier for businesses and venues to "trade later and to bring music into the centre of Byron for businesses to be more viable". Trading red tape will be cut to allow Byron Bay venues to become more viable and rebuild the night-time economy to pre-COVID highs. (Facebook: Byron Schoolies Parties) "It allows greater noise protections for venues, incentives to keep music playing, so extra trading for those venues that have music on their stages," Mr Graham said. Other SEP trials have started around the Chinatown Night Markets in Burwood and in Fairfield. This site is protected by reCAPTCHA and the Google Privacy Policy and Terms of Service apply.

title: Eating challenges on the menu as young turn away from alcohol
content: Walking through a crowd of people in North Queensland, Jimmy Judge is stopped for photos. He is 29 years old, a former amateur boxer and personal trainer, and now makes a living as a competitive eater. Over the past couple of years Mr Judge has attracted more than 200,000 followers on social media where he documents his extreme food challenges. Jimmy Judge took on 2kg of seafood this week in Townsville. (ABC North Qld: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet) One of his fastest records stands at 10 pies in four-and-a-half minutes. He has also made his way through a 1kg donut in under four minutes, 3kg of nachos in 18 minutes and 10 seconds, 14 pancakes in 15 minutes, and a 2.2kg pizza in seven minutes and 10 seconds. "I use this as entertainment for other people and it's become my job now, which I'm so blessed for," he said. "I honestly never could have imagined it would go like this." A former boxer turned competitive eater, Mr Judge is set to tour Australia. (ABC North Qld: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet) Mr Judge is about to embark on a national road trip from Queensland to WA, where he will seek out the country's best pub feeds, local cuisines and hidden gems. Hailing from Townsville and now living on the Gold Coast, Mr Judge said regional pubs would be a focus on his trip. "I'll definitely be going back out west and trying some of the famous Mount Isa pubs, coming through Charters Towers, all the gold mining towns," he said. So that's food for thought if he ever takes on a fruit-eating challenge. This week, he took on a 2kg seafood boil on stage as part of a youth festival, finishing the platter in just over 30 minutes. Bina's Kitchen owner Evelyn Billy, who cooked the seafood, said she was worried watching Mr Judge on stage. Evelyn Billy cooked the seafood for Mr Judge. (ABC North Qld: Jonathon Poulson) "I don't know if he's going to be OK, it's a lot of seafood," she said. Often making his way through kilograms of food, Mr Judge has the preparation down pat. "I always take 24 hours off before the challenge … so if I've got a challenge at lunchtime I'll normally have a big meal the day before at lunchtime but a big meal that's low calories," he said. "Five hours before, I'll cut all my liquids off so I won't drink anything between 7'o'clock and midday, but I'll get up early to make sure I can drink two or three litres of water." As young people increasingly shift away from alcohol, some pub owners say they have had to make changes to their core business. Helen Corliss is the operations manager of the Grand Hotel in Childers, one of the first stops on Judge's eating tour. Helen Corliss says the hotel launched its eating challenges after a shift in customer behaviour. (Supplied) The hotel has been running regular eating challenges for about a year. "I think it's just a bit of fun … you know cost of living pressures and everything that's going on in Australia, people when they do come out to dinner, they just want to come out and have a big meal." From 1kg steaks to a "full boar" rack of ribs and triple-stack burgers, punters must beat a time limit to eat certain meals free at the pub. Ms Corliss said there had been a "generational shift" in drinking behaviours. "We've always had the core market of the guys that come in after work, or the guys that sit there all day on a Saturday and have a pint or have a drink," she said. "The younger generation are just not like that. Mr Judge said his road trip, which will be documented on social media, was also a bid to challenge himself. "I've really struggled in the past with a lot of my own mental health battles," he said. "This is something that absolutely terrifies me to go out and be by myself for so long on the road. "I'm quite an anxious person that always needs to know what's going on next."

title: Castle conjured during slumber gives new meaning to 'dream home'
content: Selling a property that's been in the family for decades is always an emotional time – after all, as the old saying goes, every person's house is their castle. But imagine if the property was an actual castle. The castle is decorated with souvenirs from around the world, inlcuding 12 stained glass windows from Scotland. (Supplied: Rachael Moore) Welcome to the world of Rachael Moore and her husband Andre Meyer. Rachel and her siblings inherited the extraordinary property at Gleniffer, south-west of Coffs Harbour in northern NSW, when her aunt Barbara Moore passed away from brain cancer in 2021. The castle's staircase takes guests to the "Rapunzel room" upstairs. (Supplied: Rachael Moore) Barbara had a dream about a castle in the 1990s, and spent about $3.5 million to turn it into a reality. "Aunty Barb, she was very eccentric, she was a very unique human being," Rachael said. The castle, originally designed as a chapel, features 12 stained-glass windows, which were hand-picked from a church in Scotland. Upstairs, an opulent "Rapunzel room" features a Juliet balcony at the top of an elaborate winding staircase. Rachael said her aunt felt like she had never "finished" building, but relished the challenge of maintaining the property. Barbara Moore took care of Evermoore Estate until she was in her 70s. (Supplied: Rachel Moore) Rachael Moore and Andre Meyer pulling up "lunch" from their dumbwaiter. (ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager) It might sound like a fairytale, but Rachael said the property required plenty of hard work. "It's a little bit like a fairytale of Cinderella sometimes, because you're at this enchanted magical ball with the glass slipper, but you're also scrubbing the floor," she laughed. In addition to a scrubbing brush, would-be princes and princesses need to have a green thumb to trim the hedge maze and maintain the vast gardens, where Barbara spent a lot of her time. Barbara Moore designed Evermoore Estate in the 1990s. (Supplied: Rachel Moore) Family friend Linda Dalton said Barbara's personality could be seen throughout the castle in everything from a decorative bathroom chandelier to the ancient religious books on display. "Barb said herself she wasn't a minimalist; Barb hated that idea, she wanted everything," Linda said. Barbara never married or had any children. Her family said she became "married" to the land. Barbara Moore (left) inside the homestead at Evermoore Estate during construction. (Supplied: Rachel Moore) Neighbour Kevin Evans said the estate was so special due to the location of the castle. "I think most people walked into the castle and their jaws were on the floor, it was really quite extraordinary," he said. "It's not an appropriate building in terms of the landscape here in the subtropics." Evermoore Estate has been in the Moore family since the 1990s. (Supplied) In recent years, Rachel and Andre have run the property as a bed and breakfast while they live in the homestead just up from the castle. "I think she'd be stoked — we've literally brought her vision to life, which she wasn't able to do at the end of her life, because it was too much," Rachel said. Rachael Moore and Andre Meyer say it's time for someone else to enjoy the castle. (ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager) The strain of maintaining the property to Barb's lofty standards has taken its toll. "The gardening, you know, it's so much work," Andre said. The family has decided it is time to sell up and move on, leaving Barb's proud bequest for someone else to inherit. "Such is life, we can't hold onto everything forever."

title: Gold Coast light rail delays cost small businesses big money
content: From his shop on the Gold Coast Highway, Jess Firkin watches construction of a billion-dollar public transport infrastructure project. It is a 6.7 kilometre stretch of light rail that will connect about 1 million passengers a month from the shopping precinct of Broadbeach to the stunning beaches of Burleigh Heads. But it comes with road closures, a loss of parking spaces and the loud clamour of construction — something Mr Firkin says has cost his Mermaid Beach business. "We've been forgotten," he said. Mr Firkin said the state government's efforts to support businesses were falling flat as the project faced cost blow-outs and delays. Light rail arrives at Broadbeach on the Gold Coast. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale) "People that are paying commercial mortgages have still got to pay but how can we get support from the government," Mr Firkin said. "It's their project and it is affecting us." Construction of light rail stage 3 started in July 2022 under the former state Labor government. It will not be operational until at least mid-2026 — a delay of six months. The budget has also blown-out from $709 million to $1.5 billion. John Witheriff, who chairs light rail operator GoldlinQ, told a transport forum earlier this month crews were digging up decades-old infrastructure. Construction crews have uncovered buried infrastructure while building the extension. (Supplied: @lightrailstage3) "We've got no idea what's underground in our city and we've got no idea how long the stuff's been in there and when it's all going to break up," he said. Mr Witheriff said construction crews discovered broken asbestos-cement water pipes recently in Burleigh Heads, which added to the "additional time businesses and community are being chewed up about it". Mermaid Beach cafe owner Kym Hearne said her trade had dropped at least 25 per cent over the past two years. "How long can you hang on for? Our expenses don't go down [and] I've made a small amount of cuts to my staffing but that comes at the expense of our quality of service," she said. Construction is ongoing at Mermaid Beach. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale) "The only positive would have been if businesses were compensated — our income, our trade, has declined drastically." In 2023 a court found the New South Wales government liable for the financial losses suffered by some businesses along the Sydney CBD light rail route after its construction was completed a year behind schedule. But that was later overruled after the NSW Court of Appeal found that the financial loses were neither substantial or unreasonable, and that the authorities could not foresee the extent of the construction delays. Mr Firkin said he was more concerned about the immediate future of small businesses like his. "There's risk in every business," he said. Jess Firkin hopes more people will support small businesses during light rail disruptions. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale) The Queensland government has ruled out compensation for the loss of property value, trade or amenity caused by construction but has undertaken the 'Love Your Local' promotional campaign. The project's contractor, John Holland, has purchased 2,200 vouchers from almost 200 businesses since October 2022, which have been given away through local radio promotions. Mr Firkin said that approach did not make sense for his customers, who were younger and less likely to listen to radio. "They did a radio plug to give away three $50 vouchers for my store — not one of them came in to redeem it," he said. "There's just no pattern to it". Light rail construction near Mr Firkin's Mermaid Beach shop. (ABC Gold Coast: Dominic Cansdale) Ms Hearne said offering businesses promotional vouchers did not make up for more than two years of construction disruption. A Transport and Main Roads spokesperson said the light rail Instagram account, which had about 2,600 followers, also promoted local businesses. "A number of events have also been staged as part of the campaign, including a street party on the Lower Gold Coast Highway in November 2024, and a series of business networking events," the spokesperson said. The 'Love Your Local' campaign is due to finish at the end of this year.

title: Small businesses feel the pinch amid busy Easter period
content: For Marcus Booth-Remmers, Easter guarantees a sugar hit in more ways than one. From his cafe and factory in the Adelaide Hills, the chocolatier has spent the weeks leading up to the holiday period busily handcrafting and selling a range of specialty chocolate eggs, bunnies and bilbies. "It is one of the absolute busiest times of the year for us," the Red Cacao cafe owner says. "The Easter period equates for up to a third of our yearly trade, so it's really one of our peak periods." He says the boost in sales is welcome after a year of challenging business conditions. Mr Booth-Remmers says he has tried to avoid passing on increased cocoa costs to his customers, amid a global shortage of the essential chocolate-making ingredient. A global shortage of cocoa is pushing up the cost of making chocolate. (ABC News: Tim Swanston) Meanwhile, the closure of a nearby supermarket has changed foot traffic along the main thoroughfare in the area where he trades. While Mr Booth-Remmers says the public's appetite for high-end chocolates shows no sign of waning, ongoing cost of living pressures have prompted some of his customers to spend less in his cafe. "Probably in the last nine months or so we've really felt it," he says. "[People] might come in for their daily coffee still, but leave off the extra treat on the side." Marcus Booth-Remmers says customers are spending less money at his Red Cacao cafe in Stirling. (ABC News: Che Chorley) Compounding the situation is a feeling of growing unease surrounding the fast-moving trade war between the US and China. Mr Booth-Remmers's small business is not directly impacted by the situation, but he says his customers have been talking about it. "The disruption that the US is creating is real for some customers," he says. "Cost of living has definitely been on people's minds for a while and now I think what's going on in the US just throws another element onto that. "It's just uncertainty — people are not sure what to expect." In Melbourne, cake maker Matilda Chambers has taken to social media to remind customers to be "kind to your local bakers" amid the cost-of-living crisis and economic uncertainty. Like Mr Booth-Remmers, Ms Chambers's business has been affected by shortages of ingredients such as cocoa and eggs. "I have found in the past year a lot of our products have been going up — some as much as 50 per cent — which really impacts how much we can sell the cakes for," she says. "It sort of snowballs because customers don't have the money at the moment to be paying for cakes that are too expensive, so it's really hard to find the middle ground with a selling point that works for us and them." Melbourne cake maker Matilda Chambers says shortages of ingredients such as cocoa and eggs are impacting her business. (ABC News: Kate Ashton) Ms Chambers says many of her recent sales have been on the "lower end" of her pricing scale, with customers less likely to order elaborate cakes and instead opting for simpler designs. "People are conscious of what they're spending overall — especially when it's something like a cake where it's more for enjoyment and not a necessity as much," she says. The cost of doing business is also weighing heavily on Dan Keast's mind. He and his wife Tanya have spent more than four decades running DTK Textiles — an Adelaide-based wholesale business which sells printers for the clothing industry and produces commercial transfers for promotional and sports clothing. DTK Textiles director Dan Keast says the current business climate is affecting his retirement prospects. (ABC News: Che Chorley) He says in recent years he has faced "significant" increases in rent, insurance and power costs, which he sometimes struggles to absorb in pricing. "Sometimes you're saying 'no' to orders, which otherwise you would have been able to take on and make a reasonable profit," he says. "It certainly affects our prospects for retirement, because when you have a wholesaling business or you've heavily committed to stock and ongoing expenses, to walk out of a business and retire is a very expensive process. "The current climate is not a good climate for engaging in selling a business." Australian company owners say they are not getting enough support as they navigate soaring tariffs to send Chinese-made goods into the US. A report released by the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry last July found 45 per cent of the small businesses surveyed considered leaving or closing their business in the 12 months prior. "If these businesses do end up closing, more than one million small businesses will disappear, resulting in job losses for over two million Australians," the report states. Mr Keast says about two years ago he reduced his workforce from six to five employees, but within a year he was spending more on wages than before. He says he and his wife are both currently working 60-hour weeks but are hoping to retire soon. "We tend to look every day for new projects, new opportunities, and to continue to reinvent ourselves to make our business more attractive for potential buyers."

title: Opposition vows to put country of origin stamp on your back deck
content: The timber aisle in your local hardware store may look a little different if the Coalition is successful in next month's election. As part of its tilt at government the Opposition has promised to introduce country of origin labelling on timber sold by commercial hardware outlets. Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues In Australia there is no requirement for timber products to be labelled with the country they are from. Under the proposed change any timber grown and harvested in Australia would be individually marked to show its origin and imported timber would be labelled to show where it was grown. Liberal Senator Jonathan Duniam says the labels would help people choose Australian products. (Supplied: Jonathan Duniam) Opposition forestry spokesperson Jonathon Duniam said the measure would help people make an informed choice. "We should be making sure it is clear, whether it is a product that you pick up at Bunnings or Mitre 10, you can see that is a product that has come from an Australian forest," he said. Mr Dunaim said consumers should know if they were purchasing timber that had been "ripped out of the Congo Basin". "Most Australians would know enough about how good our product is to make the right choice," he said. The details of the labelling plan are yet to be established but the change is expected to apply to retail and commercial sales. A range of wood products grown in Australia and overseas are on sale in hardware stores. (ABC Rural: Warwick Long) The Australian Forest Products Association (AFPA) supports the idea, which chief executive Diana Hallam says would be similar to what is in place for food packaging. "I've lost count of the number of beautiful hardwood decks I've been shown, beautiful Merbau decks, and I say, 'Do you realise this is from Indonesia or Malaysia?'," Ms Hallam said. Diana Hallam says the labelling would give consumers more information about the timber they're buying. (Supplied: Australian Forest Products Association) According to its website Bunnings sources Merbau from West Papua, though the timber is also grown in northern Australia. A recent DNA testing trial of imported wood by the federal Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Department (DAFF) revealed up to a third of all wood traded in the world had been illegally logged. About 25 per cent of products it tested displayed inconsistencies with either the declared species, origin, or both. Ms Hallam said the incorrect identification of wood was a potential indicator of illegal activity. Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen The Labor government has not released a timber industry policy this election campaign. When questioned on timber labelling a spokesperson referred to Labor's forestry decisions while in government. "The Albanese government has made record investments in forestry, that [are] environmentally, socially and commercially sustainable," the spokesperson said. "We need timber products and we want sustainable forestry jobs. "That's why we are investing $300 million to grow plantations, modernise our timber manufacturing infrastructure, and build the skills of our forestry workforce." Labor says it supports a sustainable Australian forestry industry. (ABC Rural: Warwick Long) A label on timber sold at hardware stores may not be the deciding issue at this election, but the AFPA said it was a small change that would make a big difference to Australian forestry workers and the environment. "We are very conscious there is a cost of living crisis at the moment and a housing crisis and we don't want to exacerbate that," Ms Hallam said. title: Why exactly are STIs spreading more and more across Australia?
content: Over the last three decades, sexually transmitted infections (STIs) have quietly but steadily climbed in Australia, with bacterial diseases like chlamydia, gonorrhoea, and syphilis spreading across the country. In 2004, just over 35,724 new cases of chlamydia were recorded in Australia, according to federal government data. By 2024, that figure had roughly tripled to more than 102,000 notifications, with infections spread roughly evenly across men and women. "When we look at these data, we can see that chlamydia continues to be the most frequently notified sexually transmissible infection," said Skye McGregor, an epidemiologist with UNSW's Kirby Institute, leading its Australian STI and bloodborne virus surveillance reporting. Gonorrhoea and syphilis have followed a similar trajectory. Annual confirmed cases of the former had risen from 7,047 in 2004 to more than 44,000 in 2024. Syphilis numbers climbed by almost ninefold to 5,969 over the same period. The last three decades have seen persistent growth in sexually transmitted infections, including the bacterial disease syphilis. (Flickr: NIAID) While these infections can be treated with antibiotics and lack the harm potential of other sexual diseases like HIV, they present serious health consequences if they remain undetected, including infertility, congenital transmission and, in the case of syphilis, organ damage. Those first-line treatments are also at risk of soon becoming ineffective, with antimicrobial resistance an expanding global issue. Last year, NSW Health issued a public warning of how gonorrhoea cases resistant to azithromycin and ceftriaxone were growing in the state. "It makes infections harder to treat, which increases the risk of transmission, illness and even death," Dr McGregor said. Though the rise of bacterial STIs is well-documented — observed by health workers in the country and overseas — exactly why it's happening is something more complex and opaque. While specific populations — including men who have sex with men (MSM) — have long been associated with higher risk, the current data indicates these diseases are proliferating across age, gender and sexuality demographics. "There's a range of factors. We can't just point to one thing and go, 'This is the main reason we're seeing an increase in STIs'," Dr McGregor said. One suspected reason for an increase in cases is a decline in safe sex, a trend partially influenced by medical innovation. (ABC News: James Hancock) Included in that range of factors are the asymptomatic nature of these bacterial diseases, declining condom use and the unintended impacts of medical innovation. Research has found the widespread availability of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), a medication that prevents HIV infection, has contributed to more unprotected sex. The most immediate solution to all of this is also the most basic: Safer sexual practices alongside regular, proactive sexual health screenings. "It's really important to have the message of regular, comprehensive testing," Dr McGregor said. But despite that message's simplicity, enacting that change is difficult. One explanation held by Dr McGregor is the lack of awareness of diseases like chlamydia, gonorrhoea and syphilis alongside infection risk factors. Skye McGregor said prevention campaigns, at the scale of those targeting HIV and Hepatitis C, could raise awareness. (ABC News: Andrew Whitington) This blind spot, she said, stems in part from years of underinvestment, with few public health campaigns and research efforts matching the scale of those targeting HIV or Hepatitis C — diseases where infection rates have dropped in recent years. "It's complex, but if you take into account where the reductions have been, there's a reason for it." While greater investment in prevention initiatives could raise the necessary awareness, other experts say strategies targeting the full spectrum of those at risk are as crucial. "Traditionally we focused on what we call high-risk populations: MSM and Indigenous and so on. But maybe that's not the only group that needs all these resources poured into," Melbourne Sexual Health Centre's Jason Ong said. It's something the sexual health physician and researcher has observed firsthand. In recent years, the number of people seeking screenings has increased. Yet, infection numbers are still continuing to rise. "If you're testing more people, why aren't the STI rates dropping? And so that's also part of that story where, maybe, we're not testing the right populations," he said. "Within certain groups, we know definitely there are people that are not testing." The lack of testing may come down to awareness, but it could also be deliberate avoidance. It's long been established how the stigma surrounding STIs can dissuade someone from seeking medical care. One reason why people aren't receiving sexual health screenings is due to perceived stigma. (Pixabay) In 2021, Professor Ong co-authored a meta-analysis on what encourages young people from high-income countries to seek STI testing. Both limited awareness and stigma were named as key deterrents. "If we can address that stigma piece, I think that will help a lot so that people can feel comfortable to talk to a doctor about it — and get the proper testing and treatments if needed." But stigma isn't the only barrier to receiving sexual healthcare. The decline of bulk-billing practices within a cost-of-living crisis is keeping people away, too. "It's now expensive for people to go to the GP," said David Lewis, the conjoint professor of the University of Sydney's Sydney Medical School and a sexual health physician in the city's western suburbs. "You can do health promotion, but if you don't make the testing easily accessible for people, then it's a challenge." One workaround could be importing the strategies embraced for other sexual diseases. At-home rapid tests for HIV have been available in Australia since 2019, with a pilot program providing free access in NSW launched last year. While the equivalent technology for STIs faces questions over accuracy alongside limited accessibility — the first TGA-approved at-home kit for chlamydia and gonorrhoea relies on a vaginal swab sample — this model of private, instant healthcare could be a blueprint for increasing screening rates. "There's all these other bits of the puzzle. It's not just a question of promotion and education." Professor Lewis said. "It's very hard to shift sexual risk. What programs are successful in doing is often changing health-seeking behaviour," said Burnet Institute's head of public health Mark Stoové. Australia's leading sexual health experts say taking an antibiotic after unprotected sex could help curb rising rates of syphilis in the community, but there's a big catch. This use of new approaches that centre availability, accessibility and less visibility could be one way forward to circumnavigate those hurdles to testing and sexual healthcare. Pointing to the introduction of point-of-care testing and telehealth in response to HIV and Hepatitis C, Professor Stoové said similar adaptive models of care would — when combined with targeted education and public health messaging — close gaps in testing, in turn lowering infection rates. Any response, he added, needs to be tailored to meet the needs of wherever people are — whether that be financially, culturally, socially or geographically. "Particularly in the space of sexual health education, if we're putting a campaign out there, people need to recognise that the campaign is speaking to them."

title: Sick of paying for streaming services? These films and TV series are free
content: It's the Easter long weekend, you have to figure out a way to entertain kids on school holidays and any guests who are staying overnight. But we also know you might have been hit by numerous streaming-service price increases lately. Isn't there any way to watch quality movies and TV free of charge? There is actually a whole treasure trove of film and TV streaming right now that you can access FREE — if you know where to look. We've done the hard yards, sifting through three free Australian streaming services — iview, SBSonDemand and Brollie — to bring you the cream of the crop. So, when you've run out of egg hunts and paper craft, chuck on some of these titles and bask in your screen's warming (and free) glow. Sisterhood of the Traveling Pants | Original Theatrical Trailer Before America Ferrera was making 30-something women feel seen with her iconic monologue in Barbie, she did the same thing for young women in this coming-of-age dramedy. Four longtime friends (Ferrera, Blake Lively, Amber Tamblyn and Alexis Bledel) happen upon a pair of jeans that magically fit all of their varied body types. They use their fantastical find to connect them during the first summer they've ever had to spend apart. Equal parts heartfelt and heartbreaking, Sisterhood is a uniquely early 2000s offering that is an essential watch for any tween (and teen and young person… basically just anyone who's still coming to terms with their own emotions). Super Mario Bros. (1993) Trailer #1 Forget any billion-dollar Chris Pratt fan service, 1993's Super Mario Bros is a must-see for any Nintendo enthusiasts. Not because it's a faithful adaptation of the beloved video game series, but because it is absolutely bonkers. Mario (Bob Hoskins, in what he openly called his most hated job) and Luigi (John Leguizamo) are plumber brothers working in Brooklyn — so far, so normal. But that's before you get into the inter-dimensional travel, lizard-headed thugs and a dinosaur-inhabited realm called Dinohatten. From start to finish, Super Mario Bros is an extremely wild ride and it is exhilarating to see the IP take such massive swings when it comes to creativity (as opposed to its 2023 counterpart). Clue (1985) ORIGINAL TRAILER Now here's a board game that's guaranteed not to end in a family fight. Based on the characters from the iconic game Cluedo, Clue: The Movie is a campy romp with a sterling cast of British greats and an incredibly silly Tim Curry as suspicious butler Wadsworth. The premise is simple: mysterious rich guy Mr Boddy has gathered six strangers to his shady mansion and then has the gall to turn up murdered (bad host vibes). Characters faction off, trade sides and generally get into misfortune trying to figure out who is the killer. There's also an incredibly fun twist at the end that will keep the lounge room guessing games going. Hundreds of Beavers | Official Trailer Mike Cheslik and Ryland Tews' 2022 slapstick film might be the most lauded comedy that you've never heard of. The black-and-white marvel was the highest-rated comedy on Letterboxd for 2024 and just minutes into the film, you can understand why. It's basically 100 minutes of live-action Looney Tunes, as alcohol salesman Jean Kayak (Tews, embodying the spirit of Charlie Chaplin) fights off a hoard of mischievous beavers (actually actors in cartoonish beaver costumes). Not only is Hundreds of Beavers a gag-a-minute laugh-fest but it's also a technical achievement, weaving in slick animation on a minuscule $US150,000 budget. If blockbuster slop has got you down, then this is the film that will reinvigorate your belief in comedy cinema. BOY | Official Trailer Before Taika Waititi became Marvel's go-to guy, his domain was low-budget New Zealand comedies, and one of the first films to put him on the map was 2010's Boy. Set in mid-80s rural New Zealand, Boy is actually the name of our protagonist, played with comedic timing and pathos way beyond his years by James Rolleston. Boy spends his days impersonating Michael Jackson, hanging out with his friends and telling tall tales about his estranged father, Alamein (Waititi). Until one day, when Boy's fabled father returns home to an initially delighted son. But Alamein's questionable antics force Boy to see his father in a new, less sparkling light. Half silly comedy, half coming-of-age story, Boy is a glittering example of the humour and emotion Waititi carried on to his later work. ON THE COUNT OF THREE Jerrod Carmichael's 2021 directorial debut is as dark as comedy gets, but that doesn't mean it's not shockingly funny. Content warning: On the Count of Three is about a suicide pact, following childhood friends Val (Carmichael) and Kevin (a phenomenal Christopher Abbott) as they enjoy their "one last day" together before mutually ending their unhappy lives. While this doesn't seem like fruitful ground for a comedy, Carmichael manages to mine sparkling levity out of the serious subject. Tightly wound and incredibly action-packed for its compact 86-minute run time, On the Count of Three could have been disastrous, but in Carmichael's hands it becomes a hard and hilarious message about the value in life. How to Blow up a Pipeline - Official Trailer (2023) Loosely based on Andreas Malm's non-fiction book of the same name, How to Blow Up a Pipeline is a timely eco-thriller that sadly didn't get a lot of love when it was released locally last year. Friends Xochitl and Theo, fed up with the devastating effects of climate change in their city, band together to plan an act of environmental terrorism. Like Malm's book, How To Blow Up a Pipeline makes a stark argument that sabotage is the last bastion of self defence in a world that refuses to acknowledge the damage being done to our climate. The film is first and foremost a tight thriller, but the real-world implications will leave it lingering in your head for days. Spotlight TRAILER 1 (2015) This Best Picture Oscar-winner is a difficult but important watch. Based on The Boston Globe's 2003 Pulitzer-Prize-winning investigation, Spotlight is a jaw-dropping look at the cover-up of widespread child sex abuse by numerous priests in Boston. Populated by an all-star cast — including Mark Ruffalo, Michael Keaton and Rachel McAdams — Spotlight has been lauded for its historical accuracy and for shining a light on sexual abuse within the Catholic Church, as well as showing the importance of independent, investigative journalism. JUNGLE : Official Trailer (2017) Daniel Radcliffe Here's a real-life survival story that has an Australian connection. Based on the experiences of adventurer Yossi Ghinsberg, Jungle follows Yossi's (Daniel Radcliffe) journey into the uncharted Amazon jungle. After his hiking crew gets off track, Yossi is split up from the rest of them, leaving him to fend for himself for three weeks in the harsh wilderness. In the film, the Gold Coast Hinterland partly stands in for the unforgiving Amazon — an apt choice given the real Ghinsberg settled in Byron Bay after his ordeal. THE ROYAL HOTEL - Official Trailer Often compared to Ozploitation classic Wake In Fright, Kitty Green's The Royal Hotel is the opposite of a tourism advertisement for our county's rural outback. American backpackers Hanna (Julia Garner) and Liv (Jessica Henwick) reluctantly take up bartending work in an outback mining town. They initially try to brush off the sexist microaggressions coming from their mostly male clientele, but as it blossoms into full-blown aggression, the women are forced to evaluate the real level of danger posed by the dirt-brushed locals. Tense and building, The Royal Hotel is an uncompromising look at the misogyny still rife in some parts of Australian culture. Two Hands (1999) Trailer | Heath Ledger | Bryan Brown You'd be hard-pressed to find a film more Aussie than Two Hands. The 1999 crime comedy stars a fresh-faced Heath Ledger and Rose Byrne, and is sound-tracked by some of the most iconic Australian bands ever (we can hear 'These Days' by Powderfinger just thinking about it). While taking a dip at Bondi beach, strip-club bouncer Jimmy (Ledger) loses $10,000 loaned to him by a mob boss (Bryan Brown), sending him on a cross-city caper that includes a botched bank robbery, a hit-and-run and more Australiana than you can poke a snag at. PEN15 (Official Teaser) | Hulu This Lonely-Island-produced cringe comedy series is your typical coming-of-age, tween high school story. Except that the two 13-year-old protagonists, Maya and Anna, are played by 30-something creators Maya Erskine and Anna Konkle. Being surrounded by co-stars of appropriate age (read: 13) heightens the comedy in this side-splitting series. Set in the year 2000, Pen15 is full of relatable humiliations, surreal subplots and genuine, heartbreaking conversations on race, gender and growing up. Producing two pitch-perfect seasons before becoming a victim of COVID, Pen15 is primed to watch over one delightful weekend. Round the Twist - Series 1 Trailer Have you ever, ever felt like watching the wacky antics of a doting Dad and his three weirdo offspring as they reside in a lighthouse? No longer relegated to children's afternoon broadcast TV, all four delightful seasons of Round The Twist are available to watch FREE right now. The only decision you'll have to make is which episode to start on first: the one where Pete is impregnated by a tree sprite? Or maybe the one where Linda hooks up with a merman? OK, let's compromise and watch the one where an exotic fish allows Bronson to turn his penis into a propeller to win a swimming race. Long live weird Australian kids TV. First Look | Optics | ABC iview If you've ever enjoyed the comedic stylings of Sydney duo Freudian Nip (The Feed, your Instagram timeline), then you already know the vibe of their debut series Optics. The first season takes audiences behind the scenes of a crisis PR firm whose CEO has just carked it, leaving the keys of the castle to two of the firm's young female employees, Greta (Vic Zerbst) and Nicole (Jenna Owen). If you've ever worked in an office, then the comedy in Optics will be excruciatingly relatable as the firm's new leaders navigate scheming co-workers and disgraced clients. Its smart, quick dialogue will make the six-episode series go down easier than a decaf latte.

title: A supermarket catalogue from 2021 tells us plenty about this election
Call to insurer even worse than sight of this flood-damaged home
content: It's April 7 — a week since Thargomindah's levee broke, and nearly the entire township was inundated — and Melinda Byrne is finally returning to her home. She makes the final turn in her vehicle and pulls into the driveway, not knowing what waits for her when she opens the front door. For the past week, since being evacuated to the town's airport — the only place high enough in town to escape the floodwaters — she's tried to cling to the hope that floodwaters hadn't managed to seep into her home. Melinda Byrne said her home was always insured against floods, but she couldn't afford to continue after a recent renewal came attached to a much higher price-tag. (ABC News: Glenn Armstrong) "I think for me personally, I chose to believe that [my home] had kept it out so I didn't have to think about the carnage that would be inside," she said. But, as an SES volunteer pulls the sandbags aside and opens her front door, Ms Byrne faces a harsh reality — the water mark on her front door reveals just how high it got. Inside, puddles of mud pool on the floor, furniture has been upturned and scattered throughout her home, and water has infiltrated every cupboard, nook and cranny within a metre of the floor. "It's just hard to explain and you think, 'Yep that's the worst it can be'," she said. "But then you have a phone call with the insurance company and then it's like, 'So that's as bad as it can get'." This aerial shot shows how widespread recent flooding was across the outback town of Thargomindah. (ABC News: Glenn Armstrong) Ms Byrne said she was always covered for floods in her home insurance policy. That only changed recently, when she was sent a renewal notice — the total cost was going to be more than $30,000 a year. It was no typo. The insurance company explained to her that a recent hydrology report altered Thargomindah's flood maps. With no way to pay it, she opted out of flood cover. Now, as she rummages through what's left in her home, Ms Byrne wonders how the town is ever going to recover. Like many people in Thargomindah, Melinda Byrne's home wasn't insured against floods. (ABC News: Glenn Armstrong) Down the street at the Oasis Motel, owners Paul and Nancy Sparks are thinking the same thing. Early estimates suggest they've suffered nearly $1 million worth of damages and lost business. They're also not insured for floods. The couple said they considered the cover, but were told it would cost them an extra $25,000 per year on top of their $13,000 premium. Like most in the town, they couldn't afford to pay the exorbitant sum. Flood clean-up is underway at Oasis Motel, but owners Paul and Nancy Sparks wonder how they'll recover from such devastation without insurance coverage. (ABC News) Few people in Thargomindah were insured against floods before the waters ripped through — even some of the council assets weren't covered. Mayor John 'Tractor' Ferguson said the reason why is simple, "it's too expensive, full stop". He said many in his community could never afford to pay more than $20,000 per year for insurance; pointing out that, although house prices in the bush are cheaper, "insurance should be the same price" as the rest of Queensland. John 'Tractor' Ferguson is mayor of the Bulloo Shire, he says flood insurance in the bush shouldn't cost more than other parts of Queensland. (ABC News: Laura Lavelle) "It's rude. They take us for all mugs because we live in the bush," Mayor Ferguson said. He's called for the government to act on bringing down insurance prices in the outback, flagging the idea of a publicly-owned insurance company. With an upstream gauge out of action, Thargomindah had no way of knowing how much destruction a torrent of floodwaters would have on the outback community. The Insurance Council of Australia said worsening extreme weather conditions are putting upward pressure on premiums across the country. "Insurance prices risk, and where risk is high — as it is in Thargomindah — then premiums will reflect that," it said. It called for a $30 million investment over the next 10 years for the creation of a jointly-funded Flood Defence Fund to build disaster-resilient infrastructure. "Mitigation has proven to work," the Insurance Council of Australia said. "The construction of the flood levee in Roma in 2015 cost $15 million, protected 483 homes and 75 businesses, and reduced insurance premiums by an average of 34 per cent — with some premiums reduced by 75 per cent." The Insurance Council of Australia says flood mitigation has proven successful elsewhere. (Supplied: Bulloo Shire Council) The federal government was contacted for comment, but did not respond by deadline. Ms Byrne doesn't know the solution, but she's sure of one thing — "something has to change." "We all would have had [insurance] and we all wouldn't be in the positions that we are now," she said. "[With] the uncertainty of what our future holds." Ms Byrne says something needs to change. (ABC News: Laura Lavelle) Mayor Ferguson said he's concerned for his community and hopes that some residents won't choose to leave because they can't afford to rebuild. "If we lose them, we're not going to have the bush and we're not going to have what Australia stands for," he said. The mayor hopes locals won't decide to leave the outback community as a result of the extreme weather event. (ABC News: Laura Lavelle)

title: Coalition's tax-free lunch policy sidelined, mentioned just once in campaign
content: A Coalition policy to give businesses $20,000 in tax-free staff meals has been sidelined from the party's election campaign, with business figures admitting the policy was too easily panned, and party insiders saying it strayed from a focus on cost of living. The policy, announced in January as a "shot in the arm" for small to medium businesses and the hospitality sector, was mentioned once by leader Peter Dutton during the Liberal Party campaign launch speech — the first time it has been brought up in the first three weeks of his campaign. Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues The apparent decision not to actively campaign on the measure follows the Coalition's significant about-face on its work from home policy for the federal public sector, which saw Mr Dutton apologise and admit he made a "mistake". Mr Dutton has also faced criticism from Labor for moving nuclear power down his agenda, with the leader now referring to his energy policy as a "balanced energy mix" of "renewables, gas and nuclear", as the cost of living crisis forces parties to hone their messaging. The party's tax-free meals policy remains on the Liberal Party's website and rated a mention in Mr Dutton's budget reply speech in late March, but has been left off the "Priorities of a Dutton Coalition Government" document linked on the party's policy platform page. A Liberal politician said the policy was "not a cost of living measure" and therefore no longer a focus. The party's campaign headquarters did not respond to questions about the policy. Two senior business lobby group sources have also told the ABC a policy for tax-free lunches is "bad optics" and "too easily panned by Labor" in a cost-of-living crisis, while two Liberal backbenchers said voters were not mentioning the policy to them at all during campaign doorknocking. The Coalition unveiled a new small business strategy late on Good Friday, which also did not mention the tax-deductible meals policy, but which promises start-up small businesses new tax offsets, including the ability to pay tax on 25 per cent of their first $100,000 of income. Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen The rollout of the policy was messy, with the Coalition initially saying businesses could claim $20,000 in meal "and entertainment" expenses, excluding alcohol, leading Labor to pan the policy as a "farce", arguing bosses would use it to claim tax deductible golf trips. The Coalition soon clarified it was for meals only. In February, Treasurer Jim Chalmers asked the Treasury department to cost what Mr Dutton had announced, saying it would be a hit of at least $1.6 billion a year. The costings were quickly rejected by Shadow Treasurer Angus Taylor, who said Parliamentary Budget Office costings had estimated it would cost taxpayers around $250 million a year. Luke Achterstraat, chief executive of the Council of Small Business Organisations Australia, said it was sad the policy had been politicised. (ABC News: John Gunn) Chief executive of the Council of Small Business Organisations Australia, Luke Achterstraat, said he would have liked to have seen bipartisan support for the policy, which would see small business reduce their tax liability. "I think it's disappointing that, you know, the policy has been politicised and put into a sort of a faux class war," he said. "Rewarding staff, whether that's through breakfast or a lunch, or whether it is taking clients to a meal to win new business … that's all legitimate business expense and should be deemed so under the taxation arrangement." The Coalition has put more emphasis on its $30,000 instant asset write off for small businesses, which is more substantial than Labor's $20,000 cap. Jane Hume joked that the private sector might follow the Liberals in cracking down on work from home, but the party ran into trouble when voters came to fear the same. Mr Dutton has spoken more frequently in recent days about his nuclear plan, including during a trip to the regional New South Wales seat of Paterson, near where the Coalition has promised to turn the retired Liddell Power Station into a nuclear power plant. But it has been noted the leader has not visited a single proposed nuclear site to meet locals, with Mr Dutton explaining on Thursday that he "could not meet every Australian". The party ditched its policy that would have seen Commonwealth public servants in the office five days a week, not at home, after internal concerns that the policy alienated women. One Liberal MP told the ABC that appearing to outlaw working from home for public servants was a "silly idea" and was doing the party "massive harm". Labor has also backtracked on policies, wiping all mentions of a Makarrata Commission from its policy platform despite Prime Minister Anthony Albanese committing to establish the First Nations "truth-telling" body on the night he won the 2022 election. Mr Albanese told the ABC in March the money set aside had been re-prioritised to "economic empowerment". 1 / of 11 All fields are required unless marked optional. title: Trump says 'very good' trade deal will be made with China
content: Donald Trump says the US will strike a "very good" trade deal with China, as both countries remain locked in a tariff war. Several Asian countries have started negotiations with the US over his levy policy but despite facing the highest tariffs China has not. A White House website page states that some Chinese goods face a 245 per cent tariff in the US. Beijing has slapped a 125 per cent tariff on US imports. "I think we're going to make a very good deal with China," he said at the White House on Thursday, US time, sitting opposite Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni who was in Washington for talks on tariffs. Earlier, the US president said "big progress" had been made in negotiations with Japan on tariffs, after he met with the country's trade delegation this week. He provided no further detail about how close a trade deal may or may not be with Tokyo and later added he was in "no rush" to announce deals. "A Great Honor (sic) to have just met with the Japanese Delegation on Trade. Big Progress!" President Trump posted on social media. A photo of Japan's lead trade negotiator Ryosei Akazawa and Donald Trump at the White House was posted on X shortly after the meeting. (X: The White House) While Asia's major exporters to the US, including Japan, Vietnam and Taiwan open discussions with the Trump administration on tariffs, China is notably absent from the offices of the White House. Earlier on Thursday, he posted on social media that China "wants to meet!", despite Beijing showing no signs it wants to negotiate. China's President Xi Jinping has spent the week in South-East Asia, trying to rally support from neighbouring countries amid the tariff war. President Xi arrived in Cambodia on Thursday and said Cambodia should oppose "hegemonism" and "protectionism", echoing similar sentiments expressed in Malaysia and Vietnam earlier in the week. The US has said it was up to China to start negotiations, but that did not look likely. "The unilateral tariff increases were entirely initiated by the United States," He Yongqian, a Chinese commerce ministry spokesperson, told a weekly news conference. Ms He, quoting an old Chinese proverb said, "the person who tied the bell must be the one who unties it". While the trade war continues between the US and China, here's what we know about other countries at the negotiating table with the Trump administration. China digs in the trade war with the US, can Trump win? (Alicia Barry) Japanese negotiator Ryosei Akazawa met President Trump, Mr Greer and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in Washington on Wednesday, US time, with no detailed progress report detailed by either side. A second meeting is scheduled for the end of April. "The discussions ahead will not be easy, but the US president has expressed his willingness to give the highest priority to negotiations with Japan," Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba has said, adding that he was ready to meet President Trump himself. Japan's car industry is heavily reliant on the US market, with tariffs causing deep concerns for the future of its export market. (Reuters: Issei Kato, file photo) A close ally of Washington and the leading source of foreign investment in the United States, Japan faces an additional 24 per cent tariff on its exports as well as an existing 25 per cent automobile tax. Automobiles accounted for about 28 per cent of Japanese exports to the United States last year. Japan's Finance Minister Katsunobu Kato told Reuters he was "deeply concerned" about the global economic fall-out from the tariff chaos, saying they could have significant impacts on the country's economy. Vietnam didn't wait for President Trump to announce a 90-day pause on tariffs above 10 per cent to start discussions. The timing of his tour through South-East Asia couldn't be better for Xi, who is trying to court as many countries as possible to form a united diplomatic front against Trump's tariffs. Deputy Prime Minister Ho Duc Phoc had already been in Washington for several days before the start of the pause, meeting US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. Threatened with additional import duties of 46 per cent, Hanoi said it wanted to buy more US products, including defence equipment. The South-East Asian manufacturing powerhouse has the fourth-largest trade surplus with the United States, coming in at $123.5 billion ($193b) in 2024. To reach a compromise, Hanoi may have to overcome Washington's suspicion that Vietnam is helping China circumvent US tariffs. Is China using Vietnam as a proxy to bypass higher Trump tariffs? Taiwan said it held an initial video conference with US officials on April 11. President Lai Ching-te said the island, which hopes to protect its exporters from tariffs of up to 35 per cent, was "on the US government's first negotiation list". After the Trump administration exempted smartphones and semiconductors from tariffs, the president backtracked and warned no one was "getting off the hook". Washington is the main guarantor of Taiwan's security in the face of China, which claims the island democracy as its own. President Trump has not hesitated to link Washington's security relations with Taipei to the trade issue. About 60 per cent of Taiwan's exports to the United States are tech products, such as semiconductors. Under pressure, top Taiwanese chip maker TSMC has unveiled plans to invest a further $US100 billion ($156 billion) in the United States. "We will strive for a fair and competitive tariff for our industry," Taiwan's Economy Minister Kuo Jyh-huei said this week. Seoul has announced billions in dollars of aid for its semiconductor and automobile companies as a buffer against the tariffs. However, South Korea is also counting on talks, with Finance Minister Choi Sang-mok set to meet US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent next week. Kim Dae-jong, an economics expert at South Korea's Sejong University, said Seoul would need to "expand trade centred on the US and reduce our reliance on exports to China to less than half of current levels" to try and appease the Trump administration. Indonesia's Economy Minister Airlangga Hartarto is leading a week-long trade delegation to the United States that started on Wednesday. Chinese factories are trying to sell directly to American consumers on social media platforms in a bid to bypass the 145 per cent tariff hike imposed by Donald Trump. Jakarta, which is threatened with 32 per cent duties, plans to boost purchases of US products such as hydrocarbons to reduce its $17.9 billion ($28.3b) surplus with Washington. Thailand's Finance Minister Pichai Chunhavajira is travelling to Washington from Thursday, with Bangkok poised to commit to buying more US agricultural and energy products. Thai Prime Minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra said on Thursday that Bangkok has "strong offers" that Mr Chunhavajira will raise during negotiations on April 23. Singapore's Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong, said he spoke with Mr Greer, the US trade representative, on April 15 to explain the city-state's "unique status as a small open economy". "We just have to explain this and continue to explain this, and hopefully the US will better understand our situation," Mr Gan said. "We do have a trade deficit with the US." In Australia, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Canberra had made a proposal to the United States. "We'll engage diplomatically," he said during the ABC leaders debate with opposition leader Peter Dutton. He vowed to defend Australia's national interests in the face of the 10 per cent tariff in place. ABC/wires

title: One of Australia's biggest super funds is freezing services until June
content: Members of superannuation fund HESTA will be unable to move their money until June, in a planned outage affecting more than 1 million Australians. The industry super fund is changing its administration provider and first notified members of the move in February, but consumer advocates warn many will likely be caught out by the freeze on funds. "I expect there will be a large number of consumers that will find out for the first time that they can't access their service when they go to access them over the next seven weeks," Xavier O'Halloran, director of Super Consumers Australia, told ABC News. Director at Super Consumers Australia Xavier O'Halloran says super funds often fail to keep up-to-date contact information for customers. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine) "There's been information on their website and the media release, but I think where consumers are likely to be let down here is that we know superannuation funds often fail to keep up-to-date contact information on their members," Mr O'Halloran said. "And so have a really hard time in contacting them directly with relevant messages like this one." Half a dozen HESTA members contacted ABC News with concerns, some noting they had struggled to contact HESTA or withdraw funds leading up to the outage. Barbara Byng, who is living off regular superannuation withdrawals, said taking money from her superannuation account at the end of last month ahead of the freeze was "enormously stressful." Sydney retiree Barbara Byng is a member of HESTA. (Supplied) The retiree from Sydney said her funds arrived into her account late, after it took her three days to get through to an operator. "I know they're about to go offline … I was just more stressed about my money and also about whether my money was safe." She believes this was because lots of HESTA users were trying to withdraw money before the shutdown period. "Why [didn't they] anticipate this when they're going offline for seven weeks?" Ms Byng said being unable to access her account for seven weeks was worrying. Are you an affected superannuation member? Do you know more? Contact reporter Adelaide Miller at miller.adelaide@abc.net.au HESTA manages the funds of 1.05 million people, worth $88 billion, but from earlier this week members have been unable to access most services, including online accounts. Super contributions and investment switches won't be processed until June, and withdrawals and claims are also unavailable until then. Insurance claims, including death, terminal illness, total and permanent disability and income protection, will not be actioned until service resumes, unless they had already commenced, the HESTA website states. Given the recent cyber attacks on funds, including AustralianSuper, and share market volatility after tariff announcements, Mr O'Halloran said "people are rightly worried". "But I'd also urge a bit of caution around times of market volatility, about making big switches." Around half of Australians' superannuation balances are invested in global and local stocks, meaning the tariff-induced market ructions are hitting super savings. Here's why experts say it's not time to panic. The outage is because HESTA is transferring its member account services over to a new provider, GROW Inc. When announcing the change in late February, chief executive Debby Blakely described it as "the largest technology project in HESTA's 38-year history". A HESTA spokesperson said income stream payments falling in April or May will be paid early, and regular payment schedules will resume from mid-May. Only urgent payments may be processed, with lump sum payments of up to 80 per cent of balances able to be made. "The safety and security of members' accounts is paramount as we transition to a new provider of administration services," the spokesperson for the fund said. "Shifting to this new technology platform brings the opportunity to develop more personalised experiences for members, making it easier for them to manage their super. While HESTA said it is changing administrator providers to improve services for members, Mr O'Halloran said it reflects "a real underinvestment in services." "These kinds of delays are due to a lack of strategic vision about what superannuation funds are there to deliver, and that's good customer service to consumers," he said. In March, the Australian Securities and Investment Commission (ASIC) issued a rebuke of the superannuation sector's handling of death benefit payouts. Australia's corporate watchdog calls on superannuation funds to overhaul the way they deal with death benefit claims. The corporate watchdog called on funds to overhaul the way they deal with claims, noting excessive delays, poor customer service and ineffective claims handling. ASIC's review covered 10 funds, including HESTA, which are collectively responsible for 38 per cent of all member benefits in superannuation funds regulated by the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority. It excluded industry giants AustralianSuper and Cbus due to ongoing legal action. Earlier this month, a number of Australian superannuation funds were hit with suspected cyber attacks, with members of one fund losing $500,000 between them in retirement savings. Hostplus, Rest, AustralianSuper and Australian Retirement Trust are among the providers targeted. The attack has been called unsophisticated, and prompted calls for superannuation funds to urgently implement multi-factor authentication. AustralianSuper was questioned by its own clients about a security weakness in its accounts before cybercriminals stole hundreds of thousands of dollars in retirement savings. Customers told ABC News they had asked for multi-factor authentication (MFA) on their accounts but were rebuffed — one of them just weeks before the cyber attacks. The Financial Services Council, the industry peak body that develops standards, is recommending mandating MFA systems for superannuation companies by July 2026. Labor is pinning its hopes on a former NBL player to win the far north
content: It's hard to reach new heights when you're already six-foot-10. But if former professional basketball player Matt Smith manages to turn the federal electorate of Leichhardt red on May 3, he might just manage it. Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues The seat has long been in Labor's sights, despite it having been in Liberal National Party (LNP) hands for the better part of 30 years. Speaking with people around the electorate, this appears in large part due to Warren Entsch, who has held the seat for each of those terms but one, and is now retiring (again). When Mr Entsch was first elected, Mr Smith was a 16-year-old kid. Now, the former Cairns Taipans player is in his mid 40's with teenagers of his own, and pondering if he can be the one to get Leichhardt in Labor's column. "There's the question: Is this a Warren Entsch seat, or is this an LNP seat?" he says. Next month, Labor and the Coalition will find out. Leichhardt is enormous. Stretching from Cairns to Cape York and beyond to the Torres Strait Islands, traversing it is no easy task. And because of it vastness, there's a wide variety of issues on the agenda, but chief among them for many is the rising cost of, well, everything. But while the seat is more than twice the size of Tasmania, the majority of voters live in the suburbs of Cairns. And that's where both Matt Smith and LNP candidate Jeremy Neal are door knocking and street stalling throughout the campaign — trying to convince voters that even if there won't be another Warren, they can fill that Entsch-shaped hole. When we meet Mr Neal at a suburban Coles on a hot Monday afternoon — is there any other kind in Cairns? — he's with his wife and son manning their street stall. Former paramedic Jeremy Neal seeks to fill the shoes of retiring MP Warren Entsch. (Brendan Mounter/ABC News) It's a modest affair, but he says most people are up for a chat, especially out the front of one of the big two supermarkets. "I mean, you go in there, it seems to be no less than $50 a bag by the time you grab a couple of things," he says. Though while he criticises the supermarket duopoly — something the N (Nationals) in the LNP are threatening to unpick — he won't be drawn on whether parties should accept their campaign donations. But, he says food insecurity is the sort of thing that made him get into politics, after more than a decade as a paramedic and a brief stint on council. "The first real instance where I went 'wow, something's wrong' was when we (the paramedics) went to this mum, and she was having whatever issue early in the morning … she was crook, and we were trying to treat her and she was madly trying to get her kids ready for school so they can make breakfast club." Mr Neal says he's fighting "pretty bloody hard" against Labor's attempt to take Leichhardt. (Brendan Mounter/ABC News) Mr Neal highlights rising grocery prices as a key concern for the electorate, as did Mr Smith. Two days after we interviewed Mr Neal, a dossier of his old tweets resurfaced. In the now-deleted missives, Mr Neal labelled China "a grub of a country" after a Chinese foreign ministry spokesman posted a fake picture depicting an Australian soldier murdering an Afghan child. Mr Neal's campaign suffered a setback this week after old tweets resurfaced. (Brendan Mounter/ABC News) He also reportedly claimed Victorian COVID restrictions would have made fascist Italian dictator Benito Mussolini proud and that "feminists helped kick Trump out only to ruin 19,000,000 women's lives in Afghanistan under Biden." On the day the tweets surfaced in the media, he apologised and said they were a product of stress he was experiencing working as a paramedic during the COVID pandemic. But those comments may still sit uncomfortably with Entsch backers in Cairns, whose previous local member was known for taking a progressive stance on issues like same-sex marriage, even when it clashed with his party. Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's campaign bus rolled into town on Thursday, a signal of Labor's confidence that this seat is up for grabs. Describing Mr Neal as a "shocker and a cooker", Mr Albanese added salt into the wound, saying Mr Entsch did not support Mr Neal being preselected as the candidate for Leichhardt. This election season politicians have tried to sell you the world. The team at Gruen isn't about to buy it. They've taken a big swing at the election, showing you how the democracy sausage is made, all the sizzle and none of the meat. But Mr Neal insists Mr Entsch has been supportive of his candidacy, even acting as part-time tour guide. "He dragged me up through the Daintree, up to Cooktown and introduced me to all these people," Mr Neal says when the ABC interviewed him earlier this week. "He's quite optimistic." So is Mr Smith, who senses a growing feeling of momentum for Labor. He announced funding for the rebuild of the Barron River Bridge with the prime minister standing beside him. The next morning, the government tried to capitalise on its tropical momentum with a small amount of funding for the Great Barrier Reef. The first thing you notice about Matt Smith is his height. The second thing you notice are his bright red trainers, which match the lettering on his canvas Labor tote. Labor's Matt Smith has been carting his pamphlets around Cairns for several months. (Brendan Mounter/ABC News) We meet in a small park in Manunda, where he's just come off another round off door knocking, and volunteers have stuck around for a chat. Despite it being only week two of the official campaign, Mr Smith and his team of scarlet-clad volunteers have been at this for months, spruiking Labor's Medicare urgent care clinics, housing development ambitions and asking potential voters what they want. Volunteers on Matt Smith's campaign say they feel hopeful their side of politics can take Leichhardt. (Brendan Mounter/ABC News) "It has been hot, there were days during January when I looked down at my phone, like, 'feels like 45' and you knock on the door, just like … 'please?'" he says. While Mr Smith is quietly positive, his potential future companions in Canberra are more openly hopeful. "We've got a really good story to tell," Mr Smith says, using a refrain that will be repeated by his colleagues many times over the coming days. But a good story doesn't pay the rent. Seeking to overcome a margin of three per cent, every vote counts for former Cairns Taipan player Matt Smith. (Brendan Mounter/ABC News) Mr Smith says one of Labor's 'good stories' in the region is housing, a key issue in an area where rental vacancy rates are low, holiday rentals are many, and affordable housing is scarce. He points to Cape York in particular. "A lot of investment went into the trunk infrastructure for some of those discrete communities out to Kowanyama, Pormpuraaw, Wujal Wujal and Seisa," he says. "We're getting those communities ready to expand and to deal with some of the overcrowding issues that have been so prevalent." He also takes aim at the opposition's policy on cutting migration, a major contributor to the Cairns economy, which relies on young migrants to staff bars and tourist attractions "We are heavily, heavily reliant on skilled workers, migrant skilled workers in medicine, in our hospitality, in our teaching, and we can't afford to have this," he says. Matt Smith's red sneakers have been getting a workout since he won preselection late last year. (Brendan Mounter/ABC News) "If you cut migration like that it is going to negatively affect the economy in Cairns, and not just Cairns, but up the cape as well." Basketballer Mr Smith is used to taking long shots, but with the margin on Leichhardt close, is he nervous? "I feel pretty good, I try not to worry too much about the outcome and worry very much about the process," he says. "And that's a throwback to my time playing sport, you worry about the things that you control and the things that you can do, and everything else after that is up to the gods." 1 / of 11 All fields are required unless marked optional.
