title: 'Sorry for my cynicism': Salmon boss says he has no confidence in new fishery
content: The chief executive of salmon producer Tassal last year told the Tasmanian government he did not have any confidence in the Department of Natural Resources and Environment (NRE) delivering a proposed sardine fishery. An email released under Right to Information laws shows in June last year CEO Mark Ryan wrote to Tasmanian Business, Industry and Resources Minister Eric Abetz and NRE's then-acting general manager of marine resources, Will Joscelyne. "Sorry for my cynicism but I had the same process … relayed to me in 2022 and in 2023 … with the fishery to commence in late 2023," he said. "So it would be very helpful for me to understand some key timelines within the process please. Last November, the Tasmanian government announced its intention to set up a new commercial sardine fishery — the first new fishery in state waters in decades. In the email exchange, Mr Ryan said he hoped there was "a pathway forward for this fishery — its too important for Tasmania". A study in 2023 identified a sardine population stretching from NSW's south coast to Tasmania could rival the biggest fishery in Australia — and there's a push to make use of it. "I understand that institutional investors have contacted government about the opportunity — well, we know where that has the abalone, rick [sic] lobster and other segments since their involvement," he said. "To develop a fisheries [sic], you need to catch, process and sell the products … not just do a one off transaction and own 'rights'." Mr Ryan also asked if Tassal would be included in industry consultation with the government regarding the fishery's development. A report produced by the Institute of Marine and Antarctic Studies (IMAS) in 2023 noted that locally sourced sardines have "demonstrable ecological and socio-economic benefits" as a source of fish food for Tasmania's salmon industry. "The absence of a large-scale small pelagic fishery off Tasmania limits the opportunity for the salmon industry to obtain the tens of thousands of tonnes of forage fish that it needs annually from a sustainable local source," it said. Responding to questions about the Right to Information email, a Tassal spokesperson told the ABC the company "has no plans to participate in the proposed Tasmanian sardine fishery". Tassal is owned by Canadian seafood company Cooke and is one of three major international salmon aquaculture companies that operate in Tasmania, along with Brazilian multinational JBS (Huon Aquaculture) and New Zealand's Sealord (Petuna). Overseas, only a small amount of sardine goes to human consumption, with much if it being turned into food for other fish. (Adobe Stock: Andrea Izzotti) The Tasmanian government's Fishing Tasmania website says the sardines caught in any future fishery could be used for "high-value human consumption, recreational and commercial bait, pharmaceuticals, fish oil and fish meal". NRE's development guidelines for the fishery state that it could "allow access to a continued supply of sustainably caught Tasmanian seafood to national and local markets". Those black, circular things floating in the water off the Tasmanian coastline? They are salmon farms. Here is how many there are — and who owns them. "As a sardine fishery will produce a range of grades of product, it will be important that these products are all utilised in an economically sustainable way both to maximise the benefits of the fishery and minimise wastage," the guidelines read. An NRE spokesperson said the development guidelines would "inform the development of a fishery management plan". "The creation of rules and regulations for a new sardine fishery would involve standard processes, including statutory public consultation, which is expected to occur later this year," they said. New study confirms potential to establish a large Tasmanian sardine fishery The ABC first reported on attempts to access the fishery in 2014. It was not until November 2024 that the Tasmanian government officially announced it was investigating a new commercial fishery. Since then, community consultations and information sessions were held across the state regarding the fishery's development. The exact size and location of the fishery, and the overall catch limit, have not yet been determined. However, the Tasmanian government has indicated a commercial harvest level of a maximum of 15 per cent could be initially applied, based on research provided by IMAS. The Tasmanian government wants to establish a commercial fishery to exploit the south-eastern sardine resource. (Supplied: IMAS) The estimated size of the sardine biomass in Bass Strait is roughly 210,000 tonnes, according to the latest report released last December by the Fisheries Research and Development Corporation (FRDC). The report found the sardine stock could be harvested at an ecologically sustainable level, but the recent discovery of the size of the resource meant a "precautionary approach" should be taken when developing the fishery. Stateline report on potential for sardine fishery in Bass Strait (Clancy Balen)

title: Dutton's 'struggle street' seat the most marginal in Queensland
content: It's Queensland's most marginal seat, and it's held by the man vying to be Australia's next prime minister. The electorate of Dickson, north-west of Brisbane, is part outer-suburban mortgage belt, part rural. Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues Opposition Leader Peter Dutton — who's held it since 2001 — clings on by a margin of less than 2 per cent. Peter Dutton became the opposition leader in 2022, but has held the seat of Dickson since 2001. (ABC News: Matt Roberts) Labor, the Greens, and a new "teal-like" independent are all in a race to unseat the potential prime minister. So, is Mr Dutton in trouble? "Peter Dutton is safe in that seat," political commentator and Griffith University Professor Paul Williams says. "If the Labor Party couldn't pick up the seat of Dickson at the height of Anthony Albanese's popularity in 2022, they're certainly not going to pick it up now." An election sign promoting Opposition Leader Peter Dutton in the seat of Dickson. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi) In fact, Mr Williams says it may no longer be marginal after May 3. "Dutton should get a big swing to him and turn that seat into a fairly safe seat over five or six points," he says. Professor Williams describes Dickson as a "struggle street" seat. The vast electorate takes in the outer Brisbane mortgage belt, western rural localities, and large parts of Moreton Bay. Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen Mr Dutton lives at Dayboro, a rural country town to the west, where he polled strongly at the last election. The mortgage belt suburbs span from Kallangur down to Arana Hills, which largely split their vote between Labor and the Coalition. At the Old Petrie Town Markets, down the road from Mr Dutton's home, cost of living, interest rates, jobs and the environment are front of mind for many voters. The markets are situated in the electorate Peter Dutton has held for more than 20 years. (ABC News: Alex Brewster) Sharon Hill-Lavender juggles two jobs and began selling at the markets eight years ago. "We run at a loss here, but it's our dream, so that's why we do it," she says. "Cost of living has changed everything. No-one's got money for fun stuff, which is a shame because that's what my business is." Sharon Hill-Lavender at the Old Petrie Town Markets. (ABC News: Alex Brewster) Labor hopeful Ali France is confident her third consecutive attempt to unseat the Coalition leader will be a success. "People are getting to see Peter Dutton up close since he's become opposition leader, and I think they're seeing that he doesn't represent the things they need in this community," she says. Ali France is the Labor candidate for the seat of Dickson at the upcoming federal election. (ABC News: Alex Brewster) The former journalist and para-athlete says campaigning here for the past seven years has given her a deep understanding of what matters to the community. "My issues are their issues. I'm a single mother, I have a disability, I have a mortgage, I'm struggling with the cost of living," she says. Labor is certainly campaigning like it believes it can take Dickson, with the prime minister and a slew of frontbenchers visiting during the campaign. Ali France is confident her third consecutive attempt to unseat the Coalition leader will be a success. (ABC News: Alex Brewster) How much of this is tactical compared to real winning confidence is unclear. Also in the ring for another bout is Greens' candidate Vinnie Batten, who garnered 13 per cent of the vote in 2022. Vinnie Batten is the Greens candidate in Dickson. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi) Independent Ellie Smith is hoping to do the same as teal candidates who have unseated Coalition strongholds interstate. Despite receiving financial backing from Climate 200 — the major fundraising group behind many teal campaigns — Ms Smith dubs herself a "maroon". The first-timer has a background in environmental management, and worked with anti-coal group Lock The Gate. Ellie Smith is an independent candidate for the seat of Dickson at the upcoming federal election. (ABC News: Mark Leonardi) "There's a lot of sentiment out in the community against both of the major parties," she says. "They feel neglected by both parties, and they like the idea of having an independent representing them. "The big challenge is getting the recognition out there into the community over a short period. Peter Dutton has been here for 24 years, and my campaign started in January." Despite receiving financial backing from Climate 200, Ms Smith dubs herself a "maroon". (ABC News: Mark Leonardi) Signs promoting Mr Dutton have been swapped out for attack ads, claiming Ms Smith is a Green in disguise — suggesting the Liberals are more worried about her than Labor. Mr Williams says a teal-like candidate has "zero chance". "Queensland is not New South Wales and Victoria. It's a very different political culture, and there's no appetite for teal politics, at least outside of downtown Brisbane. "The seats the teals would have done well [in] are Brisbane, Ryan, and Griffith, but they're already sewn up by the Greens." In statement to the ABC, Mr Dutton says "he'd never taken the people of Dickson for granted". Peter Dutton has held the seat since 2001. (AAP: Alan Porritt) "As opposition leader, I have to balance responsibilities, but people in Dickson know I've always been accessible, I've always listened, and I've always delivered. "My priority is making sure our community gets the support it needs, and I'll keep working hard to do exactly that." If Mr Dutton were to be unseated, it would be a historic loss — an opposition leader has never lost their seat at a federal election. Hear the latest election news as it happens on the Election Central Playlist. Only on the ABC listen app. Two prime ministers have gone down with their losing party on election night — John Howard in 2007, and Stanley Bruce in 1929. "We've also seen premiers lose their seat. The Queensland premier, Campbell Newman, lost his seat in ... 2015," Mr Williams says. In the unlikely event Mr Dutton were to lose, replacing him as Coalition leader would take just a "matter of minutes", he adds. "That position would be declared vacant after the election, and they would have to hold a meeting of the surviving caucus members, whether the LNP is in majority government, minority government, or in opposition," Mr Williams says. "There doesn't seem to be an heir-apparent at this stage, but one would think that the most logical leader would be the deputy leader that they have today, which is Sussan Ley." 1 / of 11 All fields are required unless marked optional. title: 'I can't get out': How Andrea's country home dream turned to nightmare
content: When Andrea Martens set out to build a home to retire to in the Victorian countryside, she imagined enjoying the rural serenity with a home loan almost paid off and her troubles behind her. While a local builder would construct the home, she had a hand in its design, helping craft plans that would maximise enjoyment of the beautiful surroundings. Five years later, the building is neither a finished home nor an active construction site, but sits in limbo, barely touched after the builder left amid a deepening dispute in December 2020. Ms Martens says her dream has become a painful nightmare due to alleged defects. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson) "This is the part of the house that hurts the most: my beautiful kitchen I can't use," Ms Martens said as she stepped into the house on a recent visit. Ms Martens and her partner first brought a detailed complaint to Victoria's building watchdog in the second half of 2020, asking it to engage with their surveyor to work through about a dozen alleged potential problems at the site. In its initial response, the Victorian Building Authority (VBA) reviewed documents and photos before concluding the surveyor had acted appropriately in its attempts to resolve the potential non-compliances. Ms Martens alleges issues with the slab are among the defects at her home. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson) The authority encouraged the couple to raise other issues in further complaints, including one with Domestic Building Dispute Resolution Victoria. But it closed the detailed complaint they had already made. The incomplete home in regional Victoria was where Ms Martens had hoped to retire. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson) It was 2021 before the VBA inspected some of the site and about another year before it began formally investigating other practitioners (due in part to COVID-era delays and resourcing issues), but it warned the Martens any disciplinary action would only go so far. "I reiterate that the VBA outcomes will not resolve any outstanding building issues at the site or lead to compensation for damages," wrote an investigator, who encouraged them to pursue contractual issues before VCAT. Ms Martens says her heart breaks each time she visits the unfinished home. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson) Ms Martens's experience is one of several laid out in an independent review of the building watchdog released in November last year. Many of them sought help with defective or half-finished homes but were failed so badly that the release of the report detailing their experiences triggered a major overhaul of the VBA. The Martens have asked the state government for compensation to help finish their home. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson) Ms Martens's allegation, based on an expert report, that there are major defects in her home's slab, framing and roofing are yet to be tested. A VCAT compensation case the Martens brought in late 2021 has moved so slowly the presiding member recently described its pace as glacial. In the meantime — with rent, a mortgage and legal costs pushing her closer to financial ruin — Ms Martens has appealed to the state government for compensation over what she called the severe negligence of the VBA. The review released in October 2024 was only the latest report to confirm the state's critical building regulator was facing major defects of its own. Co-authored by lawyer and building regulation specialist Bronwyn Weir, it said poor building work standards and unethical conduct had flourished on the watch of an unresponsive watchdog that took a narrow scope to complex complaints. Complainants who were suffering life-altering financial and emotional stress as their savings and super balances depleted were described as "emotional" or "stirring up trouble" in internal documents. Matthew Bell says many homeowners tend to give up before they start a claim. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson) By statute, the VBA's role focuses on matters like builder registration and the enforcement of standards, according to University of Melbourne construction law expert Matthew Bell. He said that remit could fall short of community expectations of strong protection from a well-resourced regulator. That can leave homeowners seeking help for shoddy work through other avenues, including potentially lengthy lawsuits in complex legal areas against builders whose livelihoods are at stake, the academic said. "What we do see is that well-resourced and resilient homeowners can often get a result in VCAT if they take it all the way," he said. "But there's so many places along the line where people just give up, and quite often it's before they've even started a claim. "They'll just say, 'I'll put up with that' and just move on, or get it fixed myself, or — probably even worse — fix it myself." The Martens are one of at least two households featured anonymously in the review to have asked the state government for financial support while complicated matters progress before VCAT. The second, who for privacy reasons wanted to use the pseudonym Anne, is also embroiled in a years-long saga over an unfinished home and a terminated contract. Anne* has made several complaints to the watchdog over the years. (Supplied) Anne told the ABC she made an initial four complaints to the watchdog, hoping it would use rectification powers to resolve alleged defects such as waterproofing problems that had emerged during the build. "We thought, I suppose, that the VBA was our saviour. They would be the ones to make it right," she said. Anne lodged a further 13 complaints over the following years. While her builder and his company's registrations were cancelled in relation to a number of sites earlier this year (a decision being appealed before VCAT), her home was still incomplete after seven years, she said. The Weir review was one initiative taken by the VBA's new CEO, Anna Cronin, who is overseeing cultural transformation at the agency and of whom complainants speak highly. Anna Cronin has been overseeing a cultural transformation of the building regulator. (ABC News) Letters seeking participation in the review did not specifically mention compensation, but both women believed the government should offer support as the VBA missed critical early opportunities to intervene. "And if there were any other issues, the builder would've known that the VBA would've been on top of it," Anne said. The report found most participants believed years of expensive legal action seeking compensation could have been avoided had the VBA "done its job", but noted regulatory action alone may not have solved their issues. The government's response to both complainants and, later, the ABC's questions focused largely on series of consumer-focused building reforms but did not specifically address the question of compensation. Legislation before parliament will replace the VBA with a new Building and Plumbing Commission, bringing insurance, regulation and dispute resolution under the one roof. The watchdog would have powers to direct builders to fix defects after occupants move in, create a "first-resort" building insurance scheme and require a bond deposit from certain developers, as in New South Wales. "It could really be a game changer as these measures have been in New South Wales: an integrated regulator, so a one-stop-shop," Associate Professor Bell said. "Even at that first stage for consumers, where you are tearing your hair out and you don't know what to do, if you can at least ring somebody and the phone is answered by a regulator who can then give some advice, pathways, that's very, very helpful." Water pooling at Ms Martens's home. (Supplied) Since its review started, the VBA said it had suspended, cancelled or disciplined seven practitioners involved and is progressing investigations of more than a dozen others, including some involved in Ms Martens's home. "Some investigations remain open – these are highly complex cases with extensive documentation and we’re working hard to achieve the best possible outcomes,” a spokesperson said. In late February, Housing and Building Minister Harriet Shing also thanked Ms Martens for participating in the Weir review, saying "the courage and commitment of case study contributors including yourselves have played an important part in informing the VBA reform process". There's been extensive correspondence between the Martens and the VBA. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson) The minister's response was among dozens of emails and letters exchanged between the Martens and various authorities over the past five years reviewed by the ABC for this story. Despite the extensive correspondence, the report and a formal apology from Ms Cronin, the Martens fear little has materially changed their situation. One expert estimate said the couple would need to find $670,000 to repair their home, a figure Ms Marten said adds to many tens of thousands of dollars already spent on legal fees and expert reports. Five years after first complaining to the VBA, Andrea Martens' home is still unfinished. (ABC News: Jesse Thompson) Ms Martens described the litigation as a second full-time job, one that comes at a personal cost by day, then keeps her up at night. "I can't get out of it," she said.

title: 'Gambling without limits': How video games are fleecing kids
content: Kids playing popular video games are being targeted with harmful design tactics including gambling-like features, which fleece them of cash and trap them in gameplay, according to a new report. As a result, children were being enticed to play more and spend more, said Erin Turner, CEO of the Consumer Policy Research Centre (CPRC). "What really worries me is when we see these gambling-like features in games targeting children," she said. Researchers from CPRC and Monash University — who authored the report — looked at 20 "dark patterns" which they say deceived and manipulated gamers. The design features were not in all games but 95 per cent of adult players surveyed had come across them and 83 per cent had suffered negative consequences. Do you have a story to share? Email Specialist.Team@abc.net.au Merrick Wolski is a 17-year-old gamer who has tried to take action against gaming companies that use addictive features. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd) Of most concern was children being exposed to gambling-like features such as "paid loot boxes" and prompted to buy items with in-game currencies. Paid loot boxes require a player to pay to open a mystery box in the hope they receive something valuable in the game. Unlike the electronic gaming industry which has strict rules on how much money is returned to a player who pulls the lever of a pokie machine — Ms Turner said there's nothing forcing video game developers to even disclose that. "This is gambling without limits and real manipulation," she said. Researchers said paid loot boxes had the potential to "normalise and encourage" monetary gambling among children and young people. After questioning 800 adult gamers about their concerns, the researchers found close to half spent more money than they intended, felt pressured into buying something or made a purchase by accident, they found. Merrick Wolski spends his downtime playing and designing games on Roblox. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd) They said Australian regulators had failed to keep pace with the industry's rapid expansion — with Australians spending an estimated $4 billion annually — and a substantial overhaul was needed to keep children and adult gamers safe. Ms Turner has called for a classification system that alerts parents and players to what harmful features are included in games. However, the Australian industry body, the Interactive Games and Entertainment Association, has argued these design features were different from gambling because the items couldn't be cashed out for real money. Merrick Wolski says gaming can quickly become "toxic". (ABC News: Michael Lloyd) Brisbane gamer Merrick Wolski, 17, spends his downtime playing and designing games on Roblox — a gaming platform which allows players to create their own games. Roblox boasts 380 million users, with 42 per cent of them under the age of 13. "I like making games on the platform, because I find that fun. I like coding and modelling and stuff like that," Merrick said. Roblox earned US$3.6 billion in revenue in 2024, much of it coming from in-game transactions using the platform's currency Robux. A recent study found Australian players between the ages of four and 18 spent an average of 137 minutes a day on the platform. While Merrick is passionate about gaming he says it can quickly become "toxic". "A lot of games promote gambling content to their audiences… where you can pay to spin a wheel for different prizes." Merrick Wolski estimated over the last year he'd spent around $150 on Roblox. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd) "I found myself at times when I spin and I'm just that close to it landing on the best reward on the wheel, and it goes, 'Oh, would you like another spin for 50 Robux'." "Why not? And then I'm 10 spins down." Merrick estimated over the last year he'd spent around $150 on Roblox. "It doesn't feel great hearing that number out loud." Some of the adult gamers surveyed expressed similar concerns. "Ninety-nine per cent of them are made to create an emotional vortex of dopamine-chasing people, especially young men with a lot of anger, get sucked down, constantly chasing positive reinforcement through micro-transactions and wins while in reality hating the experience," an 18-year-old male said. Not a gamer but want to understand the lingo? Click here to see our breakdown. Researchers singled out the popular online game Stumble Guys for criticism due to its use of "trick language". The game which featured animated characters racing to the finish is marketed to kids but had complex calculations for a "Super Gem Sale" that would be difficult for many to understand, especially children. Roblox is one of the most popular platforms in the world, but there are increasing concerns over the ability for users to message each other directly through games. "It has features that look like gambling: a wheel that for anyone who's walked into a casino will look similar to a roulette wheel," Ms Turner said. "It's got randomised rewards, an overlay of fun, colourful graphics that are really about engaging children, and lots of push to spend." "There's no way we should be seeing these features in games rated for kids nine and over." In a statement the game's developer, Scopely, said age ratings were set independently by platform app stores, they followed the store policies for advertising disclosures and parents were able to use controls to limit in-game spending and screen time. "In Stumble Guys' we take additional steps to limit access to certain features for our younger players, including disabling social media plug-ins and targeted advertising," it said in a statement. Laura is part of the Heads Up Alliance, a grassroots organisation supporting parents who want their kids to be smart-phone and social media free. (ABC News: Leonie Thorne) Globally, the industry earned revenue of approximately US$223 billion in 2023 — with around $125 billion due mostly to micro-transactions, in-game ads and product placement, the report found. Ms Turner said some players spent thousands of dollars on "micro-transactions" The gamers surveyed revealed they rarely tried to get redress when something went wrong and when they did, they failed to receive help from the game developer or platform. That's something Merrick can relate to. He sent complaints to Roblox and the Australian Classification Board about gambling-like features in four games he was exposed to on the platform and believed could violate the platform's rules and breach the classification system. "They [Roblox] gave me a response that basically just said that there was nothing they could do about them." Jojo's gaming PC is in the lounge room so his parents can keep an eye on what he's doing. (ABC News: Leonie Thorne) The ABC put questions about Merrick's complaint to Roblox but it did not answer them. Roblox said safety was its "top priority" and it took action on reports of content not meeting guidelines or Australian requirements. Australia has just introduced new minimum classifications for games with gambling-like content. Games with in-game purchases linked to chance, including paid -loot boxes have an M rating and aren't recommended for children under 15. Those with simulated gambling are further restricted — rated R for adults over 18. However, Ms Turner was critical of the ratings only applying to new games and believed the definition of gambling-like content was too narrow. "It has to physically look like blackjack or poker, it has to look like a casino," she said. Laura says she tries to monitor her son Jojo's gaming. (ABC News: Leonie Thorne) Communications Minister Michelle Rowland acknowledged some active games for children still contained these purchases because the changes were not retrospective, she said if those games eventually added new purchases or rewards they would need to be re-classified. Ms Turner wants the federal government to create an independent body that would adjudicate complaints, called a digital ombudsman — something that already exists for the telecommunications and finance sectors. But she said that body would only be effective if consumer protections were strengthened — something the Albanese government said it is consulting on. Dangers still lurk for young social media users in chatrooms like Roblox (Mike Lorigan) University of Sydney research and game designer Mark Johnson said gaming companies had become incredibly skilled at "dodging and weaving" regulations. "Depending on the nature of the law, it might be as simple as just changing what something is called. So don't call it a loot box, call it something else," he said. Peak body, the Interactive Games & Entertainment Association (IGEA) said most games and platforms offered tools for parents and players to manage screen time, spending, interactions and access to content. It defended the classification system calling it "robust" and stating it provided "clear, age-appropriate guidance on game content, helping parents make informed decisions." title: Market meltdowns may have been a trial run, insiders warn
content: Are we nearly there yet? For anyone who has ever gone on a longish road trip with young children, the phrase will have been burned into the memory banks. It's also becoming the most frequently asked question from investors, most of whom have been seared by the tumult on global financial markets during the past month following US President Donald Trump's scorched-earth policy on international trade. While the past few days has seen calmness return to markets, many of the financial world's best minds fear further falls — and warn we're nowhere near the end, unless America backs away from its current policy. In last week's market chaos, traders turned their backs on US government bonds. Is Donald Trump destroying America's "exorbitant privilege"? JP Morgan chief Jamie Dimon, once a vocal Trump supporter, has shifted stance and called for the US to engage with China, concerned the trade war has begun to chip away at America's credibility. The US investment banking giant now puts the odds of a US recession at 60 per cent. Mike Wilson, the influential US stock analyst from rival firm Morgan Stanley, fears further upheaval while investors remain exposed to Mr Trump's unpredictability, and the confusing and chaotic policy shifts. Tariff impositions, repeated backflips, conflicting messages, temporary reprieves, retaliatory tariff lifts in response to retaliation from China, backdowns on repeated assurances, and clearly amateurish arithmetic to justify the blanket protectionism have shattered investor confidence. It's also unleashed a growing global feeling of distrust in the very country that controls international finance through its global reserve currency, which, ironically, features the word 'Trust' on its banknotes. Currency traders haven't been treating the US greenback as a safe haven as they typically do in times of crisis. (Reuters: Shannon Stapleton) Many rapidly are coming to the same conclusion: this is a pivotal moment in history that could go horribly wrong. "To be honest, we haven't seen a reordering of the global economic system on this scale since the 1930s," Satyajit Das, one of Australia's foremost minds on financial and economic history, tells The Business.. "That was the Smoot Hawley tariffs, which certainly didn't cause the Great Depression, but were contributors to that. "Also on the other side, on the financial side, the excesses that have built up over the last 20 years are far greater than I've ever seen before." Satyajit Das is a former banker and financial risk analyst. (ABC News) It's a combination that deeply concerns Mr Das. "I don't know how bad it could be, but all I know, looking at history, is it could be very bad," he says. Last week, the upheaval spread to the US bond market, normally a safe haven for troubled investors. Instead of cash flooding into the system, as it ordinarily would in times of a stock market meltdown, it began departing. And rather than the US dollar strengthening, it began to decline as investors abandoned US debt markets and took their cash out of the country, a deeply disturbing turn of events. The US president was confronted by a force far greater than his own and the office he now holds overnight. The bond market, an arena where brutality knows no bounds and where the participants take no prisoners. Luke Yeaman, former deputy secretary of the Australian treasury and now the Commonwealth Bank's chief economist, believes the US president will persist with his tariff policies and argues there are genuine underlying problems the new administration is trying to address. Mr Yeaman says Mr Trump sees tariffs as the balm for a range of American economic ailments: fixing the budget and trade deficits, on-shoring industry and jobs, and improving national security. "Is it going to work? I think it's going to be very challenging," he tells The Business. "Achieving those goals is not easy, and the global economy is quite good at adjusting to changes in tariffs. "That said, the US is a huge market. It's still the largest consumer market globally, accounting for around 25 to 30 per cent of global demand. "So, opportunities to avoid these tariffs are going to be quite limited compared to previous trade wars, but it's clearly doing significant damage to the US economy in the meantime." Luke Yeaman is the new chief economist at the Commonwealth Bank, joining from the federal Treasury. (Supplied: Treasury) Mr Yeaman sees clouds ahead for the US and global economies. The speed and extent of the changes to the global system will impact the economy and markets for quite some time, he argues. And there's no guarantee that Mr Trump's goals will be achieved. Mr Das agrees that the US president appears to be attempting to address serious holes that have emerged in the American economy, its financial system and its place in the world. But he is stunned at the methods. From toy brands to fashion labels, some Australian firms are facing tariffs way above the 10 per cent "baseline". Company owners say they are not getting enough support as they navigate soaring tariffs to send Chinese-made goods into the US. Imposing tariffs is just one part of the program, Mr Das explains. Another option being looked at is a radical overhaul of the bond markets, forcibly converting some or all of them to perpetual bonds or 100-year bonds with low coupon or interest rates. Capital controls are also on the table, along with an idea to charge user fees for US Treasuries, representing a complete about-face in the way America has acted in the past half century. "This is part of a plan, and the problem is we really don't know how many bits of it are going to get actually implemented or when they'll be implemented, because what we've seen is the whole process is entirely erratic," he says. Want even more? Check out our tariffs topic page Both men believe Australia is relatively well placed to cope with the impending trade war but, as a trading nation with exports heavily weighted to China, it undoubtedly will feel the pinch if China's already troubled economy takes a hit. Mr Yeaman expects Beijing to ramp up stimulus if its economy starts to waver, in a bid to defend its five per cent growth target. "I think China will certainly spend a substantial amount to ensure that its economy remains strong during this period, and we also expect them to front-load that support as much as possible to ensure that the economy doesn't dip too much in the near term," he says. Should that occur, it will further shield Australia from the impact of a protracted global slowdown as a result of the trade war. The global trading system is being rewritten, says new CBA chief economist (Kirsten Aiken) For Mr Das, the potential for longer-term damage from the way in which Mr Trump has attempted to impose his policy are the biggest concerns. "The loss of trust in the US, the loss of trust in the basic way the US has operated, is very, very critical to understand," he says. He is concerned that, once lost, that trust will be difficult to win back, that the damage being incurred may be permanent. "Mark Twain once said that he didn't know about the people who were ruling us, whether they were very smart people putting us on, or whether they were imbeciles who really meant it, and we're still trying to work that out."

title: Pacific island nation gains access to electronic banking for first time ever
content: For the first time, the Pacific island nation of Tuvalu has access to electronic banking after its first ATM was unveiled. Officials called it a "transformative" era of modern banking in the remote archipelago. For years, the nation's 12,000 residents have done all their banking in cash, with workers enduring long lines to withdraw their wages from the bank each pay day. Now they will be able to withdraw money at the swipe of a card, with five ATMs and 30 point-of-sale terminals installed. General manager of the National Bank of Tuvalu, Siose Teo, said it was a "great achievement" and "transformative switch" that was many years in the making. Prime Minister Feleti Teo said it was a "significant milestone" with a "noble objective". Dignitaries gathered in front of the ATM, on the main island of Funafuti, to mark the occasion with a chocolate cake. "It will definitely break the barriers and introduce the people to modern and reliable banking services," said Nisar Ali from Pacific Technology Limited, which helped design the machine. With a landmass of just 26 square kilometres, climate-threatened Tuvalu is one of the smallest and most remote nations on the planet. An Asian Development Bank briefing from 2019 described its banking sector as "effectively unregulated". "Key reform priorities are instituting effective banking oversight and expanding access to financial services," it said. AFP/ABC

title: US and Japan aim for deal on tariffs as Donald Trump joins talks
content: US President Donald Trump says he will join negotiations with Japan on tariffs, after both countries expressed confidence in striking a deal. President Trump issued a 90-day pause on his 24-per cent tariffs on Japan last week, but a 10 per cent tariff remains in place. Japan is the biggest investor into the United States and a close strategic and economic ally. Japanese Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba has described the levy situation as "a national crisis." The White House meeting with Tokyo's envoy is being closely watched as a possible barometer for talks with other countries, as trade officials line up to negotiate over Mr Trump's punishing tariffs. "Japan is coming in today to negotiate Tariffs, the cost of military support, and 'TRADE FAIRNESS.' I will attend the meeting, along with Treasury & Commerce Secretaries," Mr Trump posted on Truth Social. "Hopefully something can be worked out which is good (GREAT!) for Japan and the USA!" Ryosei Akazawa, Japan's Minister for Economic Revitalisation, is responsible for the country's negotiations with the US on tariffs. (AP Photo: Hiro Komae, file) As he left for the White House meeting, Japan's lead tariff negotiator, Ryosei Akazawa, spoke of seeking a "win-win" outcome, while protecting Japanese national interests. "I am confident that we will be able to build a relationship of trust and conduct good negotiations that will lead to a win-win relationship," Mr Akazawa, Japan's economic revitalisation minister, told reporters. The Trump administration has imposed steep levies on imports of Japanese cars, steel and aluminium. Automaker Honda said on Wednesday it will shift production of its hybrid Civic model from Japan to the United States in June or July, but stopped short of saying the reason was US tariffs. The rationale behind the decision "is not a single issue", a Honda spokesperson said. "The decision is based on the company's policy since its foundation that we produce cars where the demand is." The vehicle, however, represents only a small part of the Japanese company's annual output. Donald Trump's tariffs have targeted Japan's car makers, causing significant concerns for the country's export economy. (Reuters: Issei Kato, file photo) Mr Akazawa will also hold talks with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer during his trip. Purchases of US defence hardware and natural gas from Alaska could be up for negotiation, analysts said. The minister, who studied at a US university and is close to Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba, said he wants to "protect our national interests" in the talks with Mr Bessent and Mr Greer, who are "fond of Japan". The Daiwa Institute of Research warned that Trump's reciprocal tariffs could cause a decline of 1.8 per cent in Japan's real GDP by 2029. US officials are also set to hold talks with South Korea and others, but Stephen Innes at SPI Asset Management called the discussions with Japan a "canary in the tariff coal mine". "If Japan secures a deal — even a half-baked one — the template is set. If they walk away empty-handed, brace yourself. Other nations will start pricing in confrontation, not cooperation," he wrote in a newsletter. And "don't forget the elephant in the vault: Japan's still the biggest holder of US Treasuries. And that, my friend, is a whole lot of leverage", he added. Chinese factories are trying to sell directly to American consumers on social media platforms in a bid to bypass the 145 per cent tariff hike imposed by Donald Trump. Top Japanese officials including Mr Ishiba have brushed aside claims that Tokyo may have deliberately created volatility in the US Treasury market to force Trump's pause of reciprocal tariffs, saying that is not what allies would do. Mr Ishiba called Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and French President Emmanuel Macron in separate calls on Wednesday to discuss the impact of US tariffs and China's retaliatory actions. Japan's prime minister told Mr Anwar that "the current situation is serious for Japanese companies operating in South-East Asian countries" and that he was willing to listen to the voices of South-East Asian countries, according to the foreign ministry. Mr Macron and Mr Ishiba also discussed the impact of the tit-for-tat US-China tariffs "on the global economy and the multilateral trade system," and "affirmed that it is in the common interest of Japan and France to maintain and strengthen a free and open international order based on the rule of law," the ministry said. Meanwhile, China has announced a new trade negotiator as it battles the US in an escalating trade war. Beijing announced that Li Chenggang had replaced Wang Shouwen. Mr Wang was involved in previous trade negotiations with the US in 2020. It wasn't clear what prompted the change. Prior to his appointment as trade negotiator, Mr Li spent about four-and-a-half years as China's ambassador to the World Trade Organization, the body that governs global commerce. Beijing has appealed to the body in its tariff dispute with the US. The timing of his tour through South-East Asia couldn't be better for Xi, who is trying to court as many countries as possible to form a united diplomatic front against Trump's tariffs. Earlier on Wednesday, China announced its economy expanded at 5.4 per cent annual pace between January and March, supported by strong exports. Its exports helped it achieve a 5 per cent annual growth rate in 2024, but analysts forecast the world's second largest economy will slow in coming months as US tariffs take effect. Asked about the possibility of talks with the US, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said America started the tariff war and China was only taking "necessary countermeasures" to defend its rights and interests. "If the US truly wants to resolve the issue through dialogue and negotiation, it should stop using maximum pressure and stop threats and blackmail. For any dialogue to happen, it must be based on equality, respect and mutual benefit," Mr Lin told a daily briefing. President Xi Jinping has been making the case that China is a source of "stability and certainty" in global free trade as he tours South-East Asia this week — implying that China is a more reliable trade partner than the US. On a visit to Malaysia, President Xi said "China and Malaysia will stand with countries in the region to combat the undercurrents of geopolitical … confrontation, as well as the counter-currents of unilateralism and protectionism." "Together we will safeguard the bright prospects of our Asian family," he added. ABC/wires

title: Darwin Airport records rise in passengers too drunk to fly
content: The Australian Federal Police (AFP) are warning travellers in Darwin to behave after an increase in passengers too drunk to fly attending the city's airport. Both the Darwin International Airport and the AFP have recorded a recent increase in "obnoxious, abusive" drunk passengers at the facility. In the past 12 months, AFP officers have turned away 30 intoxicated travellers from the gate and been called to remove a further six passengers from planes. Rob Porter, executive general manager of the Airport Development Group, which operates the Darwin Airport, said he anticipated the upcoming Easter holidays and peak tourism season could cause those numbers to rise. The AFP will be increasing its presence near the airport's terminal gates and licensed bars. (ABC News: Lillian Rangiah) "There's some really aggressive behaviour that's unacceptable at the airport, and for the safety of everybody who flies, we'd like to see that end," he said. "We want you to come and have a great holiday, but we don't want those obnoxious, abusive behaviours." In response, AFP officers will be ramping up their presence near the terminal gates and licensed bars leading into the busy period. While it may be easy to chalk up the over-intoxication to the Northern Territory's laid-back reputation, AFP Superintendent Greg Davis said he didn't believe that was the case. Rather, he said drinking at the airport was a particular problem in Darwin because so many flights occurred overnight. Sky-high airfares, poor flight times and unexpected scheduling changes have become standard in the NT capital of Darwin. That means it isn't uncommon for holiday-makers to head straight from the city's pubs and clubs to the airport. "Our observations are, particularly with the late-night flights, people have already been out — perhaps they're celebrating or [having] farewells with their family — then they come to the airport," he said. Airline staff have the authority to prevent a passenger from boarding a plane, if they are overly intoxicated and unruly. Once a person is on a plane, Superintendent Davis said it was an offence to disobey directions from the cabin crew. Refusal to comply can result in fines and charges. Greg Davis says late-night flights at Darwin Airport appear to be contributing to the rise in drunken behaviour. (ABC News: Lillian Rangiah) Superintendent Davis said in most cases, disruptive passengers ruined the experience for others. But in the worst cases, they could become threatening or violent towards staff. "Nobody wants to be threatened or sworn at, when they're just doing their job," he said.

title: Owner of Kalgoorlie's Super Pit completes $5bn gold takeover
content: Australia's biggest gold miner Northern Star Resources will add the country's largest new gold find to its portfolio after shareholders in De Grey Mining overwhelmingly voted in favour of a $5-billion takeover. The owner of Kalgoorlie's Super Pit gold mine announced its proposed acquisition of De Grey in December in a bid to get its hands on the six-million-ounce Hemi discovery in Western Australia's Pilbara region. A shareholder meeting held in Perth on Wednesday afternoon saw 99.64 per cent vote in favour of the deal, which valued De Grey at $2.08 per share. The takeover was effectively locked in after WA miner Gold Road Resources, which holds a 17.26 per cent stake in De Grey worth more than $1.03 billion, confirmed its intention on Monday to vote in favour. The Federal Court will be asked to approve the takeover next Tuesday. The takeover comes amid record gold prices and increasing activity in the mergers and acquisitions space. The Australian dollar gold price surpassed $5,000/oz for the first time on April 1, 17 years after it first topped $1,000/oz in January 2008. Driller Zakary Kelly working at De Grey Mining's Hemi project in 2020. (Facebook: Topdrill) De Grey chairman Simon Lill said no superior proposal had emerged in the five months since the takeover was announced. "We had regard to the costs and risks associated with continuing to develop the Hemi project on a standalone basis and assessed the scheme consideration against a range of valuation benchmarks," he told the meeting. Since the takeover was announced late last year the company's shares surged from $17.51 to $22.09 at Wednesday's market close. De Grey's stocks also rose from $1.52 prior to the takeover announcement to $2.61 at Wednesday's close. Mr Lill was asked at the shareholder meeting why De Grey's board was still recommending the takeover after its share price had surpassed the offer price. He said the De Grey shares were "inextricably linked" to Northern Star shares and noted the gold price had "moved significantly". Open pit manager Sean Davies at Kalgoorlie's Super Pit gold mine. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas) The Hemi deposit, about 85 kilometres from Port Hedland, was discovered in late 2019 but the scale of the find became clearer after a major exploration campaign that saw as many as 10 drill rigs turning in 2022. The cost of bringing Hemi into production is estimated at $1.3b, but a definitive feasibility study estimated payback on that investment could be achieved in less than two years. Those studies were conducted at an Australian dollar gold price of $2,700/oz, which has since almost doubled. The mine is slated to have an initial 12-year life and is expected to create 900 construction jobs and 600 operational roles. The addition of Hemi is expected to increase Northern Star's production from a forecast two million ounces next financial year to 2.5m ounces a year by 2028-29. Northern Star chief technical officer Steve McClare and Kalgoorlie Consolidated Gold Mines general manager Nick Strong at the Fimiston Mill. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas) Canaccord Genuity analyst Tim McCormack has said the addition of Hemi would notably reduce Northern Star's exposure to the Super Pit and Mt Charlotte operations, which are forecast to represent more than 40 per cent of its production from 2027-28. The Fimiston Mill at the Super Pit is half-way through a $1.5b, three-year expansion, which is set to increase production from the operation to 900,000 ounces a year towards the end of the decade. Northern Star's managing director Stuart Tonkin has described the Hemi project as a "low-cost, long-life and large scale gold mine in a tier-one jurisdiction". "The mill expansion is the largest Australian gold project in over 10 years and provides Northern Star with the unique opportunity to de-risk the Hemi development pathway through our experience and relationships with contractors and suppliers," he said.

title: 'Going to China with an empty suitcase': US shoppers swap tips to beat tariffs
content: Chinese factories are trying to sell directly to American consumers on social media platforms in a bid to bypass the 145 per cent tariff hike imposed on Chinese products by US President Donald Trump. From furniture and appliances to laundry pods and home decors, a growing number of Chinese sellers are showcasing their products in English on platforms like TikTok and Rednote, targeting US users with captions such as "factory price for Americans" and "no middleman, no mark-up". In another clip, a factory worker pitches ultrasonic cleaning products with the line, "Trust me, trust me, Chinese people never cheat," while a Guangzhou wholesaler claims through captions, "only 10 yuan for clothes that cost hundreds." Views on these posts often climb above 200,000, and some hit over half a million. Consumers talk about how cheap products manufactured in China are on TikTok. The trend has also sparked a wave of quirky, engaging content from American users, with one TikToker declaring, "finding out I can get 20 laundry capsules for a single dollar is making my brain short-circuit." Another joked about "reverse daigou" — referring to the practice of buying goods in China on behalf of American consumers. The viral spread of these videos allowed US consumers to directly compare prices and connect across borders, making visible the once-invisible layers of profit between factories and shelves. Many users said they realised how much middle businesses and US-based companies have inflated prices for everyday goods. Ashley Dudarenok, founder of China research firm ChoZan told the ABC that while consumers can save on small purchases, they're still required to declare goods upon re-entry to the US and pay duties if they exceed exemption limits of $800. She said the manufacturers' invite for American buyers to visit "captures attention", but was a symptom of trade tensions. Buyers are expected to save a significant amount of money by buying directly in China, but they will still pay the tariff on the cheaper products. What differentiates the current trade war with the 2018 US-China trade war is that Chinese businesses explored diversifying exports away from the US rather than looking at directly selling to US consumers. Chinese President Xi Jinping has landed in Malaysia after visiting Vietnam, as he tries to secure more support from South-East Asian neighbours amid the trade war with Donald Trump. The first US-China trade war hit a wide range of export-heavy Chinese sectors, particularly electronics, textiles, toys, furniture, and machinery. According to Chinese government figures, nearly 1.9 million jobs were lost in manufacturing, and industries heavily reliant on the US market — such as those producing low-cost consumer goods — were among the hardest hit. Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which make up the bulk of exporters in China, struggled to adapt to sudden tariff hikes and shipment delays. Back then, sellers tested drop shipping, online marketplaces, and influencer partnerships. This time, they are leaning on short videos, livestreaming, and personalised messaging to tap into Western markets. Now, many of those same industries are back in the spotlight. Household goods, soft furnishings, clothing, and basic electronics are once again bearing the brunt of the renewed tariffs. Factories in Guangdong, Zhejiang and Jiangsu provinces, which serve as major manufacturing hubs for these products, are among the most active in turning to platforms like TikTok and Rednote to promote direct-to-consumer sales. Experts say this model of bypassing intermediaries may help some exporters offload surplus inventory, but turning viral reach into sustained sales will require more than digital visibility — it depends on fulfilment logistics, payment systems, and consumer trust. Companies manufacturing in China caught out by US trade war | The Business | ABC News Dr Cheng Mingming, a digital marketing professor at Curtin University, believed the direct selling trend's implications are still symbolic. "Manufacturers in a way let US consumers realise that China provides a lot of cheap products that can meet their needs, so that they would feel that America's trade tariffs actually created inconvenience in their life. An industrial park where many clothing manufacturers are located, in Guangzhou. (Reuters: Casey Hall) "It might affect how US customers perceive tariffs and the policies that Mr Trump promotes, which argue tariffs are good for the US." Meanwhile, on Rednote, China's lifestyle-sharing platform, live streamers have launched promotions under hashtags like #saveourfactory and #shopinchina, urging local consumers to buy goods originally destined for US customers. Some sellers have filled their livestream sets with boxes bearing English shipping labels and barcodes, claiming they were forced to clear out warehouses because of the US tariffs. In a post, a seller offered steep discounts on small home appliances such as rice cookers, juicers and toasters, while lamenting that US companies "cancelled our contract". "Now it's all 90 per cent off!" the post wrote. Some users even urge Americans to visit China in person for cheaper shopping, playing on both sarcasm and a growing sense of cross-border frustration. "Come to China, buy direct, save big!" reads one post on TikTok, layered over footage of a factory floor. While the message may resonate with frustrated shoppers, experts say it is unlikely to bring a surge of American shoppers to Chinese factories. He added that the passport ownership rate in the US is relatively low compared to other developed countries, and international travel remains inaccessible for many. But the goal, he believes, is not necessarily tourism. Ms Dudarenok agrees the videos are a savvy marketing strategy. She said while it's unlikely they will inspire a wave of inbound shopping tourism, they could fuel greater demand for direct-to-consumer platforms. "Failure to declare goods or pay applicable duties could result in fines or confiscation of items."

title: Footwear chain Wittner hopes for new buyer after collapse
content: Australian footwear chain Wittner is the latest local retailer to face closure, with administrators appointed to manage the 113-year-old company. Its collapse follows the closure of Jeanswest stores and chains under company Mosaic, including Katies, Rivers and Noni B. This spate of insolvencies has already led to the loss of thousands of retail jobs nationally. Wittner has 20 standalone stores nationally, and 25 stores that sit inside the floors of department stores Myer and David Jones. Its management said while online sales were up this year, so too were its costs. Are you a Wittner worker? Confidentially email our journalists on terzon.emilia@abc.net.au or em.terzon@proton.me Wittner's administrators say they will keep the stores trading, while they try to sell or restructure the footwear business. "We understand the appointment of administrators will be particularly concerning to Wittner's employees," Deloitte's Sal Algeri said in a statement. "Please be assured that trade will continue on a business-as-usual basis as we conduct an urgent review of the group's finances. "And seek expressions of interest (EOI)s from parties interested in the sale or recapitalisation of this iconic Australian brand." Wittner was first founded as a mail order business back in 1912. Deloitte did not say how many employees it has today. The Retail and Fast Food Workers Union says it represents a small number of members at Wittner, and as well as some from Jeanswest and Mosaic. “It is an ongoing concern for us particularly because these boutique brands are heavily feminised," the unions Josh Callinan told ABC News.

title: Operator of trouble-plagued power plant 'understated the gravity' of explosion
content: The operator of the trouble-plagued Callide Power Station has conceded it "understated the gravity" of an explosion at the facility, and that there has not been "adequate reporting of serious issues". One of Central Queensland power plant's generators will be offline until the end of May after a blast on April 4. Energy Minister David Janetzki has come under fire for not disclosing the incident to the public during a major address days after it occurred. The CEO and general manager of the trouble-plagued Callide Power Station have left the company after an explosion earlier this month. On Sunday, the government accused operator CS Energy of failing to communicate how serious the incident was. Two senior employees have since exited the company. This week, the government released documents, including briefing notes, outlining communications from the operator following the incident. However, the opposition accused the government of a "cover up" after it was revealed CS Energy drafted two media releases about the explosion on the day of the incident and the day after, which were not publicly issued. Shannon Fentiman says the government needs to explain why CS Energy media releases about the incident were not made public. In a statement released today, the CS Energy board acknowledged the company had "major cultural issues", and the draft media releases were its responsibility. "The recent incident has once again highlighted the deep-seated cultural problems at CS Energy that have not been addressed," the statement said. "There has not been adequate reporting of serious issues to senior management, the board and relevant ministers. "The board confirms that briefings and holding statements by CS Energy to the energy minister's office understated the gravity of the incident and the release of public statements is always a decision for CS Energy management." In a statement released last night, Mr Janetzki said any claim that his office "prevented CS Energy from releasing holding statements is categorically false". The government said it would now require energy companies to provide real-time updates following an outage — as Energex and Ergon do — to prevent a repeat of the communication failings. Mr Janetzki said any claim that his office "prevented CS Energy from releasing holding statements is categorically false". (Supplied: AAP) "The board welcomes the relevant ministers' response to introduce real-time outage reporting, seeking a full briefing into how advice is provided to relevant ministers and their offices, and a review into the operation and culture of government-owned corporations," the CS Energy board said. The Callide power station made headlines in 2021 after an explosion left nearly half a million homes without power. Callide Power Station is operated by CS Energy. (ABC News: Scout Wallen) A long-awaited report by forensic engineer Dr Sean Brady, released last year, found the operator had "substantive and longstanding issues" with safety. "The Brady Report flagged major cultural problems at CS Energy and the new board is determined to fix them," the statement from CS Energy said.

title: Zuckerberg considered 'spinning off' Instagram in 2018 amid antitrust scrutiny
content: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg considered spinning off popular photo-sharing app Instagram in 2018 over concerns about the growing risk of antitrust scrutiny, according to a document shown at a trial in Washington on Tuesday. The document was shown during Mr Zuckerberg's second day of testimony at the high-stakes trial, in which the US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is seeking to unwind Meta's acquisitions of prized assets Instagram and WhatsApp. "I wonder if we should consider the extreme step of spinning Instagram out as a separate company," Mr Zuckerberg said in the 2018 memo. Tech giant Meta used pirated books by Australian authors including Hannah Kent and Charlotte Wood to train its AI language model. At the time, Meta was mulling plans to reorganise the social media company and link its apps together more closely. Mr Zuckerberg pushed back in the memo, saying consolidation was likely to yield "strong business growth" but cautioning that it also could erode the value of flagship app Facebook's social network, with scant promise that the company would get to keep its full "family of apps" in the end. Meta ultimately did not spin off Instagram, instead proceeding with the plan to integrate its apps the following year. But the fact that Mr Zuckerberg even considered the idea is a stunning sign of how seriously he took the threat of precisely the type of antitrust trial proceeding now. "As calls to break up the big tech companies grow, there is a non-trivial chance that we will be forced to spin out Instagram and perhaps WhatsApp in the next 5-10 years anyway," he wrote then, noting the possibility that the "next Democratic president" could take action to break up tech companies. "This is one more factor that we should consider since even if we wanted to keep those apps together we may not be able to," he said. The courthouse in Washington where Meta platforms and the Federal Trade Commission are facing off in an antitrust trial. (Reuters: Nathan Howard) The FTC ultimately sued Meta in 2020, during President Donald Trump's first term. Mr Trump's antitrust enforcers sued Alphabet-owned Google the same year, accusing it of monopolising search. Mr Zuckerberg also downplayed the impact of a spin-off on the company's fortunes at the time in his memo, although Meta has argued publicly since then that attempts to break it up would be damaging. "While most companies resist break ups, the corporate history is that most companies actually perform better after they've been split up. The synergies are usually less than people think and the strategy tax is usually greater than people think," he wrote. Mr Zuckerberg's testimony comes as Meta is defending itself years after the release of other damning statements plucked from Facebook's own documents, like a 2008 email in which he said "it is better to buy than compete". The FTC accuses Meta of holding a monopoly on platforms used to share content with friends and family, where its main competitors in the United States are Snap's Snapchat and MeWe, a tiny privacy-focused social media app launched in 2016. Platforms where users broadcast content to strangers based on shared interests, such as X, TikTok, YouTube and Reddit, are not interchangeable, the FTC argues. The case is widely seen as a test of the new Trump administration's promises to take on Big Tech companies. Mr Zuckerberg testified earlier in the day that Meta bought Instagram because it had a "better" camera than the one his company was trying to build at the time. The Meta CEO acknolwedged in 2018 that separating Instagram into its own company would be an "extreme step". (Reuters: Dado Ruvic/Illustration) The acknowledgement likewise appeared to support allegations by the FTC that Meta had used a "buy or bury" strategy to snap up potential rivals, keep smaller competitors at bay and maintain an illegal monopoly. Asked by an attorney for the FTC whether he thought fast-growing Instagram could be destructive to Meta, then known as Facebook, Mr Zuckerberg said he believed Instagram had a better camera than the one his company was building. "We were doing a build vs. buy analysis," while in the process of building a camera app, Mr Zuckerberg said. "I thought that Instagram was better at that, so I thought it was better to buy them." The company argues that his past intentions are irrelevant because the FTC has defined the social media market inaccurately and failed to account for stiff competition Meta has faced from ByteDance's TikTok, Alphabet's YouTube and Apple's messaging app. Mr Zuckerberg also acknowledged that many of the company's attempts at building its own apps had failed. "Building a new app is hard and many more times than not when we have tried to build a new app, it hasn't gotten a lot of traction," he told the court. "We probably tried building dozens of apps over the history of the company and the majority of them don't go anywhere." Reuters

title: Video of 'disgusting' youth disturbance in Big W fuels police probe
content: Tasmania Police is investigating a disturbance that broke out on Tuesday at a department store in Hobart's northern suburbs, as a video of the affray reaches hundreds of thousands of viewers. The video, circulated on social media, shows a confrontation involving a large group of youths inside the Glenorchy Big W store. The young people are shown shouting in the tech area, with some jumping onto the service counter and one seen throwing punches. A Tasmania Police spokesperson said it is believed the disturbance involved two youth groups known to each other. The ABC spoke to one witness who was shopping in the store when the incident happened. Wanting to remain anonymous, the customer described it as "disgusting". "My friend and I were doing some Easter shopping and were at the front of the shop and heard some kids yelling," she said. "About five kids ran out of the shop stealing things. "One of the staff said [the youths] had just bashed someone up. "We continued shopping and were heading to the back of the shop when about 15-20 kids strolled in in one big line. The customer said she saw staff members being pushed, kicked and abused. "We couldn't stand there and watch, so we got in the middle and [were] trying to split it all up, also other people were helping as well," she said. A Woolworths Group spokesperson said team members who witnessed the incident were given access to counselling services. The customer said she wanted to see more police patrolling shops, and said she feared shops would close down because of "kids like this". "If nothing is done I can see the public taking things into their own hands." Tasmania Police has a specific taskforce to target shoplifting and anti-social behaviour in Glenorchy known as Operation Swipe. Police, Fire and Emergency Management Minister Felix Ellis said he was "appalled at the behaviour displayed last night". "Tasmanians deserve to not only feel safe, but be safe when they are going about their business. "Our government will continue to be tough on crime, and tough on the causes of crime to keep our communities safe."

title: Restaurant industry spooked by vow to crack down on immigrant workers
content: Restaurateur Amanda Scott says the process of employing skilled immigrant workers is slow, expensive, and maddeningly bureaucratic. The cafe owner fears the process will become even harder as both major parties vow to reduce immigration levels if they win the upcoming federal election. The Kedron Farm House owner said few Australians were studying cookery, with venues becoming increasingly dependent on immigrant workers. Ms Scott said overseas chefs had been filling those roles instead, but the worker visa approvals process was becoming increasingly onerous. She said skilled visa applications were now taking several years to be processed while costing upwards of $8,000 in paperwork. "It was successful until this year, but now something's happened with both sides of politics using this as an election ploy," Ms Scott said. "It's such a disincentive to go into restaurants these days because it's so complicated — you have to be a visa expert, a payroll expert, an immigration expert." Brisbane cafe mogul Philip Di Bella said the industry was badly hit when the Labor government capped the hours international students were allowed to work. Phillip Di Bella says the foreign worker cap is driving an illegal trade. (ABC Brisbane: Kenji Sato) Student visa work restrictions were scrapped in 2022 and brought back in 2023, preventing international students from working more than 24 hours per week. The Coffee Commune owner said this had served to embolden the illegal cash-in-hand market and made it more difficult for venues to fill their rosters. Want even more? "The international students didn't take all the jobs and cause unemployment," Mr Di Bella said. "If they do cap international students and migrants, it will have a big effect." Australian Hotel Association (AHA) chief executive Stephen Ferguson said the Coalition's proposed caps on foreign workers would hurt local businesses. Stephen Ferguson says there is a shortage of chefs that cannot be filled domestically. (ABC News: Matt Roberts) "The AHA is very concerned regarding the Coalition's disappointing announcement that it will decrease foreign workers by 100,000 each year," Mr Ferguson said. "Political parties often talk about the need for productivity, but in a labour-intensive industry like hospitality, a reduction in available workers will cause a severe downturn in productivity." The Hospitality Industry Award shows minimum wages for chefs have not kept up with the pace of inflation in the last five years. A casual entry-level chef earns $31.23 per hour, which is lower than the casual award for traffic controllers ($35.04 per hour), and bus drivers ($32.25 per hour). title: China halts orders of US-made Boeing jets, scrapping deals worth billions
content: China has reportedly ordered its airlines to pause all incoming deliveries of American-made Boeing aircraft in response to Donald Trump's 145 per cent tariffs on Chinese goods. The three main Chinese airlines were expected to take delivery of 179 Boeing planes between now and 2027 — more planes than the entire Qantas main fleet — in deals worth billions of dollars. But that plan has been put on hold, according to reports from Bloomberg News. In his first public comments about the US-China trade war, President Xi Jinping says there are no winners in a tariff war. International aviation consultant Neil Hansford said China would be the biggest loser from this latest trade spat. "In the end China is cutting off its nose to spite its face because [the country] has a shortage of aircraft after COVID," he said. Mr Hansford said the upheaval meant Boeing could focus on sending planes elsewhere. "It'll assist Boeing because they can actually start bringing deliveries to other customers," he said. "Everybody is short of equipment, we're all trying to give maintenance to aircraft. "So for the rest of the aviation world it's a good thing." Mr Hansford said China would still have access to jets from elsewhere, "but they need Boeing's because COVID set us years behind in the building of aircraft". The larger trade war between China and the United States shows no sign of cooling. US tariffs on China stand at 145 per cent and in return China has imposed 125 per cent tariffs on American goods entering its borders. China's Foreign Ministry spokesman Lin Jian said his country was open for business. "We will continue to expand our circle of friends in trade, strengthen the gravitational field of investment, and inject more stability and positive energy into the world economy through high-quality development and high-level opening-up." Meanwhile, a Communist Party official in Hong Kong, Xia Baolong, has clapped back to a recent reference to Chinese "peasants" made by US Vice President JD Vance. "The repeated attempts of the US to contain and suppress Hong Kong will only result in the end of its agents in Hong Kong, and will backfire, and harm itself," he said. "Those peasants from the US will soon be crying tears in front of China's 5,000 years of civilisation." Donald Trump attends a bilateral meeting with China's President Xi Jinping during the G20 leaders summit in 2019. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque) White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the US president was waiting on China to come to the table. "The president has made his position on China quite clear," she said. "The ball is in China's court — China needs to make a deal with us, we don't have to make a deal with them. "There's no difference between China and any other country except they are much larger and China wants what we have … they need our money. "The president has made it quite clear that he's open to a deal with China, but China needs to make a deal with the United States of America." Most countries are facing a 10 per cent tariff, except for some goods from Canada and Mexico.
