title: Major insurer taken to court over 'egregious' handling of storm claim
content: Australia's corporate watchdog alleges one of the country's biggest insurers took nearly three-and-a-half years to resolve a claim over storm damage to a property in regional Victoria. The Australian Securities and Investment Commission (ASIC) is suing Hollard Insurance, accusing it of breaching its "duty of utmost good faith" in its handling of the claim. A regional Victorian couple lodged a claim two days after suffering major storm damage to their home. In late October 2021, major storms battered the state, resulting in thousands of calls for help to the State Emergency Service and leaving more than half a million properties without power. ASIC said Hollard — Australia's fifth largest general insurer — deliberated for 18 months before rejecting the claim in April 2023. The watchdog claims Hollard relied on "a non-expert opinion over prior expert reports" on the cause of the damage to the property and offered the couple a small cash settlement, which was rejected. ASIC also alleged Hollard delayed decisions over repairs and took nine months to initiate an inspection by a structural engineer and delayed providing temporary accommodation to the couple. ASIC Deputy Chair Sarah Court says the couple's home is now uninhabitable. (ABC News: Billy Cooper) ASIC alleges the delays, poor communication and ignoring of expert advice "exposed the couple to unnecessary and prolonged harm" and breached Hollard's duty of good faith in handling the claim. "In the end, because of the excessive delays by Hollard and the failure to undertake make-safe works, the home has become so riddled with moisture, mould and decay that it is uninhabitable and now needs to be demolished and rebuilt," ASIC deputy chair Sarah Court said. "The egregious delay highlights ASIC's concern about the significant rise in general insurance complaints reported to AFCA since the 2022 floods, particularly those involving claim delays. ASIC is seeking a civil penalty under the Insurance Contracts Act. A spokesperson for Hollard Insurance said the insurer acknowledged the Federal Court action. "We support ASIC's work in driving positive outcomes for consumers and are cooperating with ASIC in this matter," the spokesperson said. "As this is an ongoing legal matter, we are unable to provide further comment."

title: Cause of oyster spat deaths at research facility remains a mystery
content: An investigation into fish mortalities at a South Australian Research and Development Institute (SARDI) facility has found the cause of the deaths to be "inconclusive". About 70 per cent of the state's breeding line of oyster spat, as well as significant numbers of barramundi broodstock and snapper larvae, died of unknown causes at the facility at West Beach in Adelaide late last year. South Australia's oyster industry was worth $58 million in 2022–23. (ABC News: Brittany Evins) The mass deaths were a significant setback to oyster breeding lines but SARDI executive director Mike Steer said what was lost would be recovered. "We're working closely with the oyster industry to re-establish the production of new family lines to overcome those losses. "We're effectively overcoming an environmental impact that's impacted our projects but we can recover them." Mike Steer say what was lost will be recovered. (Landline: Tony Hill) Dr Steer also played down concerns about the impact on recreational fishers. The investigation was led by three SARDI researchers, and has been independently reviewed by University of Adelaide professor Michael Goodsite. Professor Goodsite's expertise is in civil and environmental engineering. It had been speculated that the fish deaths were caused by dredging conducted by the Department for Environment and Water (DEW) at West Beach, which began in early October. However, according to the investigation, no direct evidence was identified to link the mortalities to dredged sand placement or dredging activities. The report found no link between dredging and sand carting at West Beach, and the mortalities. (ABC News: Che Chorley) South Australia's oyster industry was worth $58 million to the state in 2022–23 financial year. "The mortalities of larvae, spat, fingerlings and broodstock were unfortunate, and disappointing for all involved, not least the team at SARDI who dedicate their careers to our world-class research and breeding programs at the West Beach site," Minister for Primary Industries and Regional Development Claire Scriven said. "While there are times when causes for events such as these cannot be conclusively found, learnings can still be applied for future activities. "SARDI is already implementing mitigation measures for any future events." The SA Oyster Growers Association declined to comment.

title: Broken Hill icon set to be revitalised after years collecting dust
content: One of the main questions Shane Goodwin is asked by tourists and locals about the towering mound of ore that overlooks Broken Hill is "do you know what's happening up there?" Now he can say that after years spent collecting dust the vacant Line of Lode complex is set for a revival. NSW Crown Lands poured more than $6 million into renovating the site but it remained untouched until recently, when Broken Hill Mines struck a lease agreement with Foundation Broken Hill to establish offices at the site. Broken Hill Mines is offering to cover the rent for the business prepared to operate at the site. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde) The Australian miner purchased the Rasp Mine last year and has big plans for the city, according to Mr Goodwin, who is the company's head of corporate sustainability. "We recognise that facility as an important part of town," he said. "If we can be a big part of getting that up and running and attracting tourists and locals into that facility then we're very happy. The Broken Earth Complex has remained largely untouched since the previous tenants moved out in 2021. Foundation Broken Hill chair John Lynch hopes the development will encourage more people to enjoy the views. "Whether it's the sunset … whether it's the sunrise, if we're open, with a coffee, with something to eat," he said. "Then I think it's a real boost for the future." The challenge now will be to find tenants for the office spaces. Jim Hickey's family were the last people to run a business at the Broken Earth Complex. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde) Deputy Mayor Jim Hickey said a restaurant would not be economically viable but a cafe would be ideal. "You get a fair [amount of] patronage, but it's very hard to make a full-time living there," he said. "It will be a great secondary cafe for someone." Broken Hill Mines is confident an operator will be enticed to move in on a rent-free basis after the office is built in the existing structure. "We'd talk to them about how we'd share the utilities costs, but the leasing costs will be covered by us," Mr Goodwin said. Broken Hill Mines would also like to install an observation point that would allow people to watch the operations inside the Rasp Mine. But for now the company is focused on finding builders to get the complex up and running as soon as possible. "We'd like to see this done, certainly, within six months and up and open," Mr Goodwin said. "I need to source a builder and John needs to source a hospitality provider. title: Australian share market closes lower after week of turmoil
content: The Australian share market has ended the day 0.8 lower after seesawing through the week. Ultimately the ASX 200 lost 0.28 per cent over the week, which saw huge losses followed by historic gains when the US president hit pause on his tariff plan. The ASX 200 closed 0.8 per cent lower at 7,646 points, while the All Ords was -0.8 per cent at 7853 points. Gold miners continued to be the best performing stocks, with almost all sectors in the red on the ASX200. The uncertainty has seen the price of gold hit a record high as investors flock to the safe-haven asset, with the previous metal ending the week +0.9 per cent at US$3,202. The Aussie dollar lost some earlier gains to end the day -0.4 per cent at 62 US cents. US stocks fell overnight, reversing back some of the gains from the previous session's historic rally triggered by US President Donald Trump's announcement of a 90-day pause on some of his "reciprocal" tariffs. At the time of writing (4:30pm AEST) US futures were in positive territory over 1 per cent higher, pointing to a possible reversal on Friday's trading day. The RBA governor Michele Bullock delivered a speech last night at the Chief Executive Women Melbourne Annual Dinner, where she said as bad as things were with tariffs and the ensuing market chaos, it wasn’t reminiscent of the global financial crisis in 2008 (yet). She said the Australian financial system was strong and well placed to absorb shocks from abroad. But when it came to interest rates? She said it was still too early to know how the RBA was going to respond. “We are mindful of not adding to the uncertainty, and to that end, it’s too early for us to determine what the path will be for interest rates. Take a look back at how the session unfolded, plus the day's finance news and analysis and insights from our specialist business reporters, on the markets blog. By Nadia Daly This just in from our friends at news agency Reuters. They are reporting that Vietnam is preparing a deal to offer their US counterparts, with reported hopes to bring their tariffs down to between 22-28% or less. The country's economy is heavily reliant on exports but US officials, including the influential White House trade advisor Peter Navarro, have raised concerns about Chinese goods being sent to America with "Made in Vietnam" labels that draw lower duties. The Reuters report says Vietnam is prepared to crack down on Chinese goods being shipped to the United States via its territory and will tighten controls on sensitive exports to China, according to a person familiar with the matter and a government document seen by Reuters. Vietnam has for weeks been offering sweeteners that it hoped would persuade President Donald Trump's administration to take a benign view of its huge trade surplus with America. Instead, it was hit with a 46% tariff as part of Trump's "Liberation Day" salvo. While the tariff has been suspended for 90 days, the two countries agreed to start talks after a Vietnamese deputy prime minister met with the U.S. Trade Representative on Wednesday. The report from Reuters states Vietnam's trade ministry and the USTR's office did not return a request for comment. There are also fears China could again raise tariffs above the 84% currently on the US, in retaliation against the new 145% tariff the US has placed on China. However China has said it would be open to talks with the US, if it was based on "mutual respect". China has hit back at what it called threats and blackmail from Washington and pledged to follow through to the end if the U.S. persists, its Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yongqian told a regular press briefing. "ASIC alleges Hollard Insurance breached its duty of utmost good faith in its handling of a home building and contents insurance claim made by a couple from regional Victoria. "The insurance claim was made on 31 October 2021, two days after a major storm damaged the roof of their home, but the couple were made to wait 18 months for their claim to be rejected. The couple rejected a modest cash settlement offer by Hollard and lodged a complaint to the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA). ASIC Deputy Chair Sarah Court said the claim had an, if possible, even worse conclusion. "In the end, because of the excessive delays by Hollard and the failure to undertake make-safe works, the home has become so riddled with moisture, mould and decay that it is uninhabitable and now needs to be demolished and rebuilt." But President Trump on 9 April also announced a 90-day pause on 'reciprocal tariffs' for other countries. We believe the demonstrated willingness from the Trump administration to change its stance in response to equity and bond market turbulence indicates some sensitivity to market stress, and points to the existence of a “Trump put” in some form. It is also not certain that the pause in 'reciprocal tariffs' on other trading partners will result in more long-lasting 'deals', and we do expect additional tariffs on pharmaceuticals and semiconductors to be announced. But with many countries expressing a desire to negotiate with the US, and the Trump administration now more incentivized to demonstrate “success,” we expect a variety of “deals” or sector carveouts to materialize within the 90-day “pause” period. President Trump has even expressed the view that ultimately a deal would be struck with China. We believe that progress on negotiations should provide encouragement for investors to look through near-term tariff-induced economic weakness and toward a return to earnings growth in 2026." By Emilia Terzon Do we know who started selling American Bonds? Individuals, Funds or Nations? Was it spontaneous or a planned attack? - Cassandra Thanks for the question, Cassandra. I asked Westpac's bonds guru Martin Whetton exactly this question yesterday. Before I go further, a little refresher. As he explains, government bonds are basically a way of buying into a country's debt. The sell-off of US government bonds that happened during this week's Trump tariff turmoil was, in Martin's view, a signal from the market that investors were feeling less sure about the US economy's ability to repay their debts. His thoughts: "US government bonds are held by every country in the world, and they're held by every bank and financial institution because they are deemed to be what's called golden collateral, the simple bottom line structure of financial markets. "I genuinely think what you observed (with the sell-off), or maybe what financial markets people observed yesterday, is the breaking of this long-standing financial, almost moral, authority of the US dollar and the US government debt." The question you asked was: who was selling off? Martin says around 21% of all the US government bonds are held by investors or institutions in Asia: "Japan, China, Asian central banks and sovereign wealth funds", he says. "They hold that fairly passively. We don't know whether they sold. It'll take some months before the data actually shows. More than likely they did," he adds. I also posed another question to him, about whether those markets might have sold off US government bonds, not just because they were less attractive, but as a rage move against the US as Trump's administration put higher tariffs on them. "If you are one of these Asian nations that have just been tariffed, you may feel a little bit of antagonism towards the US government. That's probably right," he replied. "I'd make the observation that you'd hardly want to go and buy (US bonds) at the moment, when the (US) dollar is challenged, when you're going to have less in US dollars, tax, trade, receipts, and you feel aggrieved about the situation you find yourself in. "Ultimately, all you've done as a country is produce goods at a low cost (for) the American market or and global markets. Now you've been tariffed and you're hurting your industries." title: If you map financial stress, you'll find these 'aspirational Australians'
content: Paris Basra has everything she wants in life: a house with a backyard, her husband, and a young child. But like many across Australia, the cost-of-living crisis is biting hard. She lives in Ripley — a suburb of Ipswich, in Brisbane's western corridor. Paris Basra and her son Simar live in Ripley, a growing suburb west of Brisbane. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus) It is former farmland turned into expanding developments, filled with new estates and first homebuyers like Paris. Ms Basra's mortgage repayments are about $900 a week. Interest rates remain over six per cent. It's expensive — and while it is manageable by keeping a very close eye on the budget — her family's ability to live their dream of home ownership comes with major sacrifices. Her husband Manpreet works fly-in, fly-out on ships as part of the bauxite industry in Far North Queensland — so for two weeks every second fortnight he is away from home. For half the year, Ms Basra's husband works away on ships in Far North Queensland to help afford their mortgage repayments. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus) "Obviously, there isn't a lot of local jobs [in south-east Queensland] within the shipping industry, and if there is, they aren't as high paying which would probably mean I would have to work full-time," Ms Basra said. "Simar would have to go into childcare full time and then obviously there's childcare costs, so you're adding onto your budget and monthly expenses. She's part of what political commentator John Cole refers to as aspirational Australians. Associate Professor John Cole says many aspirational Australians call the western corridor of south-east Queensland home. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd) And they're increasingly calling areas like Ripley, in the federal electorate of Blair home. "If you map financial stress, you'll find it strongest in areas where you find aspirational Australians, people that have a mortgage," said Associate Professor Cole, from the University of Southern Queensland It's these voters that some, including Associate Professor Cole, believe could be crucial in the upcoming federal election. A recent ABC analysis found Blair had the highest rate of household stress in Queensland. Professor Cole says Labor have been spending "a lot of money" in an attempt to hold Blair. (ABC News: Tobi Loftus) Over 77 per cent of households were feeling some form of financial stress, including 66 per cent of those with a mortgage, and 91 per cent of renters in the region. "Blair will be no different to most of urban Australia — cost of living, cost of housing, housing affordability are all big issues," Associate Professor Cole said. That stress resonates across the generations. Ipswich resident Margaret Fielder says she wants to see more support for homeless people from politicians at this election. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd) Retired nurse Margaret Fielder lives in a small cottage she owns just outside the Ipswich CBD. "I went from rags to riches and back to rags again," the 85-year-old said. "Quite frankly, I cannot afford to pay the prices that's demanded of food in the supermarkets these days and pay my bills and maintain this house as well," she said. Ms Fielder now pays very close attention to every bill that comes in, so she doesn't have to go into debt to pay them off. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd) She's on an aged pension and receives other government support but still struggles when it's time to pay the bills. "I just have to be very careful not to get into debt … I don't have any money in the bank," she said. "If my food's getting low and that sort of thing, I'm not too proud to go to the [Foodbank] and get food that otherwise would be dumped." A number of other voters the ABC spoke with on the streets of Ipswich feel the same. Hear the latest election news as it happens on the Election Central Playlist. Only on the ABC listen app. "[Rents] are too high, property prices are also too high," one woman said. Another woman said while she was lucky enough to be a part of the social housing program, other cost-of-living issues plagued her and her children. "Food, electricity, everything," she said. Markets plunge again as US confirms China tariff even higher
content: US markets have plunged again as optimism over President Donald Trump's tariffs "pause" is overshadowed by his escalating trade war with China. At the close on Thursday, local time, the S&P 500 was down 3.5 per cent, the Dow Jones was down 2.5 per cent and the Nasdaq had fallen 4.3 per cent. That represented a wipe-out of about a third of the previous day's record gains, which followed Mr Trump's decision to "pause" his most severe tariffs for 90 days. The falls worsened after the White House clarified the tariff imposed on China — which will not be paused — equates to 145 per cent, rather than the 125 per cent previously announced. The 125 per cent figure did not account for the 20 per cent tariff placed on China earlier this year, ostensibly to punish it for doing too little to stop fentanyl shipments to the US. Mr Trump again said he was optimistic about reaching a deal with Chinese President Xi Jinping. "He's been a friend of mine for a long period of time, and I think that we'll end up working out something that's very good for both countries," Mr Trump said. Hollywood became the latest target in the bilateral trade war when China indicated it would reduce screenings of American movies. "The US government's erroneous practice of imposing excessive tariffs on China is likely to further diminish the Chinese audience's favourable perception of American films," the China Film Administration said, according to the South China Morning Post. "We will adhere to market principles, respect audience choices and moderately reduce the import volume of American films." Meanwhile, the European Union said it would pause its planned retaliatory tariffs on the US as it works to strike a deal with Washington. Mr Trump said the US would negotiate with the EU as a single bloc, rather than individual countries. Tech and banking stocks were among those hardest hit by the falls on the US markets. Speaking ahead of a cabinet meeting before the close of trade, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent indicated he was not concerned about the market volatility. "As we go through the queue and settle with these countries who are going to bring their best offers, we will end up in a place of great certainty over the next 90 days on tariffs," he said. "We had very good inflation numbers today, oil's down, we had a successful bond market. So I don't see anything unusual today." Mr Trump said "there will always be transition difficulty" but he was proud of "the biggest day in history" on the US markets on Wednesday. Mr Trump's "pause" means almost all imports are now subject to a 10 per cent "baseline" tariff, which was already the rate set for Australia. Of all Trump's miscalculations this week, his biggest miscalculation of all may be assuming that China would not hit back, using the economic power that the Chinese Communist Party has been amassing for decades, but until recently, has not fully deployed. Asked if countries could negotiate to reduce that 10 per cent tariff further, Mr Trump said: "It depends what they're adding." "Some countries we have massive deficits with or they have big surpluses with us, and others it's not that way," he said. "We have some that are pretty even, but they hurt us in other ways, and we just want to get that taken care of." The US has had a trade surplus with Australia for decades, meaning it sends more products to Australia than it imports from Australia. But early this year, there was a rare — and almost certainly temporary — reversal after an American buy-up of billions of dollars' worth of Australian gold, fuelled by fears of a trade war. Mr Trump's trade advisers also complain Australia has unfair trade barriers on meat, pharmaceuticals and tech. Want even more? Check out our tariffs topic page

title: A super payment went to the wrong account but the fund says it's not to blame
content: Warning: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised this article includes the name and image of someone who has died (used with the permission of his family). Annette Riley stands on the jetty at Derby in remote Western Australia as the harsh afternoon sun beats down on the vast body of water known as King Sound. Her youngest son Warick Deegan was a keen fisherman who worked on boats and knew this Kimberley coastline well For most of his life, Mr Deegan was "happy go lucky" but a few years ago, at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, he hit a rough patch and requested early access to $10,000 of his superannuation. When Mr Deegan didn't receive the money, he called Australian Super twice to ask why and repeatedly went into his bank. Australia's largest superannuation fund, Australian Super, is being sued by the corporate regulator for "significant delays" in processing thousands of death benefit claims. Months later, he died by suicide. His mother is still grappling with the loss. Every day she's reminded of him by a framed picture, inside the entrance way of her home. "He (would have) turned 40 this year. He was only 36 at the time (he died)," she said. Derby is a tight knit community of just over 3,000 people, more than 40 per cent of whom are Indigenous. It feels a world away — almost 5,000 kilometres — from the sleek Melbourne high-rise office tower of the country's largest retirement fund — Australian Super. Ms Riley, is speaking out about her two-year battle with the fund which she believes failed to meet the needs of her son and his beneficiaries. The Nyikina woman has been fighting to recoup the $10,000 that was sent to an account that wasn't his and she wants her son's death benefit, worth $180,000, reinstated. The company is refusing both requests. Mr Deegan's death benefit was cancelled shortly before he died because he had not made contributions for more than sixteen months, so the account was deemed inactive. Annette Riley with a photo of her son and his family. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne) Australian Super maintains it acted lawfully. "I think that's the wrong decision," Ms Riley said. "It's important for my son, but also for his daughter. "My granddaughter." Public confidence in the multi-trillion-dollar superannuation sector has been rocked in recent times. Australia's corporate watchdog calls on superannuation funds to overhaul the way they deal with death benefit claims. A cyber-attack this month sparked criticism about security and reporting processes, while a blistering review by the corporate watchdog ASIC called for a drastic overhaul of how death benefit claims are handled. The review singled out the poor experiences of First Nations members and their families. ASIC is also suing Australian Super over what it alleges were lengthy delays in processing thousands of death benefit claims. Financial counsellor Alan Gray from Bush Money Mob works across Indigenous communities in remote Western Australia. He represents Ms Riley and believes the superannuation sector is regularly failing First Nations members. Mr Deegan earned his money doing hard, physical work on cattle stations, railway lines for the mining industry and on pearling boats. Since his partner's death, John's been locked in a lengthy battle with one of Australia's largest funds to get her super paid out. He's not alone, with the country's peak advocacy group calling for an end to lengthy delays and further grief for families. But as the pandemic shut down the country, he was one of three million Australians who requested early access to their super for compassionate reasons. Mr Deegan was living in the tiny Indigenous community of Pandanus Park about 40 minutes drive from the nearest ANZ branch in Derby. His mother said he went regularly to the bank to see if the super payment had come through. After coming up empty at the bank, Mr Deegan called Australian Super twice. His family has provided recordings of the phone calls to the ABC. They also allowed us to show his face and use his name. The first time Mr Deegan called was October 15, 2020 and he told the call centre worker he'd applied for the payment through the tax office. Warick Deegan spoke with Australian Super twice over the phone about the missing money "How long ago was that?" the call operated asked. "About four weeks ago," Mr Deegan replied. The call operator sounded shocked. "Four weeks? Okay," After looking up his file, the Australian Super call operator delivered bad news. The money had been paid weeks earlier. "How much would that be?" Mr Deegan asked. "Ten thousand," the call operator answered. "Far out," Mr Deegan whispered. The operator then checked the ANZ bank account the money went into and Mr Deegan stated it was not his. "You don't have any other bank accounts?" the call operator asked. "No, I don't, um, I might have to rush into the bank or something. Someone else's account," Mr Deegan said. The second call was just days later on October 26. Mr Deegan asked the female call operator if it had been paid into someone else's account. "It will bounce back to us if the bank account details is (sic) incorrect it will bounce back to us," she reassured him. "That's what I was thinking, because it's been awhile," Mr Deegan answered. He then asked if it was certain the money would bounce back, as she had suggested. "It will bounce back, for sure, right?" he asked. "Yeah it will bounce back to Australian Super," she confirmed. The call operator then said she would get Australian Super to reprocess the payment. Mr Deegan again said he was concerned the money won't bounce back and for the third time she reassured him it would. "Look, so far, in my experience, all payments that have been made to the wrong bank account has bounced back to Australian super," she said. When Mr Deegan died he had only a small balance left in his ANZ bank account. Ms Riley said her family remains distressed because it believes based on the phone calls that he never received the money. Financial counsellor Alan Gray is working with Annette Riley and is calling on the fund to reinstate her son's death benefit. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne) She suspects financial hardship may have contributed to his death. "We were all angry when we found out," Ms Riley said. When the family asked Mr Gray for help, he in turn questioned Australian Super about the missing $10,000. At first Australian Super told him it had paid the money to Mr Deegan's ANZ account. The bank later contradicted that, confirming in an email it was not his account but refused to say more due to privacy restrictions. "Australian Super have no idea who they are paying that COVID super money to because they don't match the account name with the BSB and account number (known as confirmation of payee technology). A photograph of Warick Deegan hangs in this mother's home. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne) The ABC asked Australian Super whether it used confirmation of payee technology or if it performed other due diligence on the account prior to making payment but it did not directly answer. It said the $10,000 was paid to the bank account provided by the tax office and Mr Deegan should have checked the account details when making his early release application with the ATO. ANZ said it did not comment on individual customers and when money was sent to the wrong account it attempted to recover it. The taxation office also declined to comment. Australian Super is also refusing to reinstate $180,000 in death benefits insurance Mr Deegan had until shortly before he died. The company cancelled the cover about four months earlier, due to his account being inactive — a requirement that was put in place to stop ongoing fees eroding super balances. But his family said he never knew his insurance cover was at risk and the company missed crucial opportunities to warn him while he was on the phone. Australian Super did send two warning letters to an old address but the letters were returned to sender. Alan Gray and Annette Riley say Australian Super had many opportunities to warn Mr Deegan his death benefit was about to be cancelled. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne) The company conceded it did not have his phone number or email address but maintained the onus was on the member to make sure their contact details were up to date. Australian Super declined to be interviewed but said in a statement it was, "a tragic case" and "we feel deeply for Mr Deegan and his family". Chief Member Officer Rose Kerlin said Australian Super stood by its position because it had followed its processes and met its legal obligations. However, Ms Kerlin also said, "the outcome for Mr Deegan and his family is not what anyone would have wanted." Mr Deegan's family took a dispute to the financial ombudsman, the Australian Financial Complaints Authority (AFCA) but lost. AFCA found Australian Super had acted fair and reasonably by cancelling his insurance and processing the super payment. Financial counsellor Alan Gray. (ABC News: Andrew Seabourne) However, Mr Gray believes Australian Super should have done more to warn Mr Deegan about the loss of his death benefits and should have offered him additional support as a remote First Nations person. Mr Gray is calling on Australian Super to reverse its position on the case. Ms Kerlin from Australian Super said Warick's case showed the need for widespread change. ASIC commissioner Simone Constant says the industry needs to meet "reasonable expectations". (ABC News: Billy Cooper) "This shows systemic changes to laws and industry standards are needed to better serve vulnerable Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, particularly in remote areas," she said. The company has a phone line for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander members and those staffing it have cultural training, as have other employees including those in the dispute resolution and operations teams. Last month ASIC released a highly-critical review of how 10 super funds dealt with death benefits. It excluded Australian Super due to ASIC's ongoing lawsuit. The review uncovered lengthy delays — mostly within the trustee's control, poor customer service like phone calls not being returned and claims handling where vulnerability wasn't properly considered. Email michaelatkin@protonmail.com or contact him via the Signal secure messaging app +61 447 279 901. ASIC Commissioner Simone Constant said the industry was on notice to "lift their game now," to meet the "reasonable expectations" of grieving families. The review found outcomes were worse for First Nations members and their families and that was further exacerbated when people lived remotely. Amongst 34 recommendations, were six related to fixing these chronic issues with Indigenous Australians. "Something needs to be done here urgently," Ms Constant said. "The service failings and the gaps were amplified or exacerbated with the First Nations members and their families."

title: Australian weapon trialled by Israel's military ahead of potential sale
content: Israel's military has completed trials of an advanced weapon made by a Canberra-based defence supplier which boasts its “high precision” and “lethal” product can strike targets up to two kilometres away. The ABC can reveal the remote weapon system (RWS), designed and built by Australian company Electro Optic Systems (EOS), was one of dozens of counter drone technologies tested by the Israel Defense Forces earlier this year. A defence industry source claims the Australian-made components were first sent to an EOS entity in the United States for assembly, before being shipped to Israel without an Australian export approval. For months, the Albanese government has insisted “no Australian weaponry” has been exported to Israel, and the Defence Department has again told the ABC that “Australia has not supplied weapons or ammunition to Israel” since the Gaza war began in 2023. On Friday morning, the prime minister again insisted that Australia would not sell arms to Israel. "I am aware of this report that you refer to, we looked into this matter and the company have confirmed with the Department of Defence that the particular system was not exported from Australia," he said. "Australia does not export weapons to Israel." In a statement, EOS declined to comment on whether its R400 RWS has been demonstrated in Israel telling the ABC it “does not publicise commercially sensitive information regarding clients, existing contracts or business development campaigns”. However, documents supplied to the Australian Stock Exchange in February reveal that EOS “supported a local prime to demonstrate counter-drone capabilities in a high-profile local demonstration” in January 2025, but did not specify where it took place. Australian Army Hawkei fitted with an EOS R400-HD during a counter-drone firing (Defence department image: CPL Michael Currie) The “Market Development Update” includes a photo of Israeli Ministry of Defense officials standing behind a modified R400 and states that the “EOS’ system performed extremely well, earning high praise from the organisers”. On EOS’s website the R400 is described as “Lightweight 30mm lethality with precise mobile engagements up to 2 km” and “a high-precision weapon platform with the firepower of a 30 mm cannon”. “The R400 also supports other weapons, such as machine guns, automatic grenade launchers, and anti-tank guided missiles. It is compatible with other EOS weapon systems through ‘plug-and-play’ functionality.” Israel’s Ministry of Defence announced in February it had “successfully completed an extensive series of operational trials testing approximately 20 advanced counter-drone technologies”. “Nine Israeli defence industries and startups demonstrated various drone interception and neutralisation capabilities using both projectile-based systems and counter-drones at a testing field in southern Israel,” the Ministry said in a press release. An accompanying photograph shows Israeli Defence Ministry officials and industry representative standing behind an R400 system, which is the same image included in the EOS “Market Development Update” provided to the Australian Stock Exchange. The R400, manufactured by Electro Optic Systems (Supplied by the company, EOS) In response to questions on whether EOS sought approval to demonstrate its R400, a Defence Department spokesperson insisted Australia had “not supplied weapons or ammunition to Israel since the conflict began, and for at least the past five years. “As the circumstances of the conflict have evolved, the Government has calibrated its approach and has only approved new export permits to Israel for items for Australian defence and law enforcement that will return to Australia,” the spokesperson said. “Defence has also been undertaking a process to scrutinise the pre-existing export permits to Israel. These pre-existing permits were all approved before the conflict began and none of the permits relate to weapons or ammunition.” Asked whether it had sought permission to export the lethal technology, and whether the product had first gone to the United States, an EOS spokesperson told the ABC that that the company “complies with all relevant regulations at all times”. “EOS operates under the trade control regulations of the countries it is based in, due to the nature of its products and technologies,” the spokesperson added. “That includes detailed regulations in Australia and other host countries where EOS manufactures products, like the United States.” Greens Senator David Shoebridge says the involvement of EOS exposes the Albanese government’s “lies” that Australia has not supported Israel’s military campaign against Gaza, a position reinforced this week by the Prime Minister during a leaders’ debate. "What we can see clearly here is an Australian made weapon in the hands of the Israeli military in Israel in January this year and I think that really puts the lie to these denials we've had from the Albanese government since this appalling conflict started," Senator Shoebridge told the ABC.

title: Prada to buy rival fashion house Versace in $2.2 billion deal
content: Prada Group has announced a deal to buy Versace from the US luxury group Capri Holdings under terms that value the fashion house at 1.25 billion euros ($2.2 billion). The deal brings one of fashion's best-known Italian labels back under Italian control after it was sold to Capri Holdings, then known as Michael Kors, for $US2.15 billion ($3.4 billion) including debt in 2018. Donatella Versace is replaced as creative director of the luxury fashion house Versace. Prada said the addition of Versace's "highly recognisable aesthetic constitutes a strongly complementary addition" to its portfolio, which includes the Prada and Miu Miu fashion brands. It said Milan-based Versace offered "significant untapped growth potential.'' The final value of the deal will be adjusted at closing which is expected in the second half of the year. It will be funded by 1.5 billion euros in new debt and has been approved by the Prada and Capri Holdings board of directors. "Versace will maintain its creative DNA and cultural authenticity, while benefiting from the full strength of the Group's considerable consolidated platform, including industrial capabilities, retail execution and operational expertise,'' Prada said in a statement. Versace, founded in 1978 by the late Gianni Versace, has been owned since 2018 by Capri Holdings, which includes Michael Kors and Jimmy Choo. Capri Holdings paid $US2 billion for Versace, but had been struggling in the recent era of "quiet luxury'. Last month, Capri Holdings named Dario Vitale as creative director to replace Donatella Versace, who assumed the role after her brother's 1997 murder. Versace was given the new role of chief brand ambassador in the shake-up, which was widely viewed as setting the scene for the long-running Prada sale. The deal has revived hopes for a 'Made in Italy' luxury champion after many other family-founded brands ended up in French, Swiss or US hands, and comes as many Italian groups are outperforming the struggling sector. A model presents a creation from the Prada Fall-Winter 2025/2026 collection during the Milan Fashion Week in Italy. (Reuters: Alessandro Garofalo) Despite Italy accounting for 50 to 55 per cent of global personal luxury goods production, according to consultancy Bain's estimates, the country lacks a group with a scale that matches up to French players such as LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton SE and Gucci-owner Kering. Milan-based Prada, controlled by designer Miuccia Prada and husband Patrizio Bertelli and listed in Hong Kong with a market capitalisation of about 14 billion euros, is the largest Italian luxury fashion group by revenue. But the group, which also includes the fast-growing Miu Miu label, has been a relative minnow in terms of stock market valuation compared with the likes of Louis Vuitton-owner LVMH. The Versace deal comes after Andrea Guerra became Prada's CEO in 2023 to bridge a change in generation, with Lorenzo Bertelli, the son of the company's main owners and its chief marketing officer, regarded as the heir apparent. "Prada's ambition to become a leading Italian luxury conglomerate is a significant move in a market that is dominated by French groups," said fashion and luxury industry adviser Achim Berg. The combined revenue of the five biggest Italian-owned listed luxury groups still well below Kering's roughly 17 billion euros, even after a big fall in sales at the French group last year. AP/Reuters

title: Coalition to abolish 'ute tax' fuel efficiency standards
content: A scheme to cut the emissions of cars and encourage electric vehicle uptake will be substantially wound back under a Coalition government, with Opposition Leader Peter Dutton dubbing it an unfair car tax. The New Vehicle Efficiency Standard (NVES) will take force in July after being legislated at the request of several automotive companies in 2024. Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues It sets an emissions ceiling on the total car sales of each automaker, with heavy penalties for those who exceed it. The federal government has detailed its proposal to impose a CO2 standard on new cars. It will have a narrow road to travel to ensure it cuts emissions without driving up car prices. The Coalition will dump those penalties — keeping the framework of the efficiency standards, but not penalising breaches. It argues car manufacturers will continue to offer cleaner cars in the Australian market, but costs will not increase for consumers. The industry had asked to be regulated, saying Australia was alone with Russia in not having a fuel efficiency law — and the lack of one was making it hard to get hold of in-demand electric vehicles or other more fuel-efficient cars. However, with United States President Donald Trump's tariffs — including a substantial tariff on "foreign automobiles" — the sector is in crisis and some car makers have expressed fears when the NVES takes effect it will compound their uncertainty. Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen Industry insiders told the ABC last week that 4x2 variants of the Ford Everest and Mazda M-UX were among ranges due to be pulled from July — while other makers considered baking penalties into their business models and passing on some of that fine to consumers. The opposition leader claimed industry estimates showed some of the heaviest polluting cars could raise their prices by thousands of dollars in the long run. "This is a tax on families who need a reliable car and small businesses trying to grow. Instead of making life easier, Labor is making it harder and more expensive," Mr Dutton said. "A Coalition government will scrap this tax, so Australians can keep more of their hard-earned money when purchasing a new car." Peter Dutton has dubbed Labor's fuel efficiency standards a "tax" on families. Labor has denied its NVES will substantially affect prices, pointing to overseas markets with similar schemes that have remained competitive on price. "Let's be clear on what these standards do: they bring us into line with the rest of the world, so that Australians can have more cars that are cheaper to run," energy minister Chris Bowen told the ABC. The industry has challenged that, suggesting Australia's late adoption means it is acting harder and faster to reach similar fuel efficiency goals. However, while there is great uncertainty in the global car market under the cloud of Mr Trump's tariffs, the penalties and credits accrued under NVES don't become payable before 2028. This election season politicians have tried to sell you the world. The team at Gruen isn't about to buy it. They've taken a big swing at the election, showing you how the democracy sausage is made, all the sizzle and none of the meat. Motoring data insights agency Blue Flag has forecast the industry could be hit with as much as $2.7 billion in penalties by that date, though those who accrue credits would be set to benefit under the cap-and-trade scheme. The Coalition campaigned on Labor's planned fuel efficiency standards at previous elections, calling it a tax on utes because it dis-incentivised less fuel-efficient cars, and saying it "threatened to end the weekend". The party says it will work with industry to bring the cleanest cars on the market to Australia, without "punishing" those who cannot afford them. Shadow energy minister Ted O'Brien said the party will retain the vehicle efficiency standard without penalties, with the aim of ensuring cleaner cars continue to be brought to the Australian market. "The Coalition backs lower emitting vehicles because more fuel-efficient cars save Aussies money every time they fill up — but we won't back Labor's car tax that drives prices through the roof," he said. "Labor has got the balance wrong by imposing penalties that will be passed on to Australian families and small businesses." Mr Bowen said the Coalition would turn the standards "into a toothless tiger" and that this would be "worse than a voluntary standard". "Peter Dutton wants Australia to be a dumping ground for out-of-date models, that guzzle petrol and cost more to run, putting us in the same basket as Russia when it comes to standards," he said. "Consumer and motoring advocates, carmakers, and dealers support standards with teeth because they know their customers benefit from cars that are cheaper to run. "People can by whatever car suits their needs, from 4-wheel-drives and utes to EVs and hatchbacks. Vehicles are getting more efficient every day, and carmakers that offer those up-to-date models won't be impacted." 1 / of 11 All fields are required unless marked optional. title: How China could use its toolbox to inflict pain in US trade war
content: As the US-China trade war intensifies, Beijing is pulling out all the "tools" in its tool box to "cushion the blow". And Chinese President Xi Jinping himself is reportedly busy preparing for a tour of several South-East Asian countries to solidify its trade relations. Experts say the astonishing 125 per cent tariffs announced by Donald Trump on all goods imported from China comes at a precarious time for Beijing. But they also say Beijing has options of its own to inflict pain in the trade war. After years of momentous growth, China's economy has stalled since the country emerged from its draconian response against the COVID-19 pandemic. Mr Trump announced a 90-day pause on most of his original country-specific tariffs, except for China, which saw increased tariffs. (AFP: Getty Images) It was weighed down by weak domestic demand, a high unemployment rate and a persistent property slump. Wen-Ti Sung is a nonresident fellow with the Atlantic Council's Global China Hub. "Certainly China will be looking at this new wave of tariffs with great concern and anxiety. China's economy has been struggling over the past few years," he told the ABC. Although the US share of China's exports has been steadily declining since 2018, it still accounted for 14.7 per cent in 2024. Professor Jeanne Huang, associate professor at the University of Sydney Law School, said while she's "pessimistic" about the long-term impact of Mr Trump's 125 per cent tariff on China's economy, she believes the short-term effects can be manageable. "The Chinese government has a lot of tools to stabilise the economy," she said. On Monday, Chinese state-owned firms moved to support stock prices following sharp market declines. US President Donald Trump's trade war is facing increasing domestic criticism. (AP Photo: Seth Wenig) The People's Bank of China also allowed the yuan to weaken modestly against the US dollar, making Chinese exports cheaper while carefully managing capital outflow risks. Professor Fariborz Moshirian is director of the Institute of Global Finance at the University of New South Wales. President Xi is reportedly preparing for official visits to Malaysia, Vietnam and Cambodia, with trade high on the agenda. At the same time, Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao is engaging in dialogue with EU counterparts and the chair of ASEAN, Malaysia's Trade and Investment Minister Tengku Zafrul. Beijing has also convened meetings with representatives from more than 20 US-based companies, including Tesla, GE Healthcare, and Medtronic, to "reaffirm commitment to opening up". On Wednesday, Chinese ambassador to Australia Xiao Qiang also penned an article in The Sydney Morning Herald, calling on Australia to "join hands to defend the multilateral trading system". However, China's biggest advantage in this trade war, according to Professor Huang, is that "psychologically, Chinese people are very united." In contrast, Mr Trump's tariff escalation faces mounting skepticism at home. The US and China have participated in a series of tit-for-tat moves on tariffs. (Reuters) A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that three in four Americans expect prices to rise as a result of the new tariffs, fuelling fears of higher living costs at a time when inflation remains a major concern. This creates room for targeted retaliation, according to Mr Sung. "I can see China targeting the agricultural export sector because it's a key part of Trump's electoral base — the so-called 'Hillbilly Elegy' electorate made famous by JD Vance. Amid fears that the so-called reciprocal tariffs could cause a recession for the US, here's what it means for the global economy. "China may also focus on financial services — targeting US investment banks and management consultancies, another key part of Trump's support base." In its retaliation against Trump's tariff policy, China also announced export control of minerals critical for US' semiconductor and defence industry. In recent years, China has increasingly relied on creating regulatory hurdles and expending its "unreliable entity list" to target American firms. "They'll aim to get American businesses to pressure Trump into negotiations, even if Trump is not initially inclined to talk to China," Professor Moshirian said. "Both countries will suffer in the trade war, albeit with different levels of exposure. "Many American companies are exporting goods and services from China to the US; they will be significantly impacted, as will American consumers who will end up paying more for many low-value-added products produced and packaged in the US. "Trade war will even influence the pace of global geopolitical tensions and rivalries. They will also reduce other non-trade bilateral relationships between the US and China, including the arms race and nuclear proliferation," Professor Moshirian said. So far, it remains unclear whether Beijing will retaliate against Mr Trump's latest move to raise tariffs to 125 per cent, from the original 54 per cent announced on "Liberation Day." The initial 54 per cent tariff led China to impose a 34 per cent tariff on American goods, which then prompted the United States to escalate further, raising tariffs to 104 per cent. China replied with an 84 per cent tariff. Chinese government-owned media outlet Global Times printed a multi-page spread criticising the Trump administration's tariffs policy on April 10, 2025. (AFP: The Yomiuri Shimbun) Mr Trump responded to that with a shock reversal: a 90-day pause on many of the country-specific tariffs announced on his "Liberation Day". Except for China, because he simultaneously announced his latest gambit: raising tariffs on Chinese imports a staggering 125 per cent. However, the 10 per cent blanked tariff on almost all US imports remains. Professor Moshirian says the reversal is propelled by "a significant sell-off of US Treasury bonds and a loss of confidence in the US as a global leader". "It seems that many Republican members of Congress have now decided to collaborate with Democrats to ensure that Trump is no longer able to act unilaterally with respect to introducing tariffs and related issues without the involvement of Congress." Last Thursday, senior senators introduced new bipartisan legislation aimed at reclaiming some of Congress's authority over tariffs, although analysts note it has slim chance of passing. Mr Trump has also indicated he would veto such a bill. Economists have warned the world may face a global recession, as the China-United States trade war escalates dramatically this week. "If the trade war with high tariffs are going to continue between the US and China, there is a great chance of significant global economic slow down and even global recession," said Professor Moshirian. A series of policies have up-ended the global trade system and wiped trillions of dollars of value from the face of the Earth. Here's what could happen next. The 125 per cent tariff marks the culmination of Mr Trump's longstanding grievances over China's 20-year trade surplus with the United States, which he argues has hollowed out America's industrial base and left the US economy "a patient that was very sick." "We used to have a largely singular global economy, anchored around US leadership and institutions. Now it's far less clear. "We may end up with two rival economic blocs instead." Since Mr Trump's first term, China has accelerated trade with emerging markets as tensions with the United States have risen. In 2023, ASEAN overtook the US as China's largest export market. Meanwhile, the US had encouraged supply chain shifts toward Vietnam, India, and Mexico to reduce reliance on Chinese manufacturing — moves that were complicated when Mr Trump imposed substantial tariffs on those countries as well. The recently announced pause on "Liberation Day" tariffs also does not apply to tariffs on Canadian and Mexican goods, which remain subject to a 25 per cent fentanyl-related duty if they fail to meet the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement's rules of origin requirements. "When you make no distinction between allies and adversaries, you remove the incentive for people to be your friend." title: Regional advocates say it's 'about time' for $20 billion future fund
content: Regional leaders are welcoming a key Coalition election pledge to channel money into much needed services through a $20 billion future fund, but questions remain about how and when the fund will deliver dollars to the bush. The Regional Australia Future Fund (RAFF) is one of two new funds the Coalition outlined plans for this week, using money from windfall receipts — where revenue raised from commodities exceeds what was projected. Live results: Find out what's happening in your seat as counting continues Money for the proposed fund will also come from scrapping Labor initiatives, including an initial $5 billion from the Rewiring Australia program, which the Coalition says won't be needed under its nuclear plan. Nationals leader David Littleproud said the regional fund would provide a $1 billion dividend each year to pay for infrastructure and services that local councils cannot afford. For years, the Nationals have tried to get more money from their coalition partners for big projects like dams, railways and roads in regional areas. Through the future fund, they'll also contribute money to address shortfalls in services, like child care, health, telecommunications and internet services. The National Rural Health Alliance (NRHA) welcomed the funding proposal and said "it's about time" rural Australia received a fairer share of federal money. "Two thirds of Australia's income comes from rural, remote and regional Australia, and 50 per cent of the tourism income — despite the fact that they are only 30 per cent of the population," its chief executive Susi Tegen told ABC News. Susi Tegen, chief executive, National Rural Health Alliance (Supplied: National Rural Health Alliance) Ms Tegen said she knew of local government and rural communities trying to "raise hundreds of thousands of dollars" to keep educators and health workers employed locally. "This infrastructure funding is something that we've all been asking for," she said. The last Coalition government had a similar program called the Building Better Regions Fund, but a 2022 auditor-general's report found it funnelled money to Nationals electorates against departmental advice. Want even more? Here's where you can find all our 2025 federal election coverage Catch the latest interviews and in-depth coverage on ABC iview and ABC Listen Ms Tegen brushed away any comparison with the Coalition's latest proposal. "There is an underfunding of rural Australia in the first place," she said. "This is about equity and it's about parity." The proposed investment in health and child care has also been welcomed by Jacqui Emery, chief executive of Royal Far West, a charity specialising in the health and development of rural children. Royal Far West CEO Jacqueline Emery. (ABC North Coast: Leah White) "We can see across health and education and just general life outcomes, regional Australia is so far behind city counterparts and it has been a gap that's been widening and something really needs to be done. "This future fund is potentially a pathway forward to ensure that, rural people are not forgotten about." She said a scarcity of health professionals in regional areas was caused by a combination of factors — including the availability of housing and services like child care — and required a "holistic, long-term approach." In many areas of regional Australia families find it difficult to access child care. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde) Queensland Trucking Association's Gary Mahon said a substantial investment in roads was needed in his state, and that he was on board with the Coalition's plan provided it was not simply a reshuffling of finances. "If it's an investment fund that earns returns in its own right, that brings substantial increases to investment in our regions, that's the fund that we would find a very supportable idea," Mr Mahon said. Gary Mahon is the CEO of the Queensland Trucking Association (Supplied: Queensland Trucking Association) "If it's just another way of moving money around … that is already available and at the disposal of the government, well that's just an exercise in bureaucracy." Mr Mahon said while money had been committed to upgrading the Bruce Highway, many of the connecting roads and highways were in a poor state and needed significant improvement. "We need much more reliable, sustainable, road networks across the state, to be able to sustain, efficient movement of road freight." In Queensland, more people live outside the capital city than in it. Come on a 3,000km trip into deep Katter country to see what's really behind the regional divide. In southern New South Wales, Murray River Council's Mayor John Harvie said "any funding coming into regional areas is fantastic". But he wanted more detail on how the money would be distributed, and questioned how much would be available to the many regional communities across the country under the Coalition plan. "While $20 billion seems like a lot of money, when you invest that, if you get 3 per cent for example, that's only $600 million a year that will be available to do the things that the opposition has identified that they want to do," he said. Mr Harvie said in the long term he'd like to see sustainable federal funding for local councils restored. "You go back to the start of the century, around 2000, and local government received 1 per cent of total taxation revenues from the federal government. And here we are 20 odd years later, and we only receive 0.48 per cent." The poor state of country roads is an issue across Australian states and territories. title: EPA names composting facility as major PFAS contaminator of NSW river
content: A four-month investigation into the discovery of "forever chemicals" in a New South Wales river has identified a composting facility as a major contamination source. The NSW Environment Protection Authority (EPA) began an extensive testing program of the Belubula River in the state's central west after PFAS, or per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, were detected last year. In December it honed in on potential contamination sources from three industrial sites in the catchment, including the Australian Native Landscapes (ANL) compost site, a Blayney Council-run landfill and the Newmont Cadia gold mine. A type of PFAS, known as PFOS, was detected at 16 of 20 locations it sampled. All 16 detections breached ecological water quality guidelines for PFOS set by the Heads of EPA Australia and New Zealand (HEPA). PFAS are laboratory-made chemicals that persist in the environment, bioaccumulate and are potentially toxic. The Belubula River runs through farm land and is popular for camping. (ABC Central West: Xanthe Gregory) The Belubula River weaves through prime agricultural land between Bathurst and Orange, acting as a water source for livestock. In mid-2024 landholders raised the alarm about the health of the river after discovering foam in the waterway containing PFOS. The EPA said the results to date "indicate the risk to livestock is low, but as a precaution, the EPA will be taking soil samples for testing" at properties where livestock graze adjacent to the impacted waterways. There are no livestock and irrigation water guidelines for PFAS. Landholders noticed foam in the river mid-2024. (ABC Central West: Micaela Hambrett) The latest round of EPA testing reaffirms results from October and keeps the spotlight on ANL near Blayney, which is located on a former mine site next to Cowriga Creek. The samples taken in December show the highest levels were found in Cowriga Creek downstream of ANL and in Mackenzies Waterholes Creek near Blayney Council's landfill. Both creeks are tributaries of the Belubula River. PFOS levels upstream of the ANL site were 0.0025 ug/L (micrograms per litre), while the results immediately downstream were 0.15 ug/L. The downstream result is more than 650 times HEPA's ecological water guideline for freshwater species. Australian Native Landscapes' facility is near Blayney. (ABC Central West: Xanthe Gregory) The EPA also conducted testing near Cadia gold mine which lies to the north of the Belubula River, between Blayney and Orange. PFOS was detected at 13 of 16 sites tested on the mine while groundwater to the west and south of the site exceeded ecological guidelines in six of 10 bores. "The groundwater quality appears to pose limited risk to livestock, irrigation, or the surrounding environment," the EPA said. It will now sample Cadia's tailings facility where mine waste is stored. In a statement, Cadia said it acknowledged the findings and it would continue to work closely with the EPA in its investigations to uphold its "commitment to environmental stewardship and transparency". As a result of its investigation, the environmental watchdog has added conditions to all three sites' environmental protection licences and has ordered the operators to carry out preliminary investigations into the presence of PFAS. The operators of each site must review "all likely products and materials that may have contained PFAS" and have been used or stored on site. EPA says Blayney council-run landfill is a contamination source. (ABC Central West: Xanthe Gregory) They must also examine if any soils, surface water or groundwater have been impacted by the chemicals and whether they have posed any risks to human or environmental health. "These assessments will inform the EPA's future regulatory activities," the EPA said. "The presence of PFAS in the environment does not necessarily indicate that there is a health risk, however identifying sites that require investigation is an important precaution to reduce the risk off community exposure to PFAS." Australian Native Landscapes must report its findings to the EPA by April 25. Blayney Council must submit its results to the watchdog by May 9, while Cadia gold mine has until September 26. The ABC has contacted ANL and the council for comment.

title: Couple's gamble on forever home could mean 'torturous' forced sale
content: What would you risk for the house of your dreams? That's the question Stephanie and Paul Ryan grappled with when the opportunity arose to buy a rundown Victorian-era house in Prahran, in inner-city Melbourne, on one of the area's main thoroughfares. Located on Punt Road, the house-turned-backpackers hostel had been sitting empty and was in need of some serious TLC when it came up for sale in 2021. "I immediately started saying to Paul, 'We have to have this house'," Steph told Restoration Australia. "We first walked in ... and kind of had our breath taken away by the absolute scale of everything." Instructions: Use left and right arrow keys to control image transition Paul said the pair loved the older Victorian properties in the area, but there was a short supply of unrestored homes available within their budget. But this house became an option because it fell under a longstanding public acquisition overlay. Public acquisition overlays are a planning tool that allows the government to reserve land for future public infrastructure uses. "In theory, it means the council can widen the road, which would mean buying and [demolishing] our house," Steph explained. "I think that put off quite a few people, but that was what got us in." The house had been used as a hostel before Steph and Paul bought it. (ABC/Fremantle Media) The couple decided to go all in on the gamble, buying the house for $1.81 million, and budgeting to restore and renovate it to become the family home they had dreamed about. Unlike other residents of Punt Road subject to the acquisition overlay, the pair didn't feel like the threat of losing their house back to the government was hanging over their heads. "From our perspective, it's not something we're concerned with or stressed by," Paul said. Paul said that even if an acquisition order was made, they're hopeful the buy-back price would match, if not exceed, what they could sell the property for. "Although it would be emotionally taxing based on how much work we put in, it's not actually a financial risk to us in any meaningful sense, in our opinion," he said. Steph and Paul discuss how they feel post-restoration about the overlay. A Victorian government spokesperson told the ABC there were no current plans to acquire properties along the road under the overlay, which has been in place since 1954. Paul and Steph said the majority of the time they spend thinking about the overlay was the impact it had on the rest of the street, and the lost opportunity to provide more inner-city housing along the road. "The reason that we talk about the overlay the most … isn't because of how it would impact our property directly, but because it negatively impacts our neighbourhood," Paul said. "Up and down Punt Road, there's a whole lot of vacant, derelict buildings … [the overlay] stops them being developed by developers, and it also scares off private purchasers as well, so they're just degrading." The pair has since joined a local action group campaigning for an end to the overlay. Despite their confidence that the property won't be bought back, Steph said the reality would hurt if it did eventuate. "It would be torturous," she said. "Certainly, we are still very attached to this house, and we would be devastated if anything was to happen. "I'm really proud of us for pushing the boundaries where we did … but that doesn't mean that we can't do them somewhere else." No doubt, many homeowners would feel the same way, and while public acquisition overlays are not overly common, governments across the country have the ability to buy back any private land under compulsory acquisition laws. This is typically for a public purpose like big transport or infrastructure projects. Associate professor Duygu Yengin says the indefinite nature of public acquisition overlays can make them anxiety provoking. (Supplied) So, given it can happen with or without an overlay, is it better to know what you're getting yourself into, or have to deal with a sudden shock of having to sell your house back? According to Duygu Yengin, an associate professor of economics at Adelaide University, both have their advantages and pitfalls. In 2022, Dr Yengin led a team looking at how the compulsory acquisition process could be improved nationally. "If you buy a property knowing that there is a public acquisition overlay on it, then yes, you buy it knowing what will happen," she said. The freestanding house would otherwise have been out of Steph and Paul's budget. (ABC/Fremantle Media) But, she pointed out that the uncertainty could be difficult for owners, who might want to make long-term plans. "You cannot develop your land properly, you cannot sell your property, or you will probably not find a good buyer — things like that," Dr Yengin said. Compulsory acquisitions, on the other hand, have a finite date, but can also cause emotional stress by being unexpected, or not adequately compensating people for their properties. "[Acquisitions are] actually very common in Australia because there are lots of infrastructure needs," Dr Yengin said. "A few hundred properties are easily taken every year, but there is no central data that we can see how many are acquired in a certain year. Governments across the country are compulsorily acquiring properties to make way for massive infrastructure projects. "In almost all the interviews we made [for our research], there was a big emotional stress factor, especially when someone is really attached to their property. "Maybe it's something they thought of as their forever home, or some neighbourhood they have been living in for a very long time with family and friendship ties." While Paul may not consider the potential repurchase of their home a financial risk, Dr Yengin said adequate compensation was an issue for many people forced to sell their homes. She said compensation schemes varied from state to state, but most were based on the market value of a property and, in some jurisdictions, also included payments for emotional distress caused. "For some people, [compensation] wasn't a big issue because they didn't even think that their house was somewhere they want to live long term," Dr Yengin said. "For some others, they really were invested in their houses … they didn't feel they were treated fairly in terms of compensation." Dr Yengin's research found that clear and early communication from governments was the key to a better experience for residents going through compulsory acquisitions. title: 'We sincerely apologise': Virgin to refund 61,000 overcharged customers
content: Virgin Australia has come clean about having overcharged tens of thousands of customers over a five-year period. Customers were overcharged when changes were made to their itineraries, according to a spokesperson from Virgin Australia. The airline said 61,000 customers whose bookings were changed between April 2020 and March 2025 had been affected. Virgin Australia said the total amount owed to those customers was approximately $3.4 million, including GST. The average refund per customer was $55. "Some bookings were repriced in a way that does not align with our policy and, we are refunding all impacted guests for that amount," the spokesperson said. "We sincerely apologise to those affected guests and have launched an Itinerary Change Claim Program under which all eligible guests are being proactively contacted to process their refunds." Qantas reached a $120 million agreement with the ACCC to settle a lawsuit against the airline for selling seats on flights that had already been cancelled in 2024. The airline has appointed Deloitte to manage the claims process, which will be open for 12 months. Virgin Australia said it will contact all affected customers and any unclaimed money would be donated to a charity. "A dedicated Virgin Australia team has also been working to fix the issue and we have undertaken a range of actions to prevent this from reoccurring in the future, so our guests can be confident when making changes to their bookings," a spokesperson said. The airline said it has notified the ACCC about the "error" and will work with the regulator on any additional actions necessary. The ACCC said it is assessing whether the remedial actions taken by Virgin are suitable. You can access the online claim portal run by Deloitte here. The pricing debacle comes as Virgin Australia's US private equity fund owner Bain Capital plans to re-list the airline on the Australian Stock Exchange. In February, the federal government approved Qatar Airways' 25 per cent stake in Virgin Australia. Virgin Australia has also announced new CEO Dave Emerson, who has taken over from Jayne Hrdlicka, who announced her retirement in February 2024. Do you know more?
